items.title: Autoencoders
items.body:
## Autoencoders: compress, then reconstruct
The **autoencoder** is the foundational generative-adjacent architecture, and it is elegantly simple: a network that learns to **compress** data into a small **latent** representation (the *encoder*) and then **reconstruct** the original from that compressed code (the *decoder*).
```text
input  --encoder-->  latent code (small)  --decoder-->  reconstruction
                     (the bottleneck)                   (should match input)
```
You train it to make the reconstruction match the input (minimising reconstruction error), and the key is the **bottleneck**, the latent code is much smaller than the input, so the network cannot just copy the data through; it must learn to keep only the *essential* information needed to rebuild it. The encoder learns to distil, the decoder learns to reconstruct.

## What the bottleneck forces the network to learn
The bottleneck is the whole point, and understanding why explains what autoencoders are good for. Because the latent code is too small to hold everything, the network is forced to discover the *most important structure* in the data, the underlying factors that let it reconstruct an example from a compact code, and discard noise and redundancy. This is a learned, non-linear cousin of PCA from W7: PCA found a linear compression (top variance directions), and an autoencoder finds a *non-linear* one (via the neural network), capturing curved structure PCA cannot. The latent code becomes a useful *representation* of the data, which gives autoencoders their practical uses:
- **Anomaly detection:** train on normal data; an anomaly reconstructs *poorly* (high error) because the network never learned to represent it, the reconstruction-error method from W7, now with a neural autoencoder.
- **Denoising:** train to reconstruct clean data from noisy inputs, and the autoencoder learns to remove noise.
- **Feature extraction:** use the compact latent code as learned features for other tasks.
The autoencoder learns to *understand* data by learning to compress and rebuild it.

## The limitation that motivates everything after
Autoencoders learn great representations but have a critical limitation *for generation*: the latent space has **no structure that makes it easy to sample from**. You can encode a real input to a latent code and decode it back, but if you just pick a *random* latent code and decode it, hoping to generate a new example, you usually get garbage, because the autoencoder never organised the latent space so that arbitrary points correspond to valid data. The codes for real examples sit in unpredictable, gappy regions, and the space between them is undefined, so there is no reliable way to sample new points that decode into realistic data. This is exactly the gap that **VAEs** fill: they add structure to the latent space (organising it into a smooth, well-behaved region you *can* sample from), turning the autoencoder's representation-learning into true generation. So the autoencoder is the foundation, compress-and-reconstruct, learn a latent representation, and the limitation it has, an unsamplable latent space, is precisely the problem each later generative model improves on. Understanding this limitation is understanding why the progression exists.

## Where this fits
You understand the autoencoder: an encoder-bottleneck-decoder that learns to compress and reconstruct, forcing it to capture essential structure (a non-linear PCA), useful for anomaly detection, denoising, and features, but with a latent space you cannot reliably sample from for generation. That limitation motivates VAEs (structured, samplable latents) and the rest. Tomorrow you jump to GANs, a different and powerful route to sharp, realistic generation.

items.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
items.body:
## GANs: a generator versus a critic
**Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)** generate data through a contest between two networks, an idea both clever and famous:
- the **generator** takes random noise and tries to produce realistic fake data (a fake image).
- the **discriminator** is a classifier trying to tell real data (from the training set) apart from the generator's fakes.
They train *against* each other: the generator tries to fool the discriminator, the discriminator tries not to be fooled, and as each improves, it forces the other to improve.
```text
noise -> GENERATOR -> fake image \
                                  >-- DISCRIMINATOR -> "real or fake?"
real images --------------------/
   generator wants: fakes judged "real"   discriminator wants: catch the fakes
```
Over training, the generator gets so good that its fakes are indistinguishable from real data, at which point you have a powerful generator: feed it noise, get realistic new samples.

## Why the adversarial game produces sharp results
The adversarial setup is what gives GANs their signature strength, **sharp, realistic** samples, and understanding why illuminates the whole approach. The generator is not trained to minimise a fixed reconstruction error (which, as autoencoders show, tends to produce blurry averages); instead it is trained to *fool a learned critic* that is constantly getting better at spotting anything unrealistic. So the generator is pushed to fix exactly the flaws the discriminator learns to detect, blurriness, wrong textures, implausible details, because any such flaw is what gives it away. This is like an art forger improving by repeatedly trying to fool an expert who keeps getting sharper: the forger is driven to perfect precisely the details that betray a fake. The result is generators that produce crisp, convincing images, which is why GANs dominated image generation for years and produced the early photorealistic face generators. The adversarial pressure, a moving, learned target rather than a fixed loss, is the source of the quality.

## The catch: GANs are notoriously hard to train
GANs' power comes with serious practical difficulty, and this is the key engineering lesson about them, because it is exactly why the field largely moved on. Training two networks in competition is **unstable**: the delicate balance between generator and discriminator is easily lost, if the discriminator gets too good too fast, the generator gets no useful signal and stalls; if the generator finds one trick that fools the discriminator, it may exploit it. The most infamous failure is **mode collapse**: the generator discovers a few outputs that reliably fool the discriminator and produces only those, generating, say, the same handful of faces over and over instead of the full diversity of the data, technically fooling the critic while failing at the real goal. GANs are also hard to *evaluate* (no clean loss tells you how good the generator is) and require careful tuning and tricks to train at all. So GANs sit at a revealing trade-off: capable of stunning quality, but fragile, finicky, and prone to collapse, which is precisely the weakness that **diffusion models** address, they achieve comparable or better quality with far more *stable* training, which is why diffusion, not GANs, powers today's leading image generators. Knowing GANs' instability is knowing why the field adopted diffusion.

## Where this fits
You understand GANs: a generator and discriminator trained adversarially, which produces sharp realistic samples because the generator must fool a continually-improving critic, but at the cost of unstable training and mode collapse. Their fragility is exactly what motivated the move to diffusion. Tomorrow you meet diffusion models, the stable, high-quality approach behind modern image generation.

items.title: DDPM and DDIM
items.body:
## Diffusion: generate by removing noise
**Diffusion models** generate data through a strikingly different idea: learn to *remove noise*, step by step, until structure emerges from randomness. Training has two directions:
```text
forward (fixed):    real image --add noise--> ... --add noise--> pure noise
reverse (learned):  pure noise --remove noise--> ... --remove noise--> new image
```
The **forward** process is simple and not learned, take real data and gradually add random noise over many steps until it becomes pure noise. The model learns the **reverse**: at each step, predict and remove a bit of the noise, undoing the corruption. Once trained, you *generate* by starting from pure random noise and running the learned denoising repeatedly, step by step the model removes noise and a coherent new image emerges from nothing but randomness. (DDPM is the original formulation; DDIM is a refinement that generates in far fewer steps, addressing diffusion's main cost.)

## Why denoising is a brilliant way to generate
Diffusion's approach is clever because it breaks the impossibly hard problem of "generate a realistic image from scratch" into many easy, small problems, "remove a little noise from this slightly-noisy image", and that decomposition is the source of its advantages. Each denoising step is a manageable prediction the network can learn well, and chaining many of them turns pure noise into a detailed image gradually rather than in one impossible leap. This gives diffusion two big wins over GANs. **Stability:** there is no adversarial game, you train a single network on a clear, well-behaved objective (predict the noise), so training is far more stable and reliable than a GAN's fragile balancing act, no mode collapse, no delicate equilibrium. **Quality and diversity:** because the model learns the full distribution through denoising rather than chasing a critic, it produces both high-quality *and* diverse samples, avoiding the mode collapse that made GANs repeat themselves. The trade-off is **speed**: generating requires many denoising steps (where a GAN generates in one forward pass), making diffusion slower to sample, which is exactly why refinements like DDIM (fewer steps) and other accelerations matter. But stable training plus high, diverse quality is why diffusion overtook GANs.

## Why diffusion won, and what it powers
The practical upshot is that **diffusion models power today's leading image generators** (Stable Diffusion, and the systems behind most modern AI image tools), and they won for a concrete engineering reason that ties the week together: they deliver GAN-level-or-better quality with *trainable*, stable, reliable optimisation, trading some generation speed for that stability. This is a recurring theme you have now seen across the track, the method that wins in practice is often not the one with the highest ceiling in theory but the one that *trains reliably and predictably*, just as boosting's controllability and the Transformer's parallelism won their domains. Diffusion's stability over GANs' fragility is the same lesson again: a powerful-but-unstable method (GAN) loses to a comparably-powerful-but-stable one (diffusion), because reliability at scale beats peak potential you cannot consistently reach. Understanding diffusion, learn to denoise, generate by denoising random noise from scratch, is understanding how modern generative image AI actually works, and the next lesson shows how Stable Diffusion makes it practical and controllable.

## Where this fits
You understand diffusion models: learn to reverse a noising process, then generate by denoising pure noise into an image step by step, which gives stable training and high, diverse quality (beating GANs' fragility) at the cost of slower multi-step generation. This is the engine of modern image generation. Tomorrow you see how Stable Diffusion turns this into the practical, text-controllable system people actually use.

items.title: Stable Diffusion
items.body:
## Stable Diffusion: making diffusion practical and controllable
Raw diffusion generates images but is expensive (it denoises in the full high-resolution pixel space) and, on its own, uncontrolled (you get *a* realistic image, not the one you asked for). **Stable Diffusion** is the system that made diffusion practical and useful, through two key ideas that are worth understanding because they recur in applied generative AI:
- **Latent diffusion:** instead of denoising in pixel space, it denoises in a compressed **latent** space (using an autoencoder, this week's first lesson, to compress and decompress), which is dramatically cheaper because the latent is far smaller than the full image. This is what made high-quality diffusion fast enough to run on consumer hardware.
- **Text conditioning:** it *guides* the denoising with a text prompt (via a text encoder, a Transformer from last week), so the generated image matches your description, "an astronaut riding a horse" produces exactly that.

## How text controls the image
The text-conditioning mechanism is the heart of what makes Stable Diffusion *useful* rather than just impressive, and it ties the whole phase together. A text encoder (a Transformer, the architecture from W11) turns your prompt into a representation of its meaning, and that representation is fed into the denoising network at every step, steering the noise-removal toward images that match the text. So the model is not generating a random realistic image and hoping it fits; it is denoising *toward* the meaning of your prompt, each step nudged to be more consistent with "astronaut riding a horse." This is why prompt wording matters so much in image generation, the text representation directly steers every denoising step, and a more precise prompt steers more precisely. Notice how this single system unites the phase's ideas: an **autoencoder** (compress to latent space) + **diffusion** (denoise to generate) + a **Transformer** (encode the text prompt) working together. Stable Diffusion is a composition of exactly the architectures you learned, which is the clearest possible demonstration that these are reusable building blocks, not isolated tricks.

## Why architecture-as-composition is the real lesson
Step back from the specifics, because the deepest takeaway of this lesson is about how modern AI systems are *built*: they compose the foundational architectures into something more capable than any one alone. Stable Diffusion did not invent a monolithic new model; it combined an autoencoder, a diffusion process, and a Transformer text encoder, each handling what it is best at (compression, generation, language understanding), into a controllable text-to-image system. This compositional pattern is everywhere in modern AI, multimodal models combine vision and language encoders, RAG combines retrieval and generation, agents combine LLMs and tools, and recognising it changes how you read any new system: you decompose it into the familiar building blocks (which you now know) rather than treating it as a novel mystery. The frontier moves fast, but it moves by *recombining* a stable set of foundations, autoencoders, CNNs, Transformers, diffusion, that you have spent this phase learning. So when you meet the next impressive generative system, your first move is to ask "which known components is this composed of, and how are they wired?", and that question, answerable because you understand the parts, is what keeps you oriented on a fast-changing frontier. Understanding the building blocks is what lets you understand everything built from them.

## Where this fits
You understand Stable Diffusion: latent diffusion (denoise in a cheap compressed space) plus text conditioning (a Transformer steers each denoising step toward your prompt), a system that composes the autoencoder, diffusion, and Transformer into controllable text-to-image generation. And you see the deeper pattern, modern AI composes foundational architectures. Tomorrow you survey the modern alternatives and where generative modelling is heading, before shipping.

items.title: Modern alternatives
items.body:
## The fast-moving generative frontier
Generative modelling moves quickly, and beyond the core progression (autoencoder, VAE, GAN, diffusion) sit newer approaches worth being aware of, not to master each, but to stay oriented. A few directions matter:
- **Faster diffusion / few-step generation:** diffusion's main weakness is slow multi-step sampling, so much work shrinks the steps, consistency models and distilled diffusion that generate in one or a few steps, approaching GAN speed with diffusion's stability.
- **Flow matching and related formulations:** newer mathematical framings of the "transform noise into data" idea that aim for simpler, faster training and generation, increasingly competitive with diffusion.
- **Autoregressive generation for images/audio:** applying the next-token-prediction idea from Transformers (W11) to non-text data, generating an image or audio token by token, the same mechanism that powers LLMs, applied to other modalities.
- **Transformers as the backbone everywhere:** modern generative models increasingly use Transformer backbones (diffusion transformers), unifying the architectures.

## Choosing a generative approach is a real engineering decision
The practical point of surveying these is that, just as with clustering or forecasting, *which* generative method you choose is an engineering decision driven by your constraints, not a search for the single "best" one. The trade-offs are concrete: **diffusion** for the highest quality and stable training when you can afford multi-step generation; **few-step/distilled** variants when generation *speed* matters (real-time or high-volume); **GANs** still occasionally where single-pass speed is paramount and you can manage the training difficulty; **VAEs** where you need a clean, structured latent space (for interpolation or representation) more than peak sample quality; **autoregressive** approaches where you want one unified framework across modalities. The dimensions you weigh, sample quality, generation speed, training stability, diversity, controllability, are the same kind of trade-off table you have built all track, and the skill is matching the method to what your application actually needs. There is no universally best generative model, only the one whose trade-offs fit your constraints, which is the same recurring lesson from every "modern variants" lesson in the track.

## Stay grounded: understand the foundations, track the frontier
The meta-lesson, fitting for the last content lesson of the Deep Learning phase, is the stance to take toward a fast-moving field: **invest deeply in the foundations (which you now have) and stay lightly, currently informed on the frontier.** The specific best-performing generative model will change, possibly within months, but it will be built from the foundations you understand, learning a distribution, latent compression, denoising or its successors, attention, composed in some configuration. So you do not chase every new model anxiously; you understand the principles so well that each new system is legible as a recombination or refinement of them, and you read new work as "ah, this is diffusion but faster" or "this is autoregressive generation applied to images." That grounding is what makes a fast frontier exciting rather than overwhelming, and it is exactly the posture the AI-engineering track takes toward the models it builds products on. Understanding the foundations deeply is the durable investment; tracking the frontier is the cheap, ongoing top-up, and getting that ratio right is how you stay capable as the field moves.

## Where this fits

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a generative model that creates
You assemble the week into a generative project that demonstrates understanding of how these models work, the scope chosen to be achievable, a trained autoencoder/VAE for generation and anomaly detection, or a small diffusion model, or a thoughtful application of a pretrained generator:
- a model that **learns a data distribution** and can **sample** new examples (or reconstruct, interpolate, and flag anomalies).
- a clear demonstration of the capability, generated samples, interpolations between examples, or reconstruction-error anomaly detection.
- a write-up explaining *which* generative approach you used and *why*, in terms of the quality/speed/stability trade-offs.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Generative model: learn the distribution, sample new data + write-up"
git push
```

## The deliverable demonstrates the concept, not just an output
What makes this project meaningful is showing you understand *generative modelling as learning a distribution*, not just that you produced an output. The strongest artifact makes the concept visible: generated samples that clearly resemble but differ from the training data (you learned the distribution, not memorised examples), an **interpolation** that smoothly morphs one example into another (proving the model learned a structured space, not just a lookup), or **anomaly detection** via reconstruction error (the W7 connection, now with a neural generative model). Pair it with an honest explanation of your method choice, "I used a VAE because I wanted a structured latent space for interpolation and anomaly detection, accepting slightly blurrier samples than a GAN or diffusion would give." That demonstrates the real understanding, what generative models do, how the approaches differ, and how to choose, rather than just "I made an image generator", and it is what distinguishes someone who understands generative AI from someone who called an API.

## What generative modelling completes
Step back: this week completes your picture of what neural networks can do. You now understand models that *classify and predict* (the supervised and Transformer weeks), models that *learn features* (CNNs), and models that *create*, autoencoders (compress/represent), VAEs (structured generation), GANs (sharp adversarial samples), and diffusion (stable, high-quality denoising generation, behind today's image AI). You saw the recurring lesson, stable, trainable methods (diffusion) beat powerful-but-fragile ones (GANs), the same theme as boosting and Transformers, and you saw modern systems (Stable Diffusion) *compose* the foundational architectures you learned. That compositional understanding, knowing the building blocks well enough to recognise them inside any new system, is the durable knowledge that keeps you capable as generative AI races forward, and it directly underpins the generative capabilities you use in the AI-engineering track.

## Where this fits
You shipped a generative model and understand the full progression from autoencoders to diffusion, completing the Deep Learning phase, neural networks that predict, that learn features, and now that create. With classical ML and deep learning both mastered, the next phase, **ML Infrastructure** (W13-16), shifts from building models to the engineering that makes ML real at scale: experiment tracking, GPU training, data pipelines, and reproducibility, the systems skills that turn a trained model into reliable, production-grade machine learning.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You train a VAE on MNIST and the reconstruction loss converges well but the generated samples (sampled from the prior) look blurry and unrealistic. What is the likely cause? The KL term is being ignored, the model is converging to a standard autoencoder where the latent space is not regularised. This is called "posterior collapse" or KL vanishing. Causes: the KL weight is too high (anneal KL weight from 0 to 1 during training), the decoder is too powerful (it can reconstruct without using the latent space). Fix: add KL annealing, start training with reconstruction loss only, then gradually increase the KL term weight over the first 50 epochs.

weeks.title: Experiment Tracking, Stop Losing Track of What Worked
weeks.context:
You have now trained many models. How many of those experiments can you reproduce? How many times did you change the learning rate or the number of layers and forget which combination produced the best result? Experiment tracking is the practice of systematically recording what you tried, what it produced, and how to reproduce it. Without it, ML development is archaeology, you dig through notebooks and git blame to reconstruct decisions made weeks ago.

Weights & Biases (wandb) and MLflow are the two dominant experiment tracking tools. Both let you log hyperparameters, metrics (loss, accuracy, any custom number), artifacts (model files, plots, datasets), and environment information (Python version, library versions, git commit). Both provide a web interface for comparing runs. The practical difference: wandb is hosted and has a polished UI; MLflow is open-source and self-hostable, which matters when your data cannot leave your infrastructure.

What to track per experiment: the code version (git commit hash), the exact dataset version (not the filename, the hash of the data, or a pointer to a versioned data artifact), every hyperparameter (not just the ones you changed, all of them), every metric at every epoch, the model artifact at the end, and the training environment. If any of these is missing, you cannot fully reproduce the experiment.

The mental model shift is from "notebooks" to "runs." Each training job is a run. Each run has a unique ID, a set of recorded inputs (hyperparameters, data), and a set of recorded outputs (metrics, artifacts). A project groups related runs. You compare runs in a table to see which configuration performed best. You compare runs in charts to see how loss curves differed. This replaces the pattern of "I think that one notebook was the best, let me check."

Artifact versioning extends tracking to data and models. If you retrain on new data, you need to know which model was trained on which data version. MLflow Models and wandb Artifacts both provide this, you store each dataset and model as a versioned artifact with a name and version number. A model registered as "flightwise-v3" has a provenance chain: which data version it trained on, which hyperparameter run produced it, which code version generated it.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## The problem: you cannot reproduce your own work
You have trained dozens of models by now. Honest question: how many of those experiments could you reproduce exactly? How many times did you change the learning rate or the number of layers, get a good result, and then forget which combination produced it? This is the silent crisis of ML development, and **experiment tracking** is the cure: the practice of systematically recording what you tried, what it produced, and how to reproduce it. Without it, ML work degrades into *archaeology*, digging through old notebooks and `git blame` to reconstruct a decision you made three weeks ago, often failing, and re-running experiments you already ran because you cannot remember the result. This week you fix that permanently.

## Why ML especially needs this
Every field benefits from records, but ML needs experiment tracking acutely because of how the work happens: it is *empirical and iterative*. You do not write a model once; you run hundreds of variations, different hyperparameters, features, architectures, data, comparing results to find what works, and the knowledge of "what works" lives entirely in those comparisons. Lose the records and you lose the knowledge: you cannot tell whether your current model is better than last week's, you cannot reproduce the best one to deploy it, and you cannot explain *why* you chose the settings you did. Worse, ML results depend on many fragile details (random seeds, library versions, exact data) that are trivially easy to forget, so "I got 0.85 AUC" is meaningless without recording *how*. Experiment tracking turns ML from an unrepeatable craft into a reproducible engineering discipline, which is exactly the difference between data science and ML *engineering*.

## What a tracking system records
An experiment tracker systematically logs the things that define and reproduce a run:
- **Hyperparameters:** the settings you chose (learning rate, layers, etc.), so you know what made this run different.
- **Metrics:** the results (loss, accuracy, AUC, any number you care about), logged over training so you can compare runs and watch curves.
- **Artifacts:** the outputs (the trained model file, plots, the dataset version), so the actual products of the run are saved, not just numbers.
- **Environment:** the context needed to reproduce (Python version, library versions, the git commit), so you can recreate the exact conditions.
With these recorded for every run, "which combination was best?" becomes a query, not an archaeological dig, and any past run becomes reproducible.

## Where this fits
This opens the **ML Infrastructure phase**, where the focus shifts from building models to the engineering that makes ML reliable and reproducible at scale: experiment tracking (this week), GPU training, data pipelines, and containers. It is the natural first step, because everything else in the phase assumes you can *record and reproduce* what you do. Today's orientation: experiment tracking systematically records what you tried, what it produced, and how to reproduce it, turning ML from archaeology into engineering. Tomorrow you decide precisely *what* to track to make a run truly reproducible.

items.title: What to track
items.body:
## What to track: enough to reproduce, exactly
The core skill of experiment tracking is knowing *what* to record, and the standard is precise: **enough to reproduce the run exactly and to understand why it produced what it did.** That means four categories, and missing any one breaks reproducibility:
- **Hyperparameters / config:** every setting that affects the run, learning rate, batch size, architecture, which features, which model. If it could change the result, log it.
- **Metrics:** the outcomes, over time, training and validation loss/accuracy/AUC per epoch, plus final test metrics, so you can compare runs and diagnose training (a validation curve that diverges from training shows overfitting).
- **Artifacts:** the tangible outputs, the saved model, plots, the confusion matrix, sample predictions.
- **Environment:** the reproducibility context, library versions, Python version, hardware, and crucially the **git commit** of the code that ran.
The test for whether you tracked enough: could someone (including future-you) recreate this exact result from your records alone? If not, something is missing.

## The code version is the piece everyone forgets
Among these, the most-forgotten and most-important is the **git commit of the code**, and understanding why elevates tracking from "logging numbers" to "real reproducibility." Your hyperparameters and metrics describe the run, but the *code* is what actually produced it, the feature engineering, the model definition, the training loop, and that code changes constantly as you experiment. If you log "lr=0.01 gave 0.85 AUC" but not which version of the code computed it, you cannot reproduce it, because next week your feature code is different and `lr=0.01` now gives something else. Linking each run to the exact git commit closes this gap: the commit pins the code, the logged config pins the settings, and together they make the run genuinely reproducible. This is why a clean git history matters for ML (you commit before each significant experiment so there is a commit to reference), and it is the single discipline that most separates reproducible ML from the irreproducible kind. Numbers without the code that made them are trivia, not results.

## Track automatically, not by hand
The practical key to actually *doing* this is **automation**: a tracker that logs hyperparameters, metrics, and environment automatically as part of your training run, not notes you write manually. Manual tracking fails inevitably, you forget, you mistype, you skip it when rushing, exactly when an experiment turns out to matter, so the records have to be a byproduct of running the experiment, captured by the tooling whether or not you remember. This is why the tools (MLflow, Weights & Biases) exist: you add a few logging calls to your training loop, and every run is recorded automatically and completely, with its config, its metric curves, its artifacts, and its environment, into a queryable store. The mindset shift is to make tracking *infrastructure* rather than *effort*: set it up once so that running an experiment automatically produces a complete, reproducible record, and you never again face the archaeology of reconstructing what you did. A record you have to remember to write is a record you will eventually not have; a record the system captures for you is one you can trust.

## Where this fits
You know what to track, hyperparameters, metrics, artifacts, and environment (especially the git commit), and the standard that defines "enough": could you reproduce the run from the records alone? And you know it must be automatic, not manual, to be reliable. Tomorrow you set up MLflow to capture all of this automatically for every run.

items.title: MLflow
items.body:
## MLflow: tracking as infrastructure
**MLflow** is one of the two dominant experiment-tracking tools (Weights & Biases is the other), and it turns yesterday's principles into a running system with a few lines in your training code:
```python
import mlflow
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_params({"lr": 0.01, "layers": 3, "batch_size": 64})
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # ... train ...
        mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", val_auc, step=epoch)   # logged over time
    mlflow.log_artifact("model.pkl")                         # save the model
    mlflow.set_tag("git_commit", current_commit())           # pin the code
```
Run your training and MLflow records everything to a store with a **web UI** where you compare runs side by side, sort by any metric, and view the curves and artifacts of any past experiment. The archaeology is gone: every run is a queryable, comparable record.

## What the tool gives you beyond logging
The value of a tracking tool is not just storage, it is *comparison and organisation*, which is what makes experimentation productive. The web UI lets you do the things that were impossible with scattered notebooks: **compare runs** in a table sorted by validation AUC to instantly see your best configuration, **overlay metric curves** from multiple runs to see which trained better and whether any overfit, **filter and search** runs by hyperparameter ("show me all runs with lr < 0.05"), and **drill into any run** to see its full config, metrics, artifacts, and environment. This transforms how you iterate: instead of vaguely remembering that "the deeper model seemed better," you *see* that the 4-layer run hit 0.84 and the 3-layer hit 0.81, with the curves to prove it, and you make decisions from data rather than fading memory. The tool makes the comparison that *is* ML experimentation fast, reliable, and shareable, which is why it pays for itself immediately on any project with more than a handful of runs.

## Hosted vs self-hosted: the recurring choice
The practical difference between the two main tools is one you have seen before in this track, the build/host trade-off. **Weights & Biases (wandb)** is hosted (cloud) with a notably polished UI, easy to start, your run data lives on their servers. **MLflow** is open-source and **self-hostable**, which matters precisely when your data cannot leave your infrastructure, regulated industries, proprietary data, privacy requirements, the same consideration that drove the self-hosted choice for observability (AI-engineering W18) and the local-vs-API choice for transcription. So you pick on the same axis: wandb for convenience and polish when sending run data to a third party is fine, MLflow (self-hosted) for control and privacy when it is not. Both log the same things and provide the same comparison capabilities; the decision is about where the data lives, and recognising this as the same recurring build-versus-host trade-off (not a new dilemma) is part of developing infrastructure judgement. For learning and most projects, either works and the choice is reversible.

## Where this fits
You can set up MLflow to automatically record every run's config, metrics, artifacts, and environment, with a web UI for the comparison and search that make experimentation productive, and you understand the hosted-vs-self-hosted choice (wandb vs MLflow) as the familiar privacy/convenience trade-off. Your experiments are now systematically tracked. Tomorrow you tackle the subtler half of reproducibility: making a run produce the *same* result twice, via determinism and seeding.

items.title: Determinism and seeding
items.body:
## The uncomfortable truth: ML is random by default
You have tracked everything, code, config, environment, and you re-run the exact same experiment, and get a *different* result. This is normal and unsettling, and it is because ML training is full of **randomness**: weights are randomly initialised, data is randomly shuffled each epoch, dropout drops random neurons, augmentation applies random transforms. Run twice, get two different models with two different scores, even with identical code and settings. **Determinism and seeding** is the practice of controlling that randomness so a run is *exactly* reproducible, which is the other half of reproducibility that tracking alone does not provide. Tracking records *what* you did; seeding ensures that doing it again gives the *same* answer.

## Seeding: pin the randomness
The fix is to set the **random seeds** for every source of randomness, which makes the "random" choices deterministic, the same sequence of pseudo-random numbers every time, so initialisation, shuffling, and dropout all behave identically across runs:
```python
import torch, numpy as np, random
SEED = 42
random.seed(SEED); np.random.seed(SEED); torch.manual_seed(SEED)
torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(SEED)
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True   # make GPU ops deterministic too
```
You must seed *all* the libraries involved (Python's `random`, NumPy, PyTorch, and the GPU), because randomness anywhere unpinned breaks determinism, missing the GPU seed is a classic reason "I seeded everything and it's still not reproducible." And you **log the seed** as a hyperparameter, because the seed is part of what defines the run: to reproduce a result exactly, you need its seed alongside its code and config. With seeds set and logged, re-running gives the identical model, the reproducibility that tracking promised is now real.

## Why determinism matters, and its honest limits
Determinism matters for two concrete reasons beyond tidiness. First, **debugging and fair comparison:** if results vary run to run, you cannot tell whether a change *you* made improved the model or whether you just got a luckier random seed, the signal is drowned in noise, so to compare "feature A vs feature B" fairly you fix the seed and change only the feature, isolating the real effect (the controlled-experiment discipline from the classical weeks, now enforced via seeding). Second, **reproducibility for others and production:** a result a teammate or a regulator can reproduce exactly is trustworthy in a way a result that drifts is not. But there are honest limits worth knowing: full determinism can be hard to achieve across different hardware (a model trained on one GPU may not reproduce bit-identically on another), and enforcing deterministic GPU operations can *slow training*, so in practice you seed for reproducibility during development and comparison, and sometimes relax strict determinism for speed in large production training, accepting that results will be *statistically* consistent rather than bit-identical. The judgement is to control randomness enough that your comparisons are fair and your key results reproducible, while knowing perfect bit-determinism is not always worth its cost. The deeper point: randomness in ML is real and must be *managed*, not ignored, and an unseeded experiment is one whose results you cannot fully trust or defend.

## Where this fits
You can make runs reproducible by seeding every source of randomness (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, GPU) and logging the seed, which enables exact reproduction and, just as importantly, fair comparison where only the variable you changed differs. You understand both the value and the practical limits of determinism. Tomorrow you handle versioning the *outputs* of runs, the models and datasets, with artifact versioning.

items.title: Artifact versioning
items.body:
## Versioning the things runs produce and consume
Tracking records the *numbers* of a run; **artifact versioning** manages its *files*, the trained models, the datasets, the plots, so you can always retrieve the exact model a run produced and know exactly which data it was trained on. This matters because the model file *is* the deliverable, and "which model is in production, and what produced it?" must have a precise answer. An artifact store (built into MLflow/wandb) versions these files and links them to the run that created them:
```python
mlflow.log_artifact("model_v3.pkl")        # this run's model, versioned + linked
mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")
# later: retrieve the exact model any past run produced
```
Now every run has its actual outputs saved and traceable, not just a logged accuracy number with the model long since overwritten.

## Why model and data versions must be linked
The crucial idea is **lineage**: every model artifact should be traceable to the exact code, config, *and data* that produced it, so a model is never an orphan file but a known result of known inputs. This closes the reproducibility loop, you can answer not just "what was the model's accuracy?" but "here is the model, the code commit, the hyperparameters, the random seed, and the dataset version that made it", a complete, reproducible chain. The **data version** is the often-missing link, and it is vital because the same code on different data gives a different model, so a model is only reproducible if you know precisely which data slice trained it. This is exactly the problem next week's data versioning (DVC) solves at scale (datasets too big for git), but the principle starts here: a model artifact is meaningful only with its data and code lineage attached. Without lineage, you have a `model.pkl` in production that nobody can reproduce, re-train, or even explain, which is a serious liability when it inevitably needs updating or its decisions get questioned.

## Lineage is what makes production ML accountable
The payoff of artifact versioning and lineage is accountability and safe iteration, which production ML demands. When the model in production starts misbehaving, lineage lets you trace it back to its exact training conditions and diagnose what changed. When you need to **roll back** to a previous model (the new one regressed), versioned artifacts mean the old one is sitting there, retrievable, with its full provenance, not lost to an overwrite. When a regulator, auditor, or stakeholder asks "how was this model that made this decision built?", lineage gives a complete, honest answer. And when you improve the model, you can compare the new artifact against the old precisely because both are versioned and traceable. This is the same versioning discipline you applied to FlightWise with git tags (v0.1 to v0.4), now extended to the large binary artifacts (models, datasets) that git cannot handle well, and unified with the experiment tracking so that every artifact knows its origin. The mature stance is that a model without lineage is a risk, a black box you cannot reproduce or account for, and artifact versioning with full lineage is what makes a deployed model a known, reproducible, auditable thing rather than a mystery binary.

## Where this fits
You can version artifacts (models, datasets, plots) and link them to the code, config, seed, and data that produced them, establishing the *lineage* that makes any model reproducible, rollback-able, and auditable, the foundation of accountable production ML. Tomorrow you turn all of this into a sustainable team practice with experiment hygiene.

items.title: Experiment hygiene
items.body:
## From tools to discipline: experiment hygiene
You now have the tools (tracking, seeding, artifact versioning); **experiment hygiene** is the *discipline* of using them well so that, over hundreds of runs and possibly a team, the records stay useful rather than becoming their own mess. Tools alone do not save you, a tracker full of 500 runs named "test", "test2", "final", "final_real" with no organisation is nearly as useless as no tracker at all. Hygiene is the set of habits that keep the experiment record navigable and meaningful: naming runs sensibly, organising them, recording *why* you ran each one, and cleaning up, so that the accumulated experiments form a coherent, searchable history of what you learned rather than an undifferentiated pile.

## The habits that keep experiments useful
Good experiment hygiene is a handful of concrete practices:
- **Meaningful names and tags:** name runs and group them by experiment (`baseline`, `lr-sweep`, `add-augmentation`) and tag them with their purpose, so you can find and compare related runs instead of scrolling through hundreds of anonymous IDs.
- **Record the hypothesis:** note *why* you ran each experiment, what you were testing and what you expected, because a result is far more useful when you remember the question it answered ("testing whether deeper helps", not just "run #347").
- **Change one thing at a time:** structure experiments so each run isolates one variable where possible, so a difference in results is attributable to a known cause, the controlled-experiment discipline, now as an organising habit.
- **Clean up:** delete or archive junk runs (the broken ones, the typos), and mark the important ones (the current best, the chosen baseline), so the signal does not drown in noise.
These habits cost a little discipline per run and save enormous time later when you need to understand what you have done.

## Why hygiene is a force multiplier, especially on a team
The deeper reason experiment hygiene matters is that the *value* of experiment tracking compounds with its organisation, and collapses without it. A well-kept experiment history is a knowledge base: months later you (or a teammate) can see exactly what was tried, what worked, what failed and why, and build on it instead of re-running settled questions, the records *teach*. A messy one is write-only, technically complete but practically unsearchable, so people re-run experiments that were already done because finding the prior result is harder than redoing it, the exact archaeology tracking was supposed to end, reintroduced through neglect. On a *team* this multiplies: shared, well-organised experiment tracking lets people build on each other's work and avoid duplicating it, while a shared mess means everyone wastes time deciphering everyone else's runs. So hygiene is not bureaucratic neatness; it is what makes the experiment record a genuine, growing asset, individually and collectively. The habit to internalise is that *running* an experiment is only half the job, *recording it cleanly enough that it teaches your future self and your team* is the other half, and it is the difference between accumulating knowledge and accumulating clutter.

## Where this fits
You understand experiment hygiene, meaningful names and tags, recorded hypotheses, one-variable-at-a-time, and cleanup, the discipline that keeps tracking a useful, growing knowledge base rather than a write-only pile, and that compounds in value especially across a team. With tools and discipline together, tomorrow you assemble a fully tracked, reproducible experiment workflow and ship it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a reproducible experiment workflow
You assemble the week into a complete, tracked, reproducible experimentation setup, demonstrated on a real modelling problem (FlightWise, or any model from the track):
- **MLflow** (or wandb) logging every run's config, metrics, artifacts, and environment automatically.
- **seeding** for reproducibility, with the seed logged, so any run reproduces exactly.
- **artifact versioning** with lineage linking each model to its code commit, config, and data.
- **hygiene**: well-named, organised, documented runs comparing several configurations.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Reproducible experiment workflow: MLflow tracking + seeding + lineage"
git push
```

## The deliverable is a workflow, demonstrated
What makes this valuable is showing a *workflow*, not a single model, the ability to run experiments systematically and reproducibly, which is core ML-engineering competence that pure modelling projects never demonstrate. The strongest artifact is a tracked experiment campaign: several runs (different hyperparameters or features) logged to MLflow, compared in the UI to show how you found the best configuration, with the proof that any run reproduces exactly (same seed, same code commit gives the same result) and that each model traces to its full lineage. Show the comparison view ("here are my 8 runs sorted by validation AUC; run #5 won, here is its exact config, seed, and code commit"). That demonstrates you can do ML the disciplined, reproducible way, the way that scales to a team and to production, rather than the irreproducible notebook-archaeology way, which is precisely the maturity the ML Infrastructure phase is building.

## What experiment tracking established
Step back: you have ended the era of losing track of your own work. You can now record every experiment completely (config, metrics, artifacts, environment), reproduce any run exactly (seeding), trace every model to its origins (lineage), and keep it all organised into a knowledge base (hygiene). This is the foundation the rest of the infrastructure phase builds on, every later practice (scaled GPU training, data pipelines, containerised reproducibility) assumes you are tracking and reproducing what you do, and it is the practice that most distinguishes ML *engineering* from ad-hoc model-tinkering. The throughline: ML is empirical and randomised, so without systematic tracking and reproducibility its knowledge is unreliable and unrepeatable, and you have now built the discipline that makes it solid.

## Where this fits
You shipped a reproducible experiment workflow, tracked, seeded, lineage-linked, and organised, ending the archaeology and turning your ML work into a reliable, repeatable engineering practice. This is the foundation of the ML Infrastructure phase. Next week you tackle the hardware that makes serious training possible, **GPU training**: using a single GPU effectively, then scaling to multiple GPUs and training models too large to fit, where the memory constraints you first met in W9 become the central engineering challenge.

weeks.title: GPU Training, Single GPU, Then Multi-GPU
weeks.context:
A GPU is a massively parallel processor with thousands of cores optimised for the matrix multiplications that underpin deep learning. Using one effectively requires understanding its memory model, its programming constraints, and the tradeoffs between batch size, precision, and throughput. This week you take a training loop that ran on CPU and run it on a GPU, then go further: mixed precision training and gradient accumulation to train models that would otherwise not fit.

GPU memory is the binding constraint. A single A100 has 40-80GB. A GeForce RTX 4090 has 24GB. Your model weights, activations (intermediate computations kept for the backward pass), gradients, and optimizer states all compete for this memory. For a large model in full float32 precision: a 100M parameter model uses 400MB for weights, 400MB for gradients, and 800MB for Adam optimizer states (two moment estimates per parameter), 1.6GB before any activations. Activations scale with batch size and sequence length.

Mixed precision training uses float16 or bfloat16 for most computations and float32 only where needed for numerical stability. The practical effect: roughly 2x throughput (tensor cores on modern GPUs are optimised for 16-bit), 2x memory reduction for activations, and little to no quality loss when done correctly. PyTorch's automatic mixed precision (torch.cuda.amp) handles the details: the GradScaler prevents gradient underflow in float16, and autocasting handles the precision decisions.

Gradient accumulation simulates larger batch sizes without the memory cost. Instead of passing batch_size=128 samples through the model at once, you pass 16 samples, compute the loss, divide by 8, call backward(), then repeat 8 times before calling optimizer.step(). After 8 iterations, the accumulated gradients are equivalent to one batch of 128. The model update is identical; the memory peak is 1/8th.

Multi-GPU training with Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) is the next step when one GPU is not enough. DDP replicates the model on each GPU. Each GPU processes a different batch of data. After the backward pass, DDP all-reduces the gradients across all GPUs (summing them) and divides by the number of GPUs. Each GPU's optimizer step now uses the average gradient across all GPUs, equivalent to training with a batch size of num_gpus times the per-GPU batch size.

concept_check.q: You increase batch size from 32 to 128 and GPU memory usage quadruples. Why? Activations (intermediate computations) are stored during the forward pass for use in the backward pass. For a batch of 32?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You implement mixed precision training with torch.cuda.amp. The training is faster but after 100 steps, you see "inf" in the gradient scaler's scale factor, then the scale drops dramatically. What is?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You implement gradient accumulation with accumulate_steps=8. Where exactly does optimizer.zero_grad() go in the training loop? Zero the gradients at the start of each accumulation sequence, not at the?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Using the hardware deep learning actually needs
You met the GPU briefly in W9; this week you learn to use it *well*. A GPU is a massively parallel processor, thousands of cores built for the matrix multiplications that are 99% of deep learning, and using one effectively means understanding its memory model, its constraints, and the trade-offs between batch size, precision, and throughput. You take a training loop that ran on CPU, run it on a GPU, and then go further: **mixed precision** and **gradient accumulation** to train models that would otherwise not fit at all, and finally **multi-GPU** training for when one GPU is not enough. This is the hands-on hardware skill that separates someone who can train a toy model from someone who can train a real one.

## The binding constraint: GPU memory
The single fact that shapes all GPU training is that **memory is the binding constraint**, and the numbers make it concrete. A high-end A100 has 40-80GB; a consumer RTX 4090 has 24GB, and everything your training needs competes for that fixed space:
```text
For a 100M-parameter model in float32:
  weights:           400 MB   (4 bytes x 100M)
  gradients:         400 MB   (one per weight)
  Adam optimizer:    800 MB   (TWO moment estimates per weight)
  ---------------------------------
  ~1.6 GB before a single activation
  + activations (intermediate values kept for the backward pass) -- often the BIGGEST part
```
So a "100M-parameter" model is not 400MB to train, it is well over 1.6GB before activations, and activations (which scale with batch size) often dominate. This is why "CUDA out of memory" is the most common error in deep learning, and why understanding the memory budget is the prerequisite for training anything non-trivial.

## What competes for memory, and why it matters
Naming the four memory consumers explains every GPU-training technique you will learn:
- **Weights:** the model's parameters, fixed by model size.
- **Gradients:** one per weight, for the backward pass, also fixed by model size.
- **Optimizer states:** extra per-weight values, Adam keeps *two* (momentum and variance), so it doubles the per-parameter overhead beyond weights and gradients, a big and surprising cost.
- **Activations:** the intermediate computations saved during the forward pass so the backward pass can compute gradients. These scale with **batch size**, so they are the part you can most control.
Every technique this week targets one of these: smaller batches and gradient accumulation cut activations, mixed precision halves the bytes per value, multi-GPU and sharding split the fixed costs across devices. Understanding *what* is using your memory tells you *which* lever to pull when you run out, which is the core skill of fitting real models onto real GPUs.

## Where this fits
This week is the hands-on hardware engineering of the ML Infrastructure phase: making training actually run and fit on GPUs, single, then multiple, then for models bigger than one GPU. It builds on the W9 GPU basics and the memory awareness that has recurred since, now as a central engineering discipline. It also underpins everything large-scale in ML: you cannot train serious models without managing GPU memory and parallelism. Today's orientation: GPU memory is the binding constraint, divided among weights, gradients, optimizer states, and activations, and every technique this week is a way to fit training into that budget. Tomorrow you go deeper into the GPU's memory hierarchy.

items.title: GPU memory hierarchy
items.body:
## Inside the GPU's memory
To use a GPU well you need a clearer picture of its memory than "there is some and it runs out." A GPU has a **memory hierarchy**, layers of memory trading capacity for speed, and the one that matters most for fitting your model is the large **global memory** (the 24GB or 80GB figure), which is what holds your weights, gradients, optimizer states, and activations, and what "out of memory" refers to. There is also much smaller, much faster on-chip memory (shared memory, registers) that the GPU uses internally during computation, which is why *how* an operation is implemented (like FlashAttention from W11) affects speed and memory, but for training-level decisions, **global memory is the budget you manage**. Knowing the GPU has this hierarchy explains why some operations are memory-bound (waiting on global memory) rather than compute-bound, and why efficient implementations matter.

## The activation memory problem
The subtlest and most controllable memory consumer is **activations**, and understanding them is key to fitting larger models. During the forward pass, the GPU must *save* the intermediate output of each layer, because the backward pass needs those values to compute gradients (the chain rule reuses the forward values). So a deep network holds the activations of *every* layer in memory simultaneously during a training step, and this scales with both model depth and **batch size**, double the batch and you roughly double the activation memory. This is why activations often dwarf the weights: a model whose parameters fit easily can still blow up on activations with a large batch. The good news is that activations are the lever you control most directly, through batch size (smaller batch, less activation memory, tomorrow's gradient accumulation recovers the effect of a large batch without the memory) and through a technique called **gradient checkpointing** (recompute some activations during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading compute for memory). Recognising that activations, not just weights, are what fill your GPU, and that they scale with batch size, is the insight that lets you fit training that seemed impossible.

## Reading and reasoning about memory
The practical skill is to *reason about* and *measure* GPU memory rather than just hitting the wall and guessing. You can estimate the fixed costs (weights + gradients + optimizer states from the model size, as in D1) and you can watch actual usage with `nvidia-smi` (the GPU's status tool) or PyTorch's memory utilities, so when you get an out-of-memory error you can diagnose *which* consumer overflowed and pick the right fix: if activations (large batch), reduce batch size or use gradient accumulation/checkpointing; if the fixed model costs are too big for the GPU at all, you need mixed precision (smaller bytes) or multi-GPU sharding (split across devices). This turns "CUDA out of memory" from a frustrating dead-end into a solvable engineering problem with a clear diagnosis and a matching remedy, which is exactly the difference between flailing and engineering. The memory hierarchy and the activation insight together give you the mental model to fit real training onto the GPU you actually have, the foundational skill of the week, and the rest of the week is specific techniques (gradient accumulation, mixed precision, multi-GPU) for when the basic budget is not enough.

## Where this fits
You understand the GPU's memory: global memory as the budget you manage, and activations (saved for the backward pass, scaling with batch size) as the large, controllable consumer that often dominates, plus the ability to measure and diagnose memory so out-of-memory errors become solvable. Tomorrow you learn gradient accumulation, the technique that lets you get a large effective batch size without the activation memory a large batch normally costs.

items.title: Gradient accumulation
items.body:
## The problem: you want a big batch but cannot fit one
Larger batch sizes give smoother, more stable gradient estimates and better GPU utilisation, but a large batch means large activation memory (yesterday's lesson), so you often cannot fit the batch size you *want* on your GPU. **Gradient accumulation** is the clever trick that resolves this: it lets you get the *effect* of a large batch while only ever holding a small batch's worth of activations in memory. The idea is to process the large batch in small pieces, accumulate their gradients, and only update once:
```text
want effective batch 256, but only 64 fits:
  for 4 micro-batches of 64:
      forward + backward   (gradients ADD UP, not overwritten)
      DO NOT update yet
  after 4 micro-batches:  optimizer.step()   # one update, as if batch was 256
```

## Why this works: gradients add
Gradient accumulation works because of a simple mathematical fact: the gradient over a big batch equals the *sum* (or average) of the gradients over its parts, so you can compute the parts one at a time and add them up to get exactly the big-batch gradient. In PyTorch this is almost free to implement, because PyTorch *accumulates* gradients by default (the very behaviour that requires `zero_grad` normally), you simply run several forward-backward passes *without* calling `zero_grad` or `step`, letting the gradients pile up, then `step` once and `zero_grad`:
```python
optimizer.zero_grad()
for i, (X, y) in enumerate(loader):
    loss = loss_fn(model(X), y) / accum_steps   # scale so it averages
    loss.backward()                              # gradients accumulate
    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()                         # update after accum_steps micro-batches
        optimizer.zero_grad()
```
Only one micro-batch's activations exist at a time, so memory stays low, while the *update* is computed from the full effective batch. You have decoupled "how much fits in memory" from "how big a batch the optimizer sees," which is exactly the freedom you wanted.

## Why this matters: training big on small hardware
Gradient accumulation is one of the most practically important techniques in GPU training because it democratises larger-scale training: it lets you train with the large effective batch sizes that big models and stable training often require, on hardware that could never hold such a batch directly. Without it, your batch size is capped by your GPU memory, and some models simply will not train well at the tiny batch a small GPU forces; with it, a modest GPU can train with an effective batch of hundreds or thousands by accumulating over many micro-batches, trading a bit of *time* (you do several forward-backward passes per update) for the *memory* you do not have. This is the recurring GPU-training trade, spend time to save memory, and it appears again in gradient checkpointing (recompute activations to save memory) and is the conceptual cousin of the sharding you will meet later. The broader lesson is that GPU memory limits are not hard walls but *engineering constraints with workarounds*: when you cannot fit what you need, there is usually a technique that trades a resource you have (time, extra computation) for the one you lack (memory), and knowing these techniques is what lets you train ambitious models without ambitious hardware. Gradient accumulation is the first and most useful of them.

## Where this fits
You can use gradient accumulation to get a large effective batch size on limited memory, processing micro-batches and accumulating their gradients before a single update, trading time for memory. This is a core technique for training real models on modest GPUs. Tomorrow you learn mixed precision, which attacks memory (and speed) from a different angle, using smaller-precision numbers.

items.title: DataParallel vs DistributedDataParallel
items.body:
## Half the bytes: mixed precision training
Every number in your model is stored at some precision, and by default that is **float32** (32 bits, 4 bytes each). **Mixed precision training** uses **float16** (16 bits, 2 bytes) for most of the computation, which roughly *halves* the memory for activations and gradients *and* makes the math faster on modern GPUs (which have dedicated hardware for 16-bit operations). "Mixed" because it keeps a few sensitive parts in float32 for numerical stability while doing the bulk in float16, getting most of the memory and speed benefit without breaking training. In PyTorch it is nearly automatic:
```python
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
for X, y in loader:
    with torch.autocast("cuda"):          # run the forward pass in float16
        loss = loss_fn(model(X), y)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()          # scaled to avoid float16 underflow
    scaler.step(optimizer); scaler.update()
```

## Why it is nearly free, and what the catch is
Mixed precision is one of the highest-return techniques in deep learning because it gives you *two* wins for almost no cost: about **half the memory** (so you can fit bigger models or larger batches) and often **substantially faster training** (modern GPUs run 16-bit matrix math much faster than 32-bit), with usually *negligible* loss in final model quality. That combination, less memory, more speed, same accuracy, is why mixed precision is standard in essentially all modern training. The catch it manages is numerical: float16 has a much smaller range than float32, so very small gradient values can **underflow** to zero (vanishing in the limited precision) and break learning, which is why the technique keeps certain operations in float32 and uses **gradient scaling** (multiply the loss up before the backward pass so small gradients stay representable, then scale back down before the update), the `GradScaler` above. You do not have to manage this by hand, the framework handles the mixing and scaling, but understanding *why* it scales (to keep tiny float16 gradients from vanishing) is what lets you debug the occasional instability and trust the technique rather than treating it as a magic flag.

## The precision dimension of the memory budget
Mixed precision adds a new lever to the memory-management mental model from this week: besides controlling *how many* activations you hold (batch size, gradient accumulation) and *how* you split across devices (multi-GPU, coming up), you can control *how many bytes each value costs* (precision). This is increasingly central as models grow, and the frontier pushes it further with even smaller formats (bfloat16, and 8-bit or 4-bit *quantization* for inference and even some training), each trading a little numerical precision for large memory and speed savings, the same quantization idea you met in QLoRA for fine-tuning (W11/AI-eng). The unifying insight is that *precision is a resource you spend deliberately*: full float32 is rarely necessary, and using fewer bits where accuracy permits is one of the cheapest ways to fit and speed up large models. So your GPU-training toolkit now has three independent dimensions, manage activation count (batching), split fixed costs across devices (parallelism, next), and reduce bytes per value (precision), and a real training-engineering problem is solved by combining them: mixed precision to halve the bytes, gradient accumulation for the batch, and multi-GPU for what still does not fit. Knowing all three, and that they compose, is what lets you train models far larger than any single naive approach allows.

## Where this fits
You can use mixed precision to roughly halve memory and speed up training by computing in float16 (with float32 for stability and gradient scaling to prevent underflow), adding *precision* as a third lever alongside batching and parallelism in your memory toolkit. Mixed precision and accumulation handle a single GPU's limits; tomorrow you scale *out* to multiple GPUs with DataParallel and DistributedDataParallel.

items.title: Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)
items.body:
## When one GPU is not enough: data parallelism
Single-GPU techniques eventually hit a wall, the data is too big to train in reasonable time, or the model is too big to fit at all, and the answer is **multiple GPUs**. The most common form is **data parallelism**: put a *copy* of the model on each GPU, split each batch across the GPUs so each processes a different slice, then combine their gradients so all copies update identically and stay in sync.
```text
batch of 256, 4 GPUs:
  GPU0: model copy + 64 examples \
  GPU1: model copy + 64 examples  >  each computes gradients on its slice
  GPU2: model copy + 64 examples  >  gradients averaged across GPUs (all-reduce)
  GPU3: model copy + 64 examples /   all copies update identically
```
Four GPUs process four slices at once, so you train roughly four times faster (or with a four-times-larger effective batch), the throughput win of going multi-GPU.

## DataParallel vs DistributedDataParallel: use the right one
PyTorch offers two data-parallel implementations, and knowing which to use matters because one is much better:
- **DataParallel (DP):** the simple, single-line option that splits a batch across GPUs *on one machine*. It is easy but **inefficient**, it has a single-process bottleneck (one GPU coordinates and gets overloaded) and does not scale well, so it is mostly a quick-and-dirty choice you will outgrow.
- **DistributedDataParallel (DDP):** the production standard. It runs a separate process per GPU, each handling its own GPU efficiently, and synchronises gradients between them with an optimised **all-reduce** operation. It is more setup but *much* faster and scales across many GPUs and even multiple machines.
The practical guidance is clear: **use DDP**, not DP, for any real multi-GPU training, because DP's bottleneck wastes most of the benefit of extra GPUs. Knowing that DDP (per-process, efficient gradient sync) is the right tool, and DP is the deprecated convenience, saves you from the common mistake of scaling to 8 GPUs with DataParallel and getting barely 2x the throughput.

## The real cost of parallelism: communication
The crucial concept that makes you *think* clearly about multi-GPU is **communication overhead**, and it explains why N GPUs never give exactly N times the speed. After each step, the GPUs must *synchronise* their gradients (the all-reduce), which means moving data between GPUs over their interconnect, and that communication takes time, so the speedup is always less than perfectly linear: 4 GPUs might give 3.5x, not 4x, because some time is spent talking instead of computing. This communication cost is why the *interconnect* matters (fast GPU-to-GPU links like NVLink reduce it; GPUs talking over a slow network reduce the benefit), why parallelism efficiency *degrades* as you add more GPUs (more participants, more synchronisation), and why a well-engineered setup overlaps communication with computation to hide it. The deeper lesson, which recurs through all distributed systems (you saw it in multi-agent and shared-memory contexts in AI-eng), is that distributing work introduces *coordination cost*, and the art is keeping that cost small relative to the work, so you parallelise when the computation per GPU is large enough to dwarf the synchronisation, and you do not naively assume more GPUs means proportionally faster. Understanding that the bottleneck in multi-GPU training is often *communication, not computation* is what separates someone who throws GPUs at a problem from someone who scales it efficiently.

## Where this fits
You can scale training across GPUs with data parallelism, using DDP (efficient per-process gradient sync) over DP, while understanding that communication overhead makes the speedup sub-linear and is the real constraint on scaling. Data parallelism replicates the model on each GPU; tomorrow you handle the case where the model is too big to fit on even one GPU, with Fully Sharded Data Parallel.

items.title: Cloud GPU rentals
items.body:
## When the model itself does not fit: FSDP
Data parallelism assumes a copy of the model fits on each GPU. But the largest models, billions of parameters, do *not* fit on a single GPU at all, weights plus gradients plus optimizer states exceed even an 80GB card. **Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)** solves this by *sharding* the model itself across GPUs: instead of each GPU holding a full copy, each holds only a *slice* (shard) of the parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, and the GPUs gather the pieces they need just in time during computation, then release them.
```text
Data parallel:  each GPU = FULL model copy        (model must fit on one GPU)
FSDP:           each GPU = a SHARD of the model    (model split across GPUs; none holds it all)
                gather the needed shard for each layer, compute, then free it
```
This is what makes training models larger than a single GPU's memory possible, by spreading the model's memory footprint across the whole cluster.

## The trade: more communication for more capacity
FSDP fits enormous models by trading *memory* for *communication*, the same kind of trade you have seen all week, now at the model-sharding level. Because no GPU holds the whole model, the GPUs must constantly **gather** the relevant shards from each other before computing a layer (and discard them after to free memory), which means much more inter-GPU communication than plain data parallelism, where each GPU already had the full model and only synced gradients. So FSDP enables training that is otherwise impossible (the model would not fit any other way), at the cost of heavier communication overhead, which makes the fast interconnect from yesterday even more critical. This sits on a spectrum of parallelism strategies: **data parallel** (replicate the model, split the data, simplest, needs the model to fit) for when the model fits but you want speed/throughput, and **sharded/model-parallel** approaches like FSDP for when the model is too big to fit, accepting more communication to gain the capacity. Real frontier training often combines them (data parallel across groups, sharding within), but the conceptual split, replicate when it fits, shard when it does not, is the key judgement.

## Where this leaves you: the full scaling toolkit
Step back and see the complete picture of how training scales, because this lesson completes it. To fit and accelerate training you now have a layered toolkit, applied in roughly this order as needs grow: on a **single GPU**, manage activations (batch size, gradient accumulation, checkpointing) and reduce bytes (mixed precision); when one GPU is too *slow*, replicate across GPUs with **DDP** (data parallel); when the model is too *big* for one GPU, **shard** it with FSDP. Each step trades a resource you have for one you lack, time and communication traded for memory and speed, and they compose into the ability to train almost anything given enough hardware. You do not need to train billion-parameter models to benefit from understanding this: it tells you *why* large models require clusters, *what* the engineering challenges are (memory, communication), and *how* to reason about scaling your own training as it grows. This is the knowledge that lets you read a paper saying "trained with FSDP on 256 GPUs" and understand exactly what that means and why it was necessary, and that orients you in the world of large-scale ML even when your own work is smaller. Most engineers treat large-scale training as a mystery; you now understand its mechanics.

## Where this fits
You understand FSDP, sharding the model across GPUs so models larger than one GPU can train, trading communication for capacity, and you hold the full scaling toolkit: manage activations and precision on one GPU, replicate with DDP for speed, shard with FSDP for size. With the techniques understood, tomorrow you handle the practical reality of *getting* GPUs, cloud GPU rentals, before shipping.
