items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Renting the hardware: cloud GPUs
Most people do not own A100s, so real GPU training usually means **renting** them from the cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure, or GPU-focused providers like Lambda, RunPod, Vast.ai), and using them cost-effectively is its own skill, the practical bookend to the week's techniques. GPUs are expensive by the hour (a high-end card can be several dollars an hour, more on the big clouds), so the engineering goal is to get your training done while spending as little GPU time as possible:
```text
cost = (GPU hourly rate) x (hours of training) x (number of GPUs)
minimise by: right-sized GPU, efficient code, spot/preemptible pricing, no idle time
```

## Spending GPU money wisely
A handful of practices keep cloud GPU costs sane, and they tie the whole week together:
- **Right-size the GPU:** do not rent an 80GB A100 to train a model that fits on a 24GB card, match the GPU to the job's actual memory and compute needs (which you can now estimate from the memory budget).
- **Use spot / preemptible instances:** these are much cheaper (often 50-70% off) GPUs that the provider can reclaim with little notice, ideal for training *if* you **checkpoint** regularly (save the model state periodically) so a preemption costs you minutes, not the whole run. This makes checkpointing not just good hygiene but a cost strategy.
- **Eliminate idle time:** a rented GPU sitting idle while you debug or prepare data is pure waste, so you develop and debug on CPU or a tiny dataset *first*, then spin up the GPU only when the code is correct and ready to train at full scale, and shut it down the moment training finishes. Never pay for a GPU that is not computing.
- **Use the efficiency techniques:** mixed precision and good utilisation mean fewer GPU-hours for the same result, so the week's techniques are *also* cost savings, faster training is cheaper training.

## GPU efficiency is cost efficiency, and that is an engineering responsibility
The deeper lesson is that on rented hardware, **technical efficiency and cost efficiency are the same thing**, and managing that is a real ML-engineering responsibility, not an afterthought. Every technique this week, fitting the model so you do not need a bigger GPU, mixed precision so training runs faster, gradient accumulation so a cheaper card suffices, efficient DDP so extra GPUs are not wasted, translates directly into money saved, because cloud GPU time is metered and expensive. An engineer who can train a model on one well-utilised 24GB GPU with mixed precision and accumulation, while another rents four A100s and uses DataParallel inefficiently, does the same job for a fraction of the cost, and at scale that difference is enormous. This is the same cost-consciousness that ran through the AI-engineering production phase, now applied to *training* rather than inference: the GPU is a scarce, expensive resource, and using it deliberately, right-sized, efficiently utilised, never idle, on the cheapest viable pricing, is part of doing the job well. The mature stance is that "make the training efficient" and "make the training affordable" are one goal, and the GPU skills of this week serve both.

## Where this fits
You can train on rented cloud GPUs cost-effectively, right-sizing the GPU, using spot instances with checkpointing, eliminating idle time, and leaning on the week's efficiency techniques, recognising that GPU efficiency *is* cost efficiency. You now command GPU training end to end: memory, single-GPU optimisation, multi-GPU scaling, and the economics. Next week you move from the hardware to the *pipelines*, data versioning and automated workflows that take ML beyond notebooks into reproducible, production-grade systems.

## What GPU training gave you
You have turned the GPU from a vague "thing that makes training fast" into a resource you manage deliberately: you understand its memory budget (weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations), you can fit models that seemed too big (gradient accumulation, mixed precision, sharding), you can scale across GPUs efficiently (DDP over DP, with communication as the real cost), and you can do it affordably in the cloud. This is the hands-on hardware competence that makes serious deep learning possible, and it is exactly the engineering, not the math, that most distinguishes someone who can only train toy models from someone who can train real ones.

weeks.title: Data Versioning and Pipelines, Beyond Notebooks
weeks.context:
Notebooks are for exploration. Production ML runs in scripts, pipelines, and version-controlled code. The transition from "works in a Jupyter notebook" to "reproducible, automated, reviewable" is where ML engineering diverges from data science. This week you build the infrastructure that makes your training reproducible, versioned, and automated: DVC for data versioning, a pipeline DAG, and a testing framework for ML code.

Data Version Control (DVC) handles the problem that git handles for code: tracking changes, enabling rollback, and synchronising across team members. The difference: ML datasets are gigabytes or terabytes, too large to commit to git. DVC stores the data in remote storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) and commits only a small .dvc pointer file to git. When a teammate clones the repo and runs dvc pull, they get the exact data version referenced in the pointer file.

Pipelines as DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) are the architecture that makes ML workflows reproducible. Each step in the pipeline (data ingestion, preprocessing, feature engineering, training, evaluation) is a node. Edges represent dependencies. If the preprocessing output has not changed since the last run, the training step uses the cached result rather than re-running preprocessing. DVC stages define these dependencies declaratively: inputs, outputs, the command to run, and the dependencies between stages.

Idempotency is the property that running a step twice produces the same result as running it once. An idempotent pipeline can be safely retried after failure, run in CI without side effects, and shared with teammates who can reproduce any historical result. Achieving idempotency requires: fixed random seeds, version-pinned dependencies, deterministic data loading (fixed shuffle order), and no side effects outside the declared outputs.

Testing ML code is genuinely different from testing regular software. The model output is probabilistic, you cannot assert an exact output. Instead you test properties: the model's output shape is correct, the loss decreases over the first 10 training steps, the preprocessing preserves row counts, the feature engineering function produces the expected column set. Behavioural tests go one level higher: the model should score higher on clean data than on corrupted data, the model's performance should not degrade more than 2% when a single feature is removed.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Beyond notebooks: ML as engineered software
Notebooks are wonderful for exploration, and terrible for production. This week is about the transition that *defines* ML engineering: moving from "it works in my Jupyter notebook" to "it is reproducible, automated, versioned, and reviewable." Production ML does not run in notebooks; it runs in scripts and **pipelines**, version-controlled, tested, and automated. You will build the infrastructure that makes your training a real software system: **DVC** for versioning data, a **pipeline** that runs your ML steps as an automated graph, and the practices that make ML code testable and reviewable. This is precisely where ML engineering diverges from data science, the data scientist explores and proves a model possible; the ML engineer makes it a reliable, repeatable, automated system.

## Why notebooks do not scale to production
A notebook hides problems that production cannot tolerate, and naming them motivates the whole week. Notebooks run **out of order** (you can run cell 5 before cell 3, so the result depends on hidden execution history nobody can reconstruct), they **mix everything** (data loading, training, plotting, and one-off debugging all tangled together), they are **hard to test and review** (you cannot easily unit-test a notebook cell or review it cleanly in a pull request), and they **do not automate** (you cannot reliably schedule or trigger a notebook to retrain on new data). For exploration none of this matters; for a system that must retrain reliably, be reviewed by teammates, and run unattended, all of it is disqualifying. So the move to pipelines is not bureaucratic ceremony, it is what makes ML *operable*: code that runs the same way every time, can be tested before it ships, reviewed before it merges, and automated to run on its own.

## What you will build: versioned data and automated pipelines
The week's infrastructure has two pillars:
- **Data versioning (DVC):** git for your *data*. Just as you version code, you version the datasets, so any model traces to the exact data that trained it, and a teammate can fetch the precise data version your results used.
- **Pipelines as automated workflows:** your ML steps (load, preprocess, train, evaluate) expressed as a connected, automated **graph** that runs reproducibly, with caching so unchanged steps are skipped, orchestration so it runs on schedule or trigger, and observability so you can see what happened.
Together these turn an ad-hoc notebook into a versioned, automated, reproducible ML *system*, the foundation for everything in production ML.

## Where this fits
This week continues the ML Infrastructure phase by building the pipelines and data versioning that take ML out of notebooks and into engineered software, pairing with experiment tracking (W13, reproducible *experiments*) and GPU training (W14, scalable *training*) to make ML reliable end to end. It directly enables the production phases ahead: you cannot serve, monitor, or continuously retrain a model that lives in an un-versioned, un-automated notebook. Today's orientation: production ML runs in versioned, automated, testable pipelines, not notebooks, and the gap between the two is exactly where ML engineering lives. Tomorrow you learn the core structure of a pipeline: the DAG.

items.title: Pipelines as DAGs
items.body:
## Pipelines as DAGs: ML steps as a graph
An ML workflow is a sequence of steps, load data, preprocess, engineer features, train, evaluate, and the right way to express it is as a **DAG** (Directed Acyclic Graph): each step is a node, and the arrows show dependencies (which step's output feeds which next step), with no cycles (nothing depends on itself, directly or indirectly).
```text
load_data --> preprocess --> train --> evaluate
                  \--> feature_engineering --/
(each node = a step;  arrows = "this output feeds that step")
```
Instead of a notebook's implicit top-to-bottom-if-you-remember order, the DAG makes the dependencies *explicit*: the pipeline knows that `train` needs `preprocess`'s output, so it runs them in the correct order automatically, every time.

## Why the DAG structure is exactly right for ML
Expressing the pipeline as a DAG is not arbitrary, the structure encodes precisely what an ML workflow *is*, and that yields concrete benefits. **Explicit dependencies** mean the system knows the correct execution order and can enforce it, ending the notebook's "did I run preprocessing before training?" ambiguity, the order is defined by the graph, not by what you happened to click. **Reproducibility** follows: given the same inputs, running the DAG produces the same outputs in the same order, every time, because the steps and their connections are fixed code, not a stateful notebook session. **Modularity** follows too: each node is a discrete, testable unit with defined inputs and outputs, so you can test `preprocess` in isolation, swap one step without touching the others, and review each step's code cleanly, exactly the software-engineering qualities notebooks lack. And the **acyclic** part matters: ML workflows genuinely have no cycles (you do not preprocess the output of training), so a DAG fits naturally, and the absence of cycles is what lets the system reason about order and caching. The DAG is the data structure that turns a tangle of notebook cells into an ordered, reproducible, modular system.

## The DAG enables everything else this week
The reason the DAG comes first is that it is the foundation the rest of the week builds on, each later capability is something the graph structure makes possible. **Caching** (tomorrow): because the DAG knows each step's inputs, it can skip a step whose inputs did not change and reuse its cached output, only re-running what actually needs re-running. **Orchestration** (D4): because the workflow is an explicit graph, an orchestrator can run it on a schedule, retry failed nodes, and run independent branches in parallel. **Observability** (D6): because each node is a defined unit, you can monitor each step's status, duration, and outputs. None of these are possible with a notebook's implicit, stateful flow; they all require the work to be expressed as an explicit graph of discrete, dependency-linked steps. So learning to *think* in DAGs, decomposing your ML workflow into clean nodes with explicit dependencies, is the foundational skill of the week, and it is a mental model that transfers far beyond ML (build systems, data engineering, and workflow tools everywhere use DAGs for exactly these reasons). Structuring your work as a DAG is the first and most important step out of the notebook.

## Where this fits
You understand pipelines as DAGs: ML steps as nodes with explicit dependency arrows, no cycles, which gives reproducible ordering, modular testable steps, and the structure that enables caching, orchestration, and observability. This is the foundation of pipeline engineering. Tomorrow you exploit the DAG's first big payoff: caching, so you only re-run the steps that actually changed.

items.title: Caching
items.body:
## Caching: do not redo work that has not changed
ML pipelines have expensive steps, preprocessing gigabytes of data, training for hours, and re-running the *entire* pipeline every time you change one thing is wasteful. **Caching** exploits the DAG to avoid that: because the pipeline knows each step's inputs, it can detect when a step's inputs are *unchanged* and reuse its previously-computed output instead of recomputing it.
```text
change only the training code:
  load_data     -> CACHED (inputs unchanged, skip)
  preprocess    -> CACHED (inputs unchanged, skip)
  train         -> RE-RUN (its code changed)
  evaluate      -> RE-RUN (depends on the new model)
```
So tweaking your model and re-running the pipeline does *not* re-load and re-preprocess the data, it skips straight to retraining, turning a multi-hour full run into a few-minute incremental one. This is what makes iterative development with pipelines practical rather than painful.

## How caching knows what changed
Caching works by *fingerprinting* each step's inputs, the data it consumes, the parameters it uses, and the code that runs it, typically by hashing them. When you re-run the pipeline, it recomputes each step's fingerprint and compares to last time: if the fingerprint matches (nothing the step depends on changed), the cached output is still valid and the step is skipped; if it differs (data, params, or code changed), the step re-runs and everything *downstream* of it re-runs too (because their inputs, the changed step's output, are now different). This dependency-aware invalidation is the clever part and exactly why the DAG matters: the pipeline propagates "this changed" correctly through the graph, re-running precisely the affected steps and no more. Tools like DVC pipelines and the workflow orchestrators do this fingerprinting for you, you declare each step's inputs, outputs, and parameters, and the tool tracks the rest. The key insight is that correct caching requires *accurately declaring each step's true dependencies*: if you forget to tell the pipeline that a step depends on a particular config value, it will wrongly skip the step when that value changes and silently serve a stale result, the one real hazard of caching.

## Why caching transforms how you work
The payoff of caching is not just speed, it changes the *economics of iteration* and thus how freely you experiment, which compounds over a project. When re-running the pipeline after a small change takes minutes instead of hours (because only the changed step and its descendants re-run), you iterate far more, try more variations, fix more issues, improve the model faster, the same way fast tests encourage more frequent testing. Slow full re-runs, by contrast, discourage experimentation (you avoid changes because re-running is painful) and waste compute (and on rented hardware, money, recomputing unchanged preprocessing every time is paying to redo settled work). Caching also makes pipelines *trustworthy* to re-run: you can safely re-execute the whole pipeline knowing it will only do necessary work, so "just run the pipeline" becomes a cheap, routine operation rather than a heavyweight commitment. This is the same principle as build-system incremental compilation or fast test suites, only redo what changed, applied to ML, and it is a large part of what makes pipeline-based ML *more* productive than notebooks despite the upfront structure, because the structure (the DAG) is exactly what enables the caching that makes iteration fast. Cheap, correct re-runs are a productivity multiplier.

## Where this fits
You understand pipeline caching: fingerprinting each step's inputs (data, params, code) to skip unchanged steps and re-run only what changed and its descendants, which makes iteration fast and cheap, provided you declare dependencies accurately. This is the payoff that makes pipelines more productive than notebooks. Tomorrow you learn orchestrators, the tools that *run* pipelines on schedules and triggers, handling failures and scale.

items.title: Orchestrators
items.body:
## Orchestrators: running pipelines for real
A pipeline you run by hand on your laptop is a start; a *production* pipeline needs to run automatically, on a schedule or a trigger, recover from failures, and scale, and that is the job of an **orchestrator** (tools like Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, Kubeflow). An orchestrator takes your DAG and *operates* it: it runs the steps in dependency order, on a schedule (retrain every night) or a trigger (when new data arrives), retries failed steps, runs independent branches in parallel, and gives you a control plane to see and manage it all. It is the difference between "I run my pipeline when I remember to" and "the pipeline runs reliably on its own, and tells me when something breaks."

## What an orchestrator handles that you would not want to
The value of an orchestrator is everything it handles so you do not have to hand-roll it, and each capability addresses a real production need:
- **Scheduling and triggering:** run the pipeline at set times or in response to events (new data, a code push), so retraining and processing happen automatically rather than relying on someone to launch them.
- **Failure handling:** when a step fails (a transient network error, a flaky data source), the orchestrator retries it per your policy, and if it still fails, alerts you and stops cleanly, rather than the whole pipeline silently dying or producing a half-finished result.
- **Parallelism:** independent branches of the DAG (two preprocessing steps that do not depend on each other) run *concurrently*, using your resources efficiently, the orchestrator reads the graph to know what can run in parallel.
- **Dependency management across runs and resources:** it coordinates which steps run where (this on a GPU, that on a CPU), and manages backfills and reruns.
Building all of this yourself, scheduling, retries, parallelism, alerting, would be a large, error-prone project; the orchestrator provides it as infrastructure, which is why production ML teams use one rather than cron jobs and shell scripts.

## Choosing and using an orchestrator wisely
The practical judgement is to match the orchestrator's power to your actual needs and not over-engineer, the recurring discipline of the track. For a learning project or a simple pipeline, a heavyweight orchestrator like Airflow is overkill, the DVC pipeline or a simple scheduled script may be all you need, and reaching for a full orchestration platform adds real operational complexity (it is itself a system to run and maintain). You adopt an orchestrator when the needs genuinely arrive: scheduled or triggered retraining, multi-step pipelines with failure-recovery requirements, parallelism across many steps, a team that needs shared visibility and control. The different tools also have different philosophies (Airflow is mature and config-heavy; Prefect and Dagster are more modern and Python-native; Kubeflow is Kubernetes-centric for scale), and you choose based on your stack and scale rather than hype. The deeper point is that orchestration is what makes ML pipelines *operational*, run reliably, automatically, and recoverably in production, and recognising *when* a workflow has graduated from "run it manually" to "needs orchestration" (it needs to run on its own, recover from failures, and be visible to a team) is the engineering judgement, just as much as knowing the tools. Orchestration turns a pipeline from a script you run into a service that runs itself.

## Where this fits
You understand orchestrators: tools that run your pipeline DAG automatically on schedules and triggers, with retries, parallelism, and alerting, turning a manual pipeline into an operational service, adopted when the workflow genuinely needs automation, recovery, and shared visibility. Tomorrow you handle how pipelines themselves are defined and maintained: workflow as code.

items.title: Workflow as code
items.body:
## Workflow as code: the pipeline is software too
A crucial principle ties the week together: your pipeline, the steps, their dependencies, their schedule, is itself defined in **code**, version-controlled, reviewed, and tested like any other software, not configured by hand in a UI or held together by manual steps. "Workflow as code" means the entire pipeline definition lives in your repository as files you commit, so the pipeline's structure has a history, can be code-reviewed in a pull request, can be rolled back, and is reproducible from the repo alone.
```text
the pipeline DEFINITION (which steps, what depends on what, the schedule)
  -> lives in version-controlled code, not clicked together in a dashboard
  -> reviewed in PRs, tested, rolled back, reproduced from git
```
This is the same move you made for the model (versioned) and the data (versioned next, via DVC), now applied to the *workflow itself*: it becomes a first-class, versioned software artifact.

## Why defining workflows in code matters so much
Workflow-as-code earns its place because it brings every software-engineering discipline to bear on the pipeline, which a hand-configured or manual workflow cannot have. **Version control:** the pipeline's evolution is tracked, so you can see when and why a step was added, diff changes, and roll back a workflow change that broke things, exactly the benefits git gives code, now for your workflow. **Code review:** a change to the pipeline (a new step, a different schedule) goes through a pull request where a teammate reviews it before it runs in production, catching mistakes before they cause a bad retraining run, where a UI-configured change has no such gate. **Testing:** because the workflow is code, you can test it, validate the DAG is well-formed, test individual steps, even dry-run the pipeline, before it touches production. **Reproducibility:** anyone can recreate the entire pipeline from the versioned definition in the repo, with no "and then click these settings in the dashboard" tribal knowledge. The contrast is stark: a workflow clicked together in a GUI is unversioned, unreviewable, untestable, and exists only in that GUI's state, which is fragile and opaque; a workflow defined in code is a durable, auditable, collaborative software asset.

## The unifying principle: everything is versioned code
Workflow-as-code is the capstone of a principle that runs through this entire phase and is the deepest lesson of ML infrastructure: **make everything a versioned, reproducible artifact, code, data, models, experiments, and the workflow itself.** Each week added a piece: experiment tracking versioned the *runs*, artifact lineage versioned the *models*, DVC (next) versions the *data*, and workflow-as-code versions the *pipeline*. The reason this matters is reproducibility and reliability at the system level: when code, data, model, and workflow are *all* versioned and defined as artifacts, you can reproduce any past result completely (this code, on this data, run by this workflow, produced this model), roll back any part, review any change, and operate the whole ML system with the same rigour as mature software engineering. This is the precise difference between data science (a model proven possible in a notebook) and ML engineering (a model produced by a versioned, reviewable, reproducible, automated system), and workflow-as-code completes the picture by ensuring the *process* that ties everything together is itself engineered, not improvised. The mature ML system has no un-versioned, un-reviewed, manually-configured pieces, and treating the workflow as code is what closes the last gap. Everything that defines how your ML is produced lives in the repo.

## Where this fits
You understand workflow-as-code: defining the pipeline itself in version-controlled, reviewable, testable code, which completes the phase's unifying principle that *everything*, code, data, models, experiments, and workflow, should be a versioned, reproducible artifact. This is what makes ML a true engineering discipline. Tomorrow you add the operational visibility that keeps running pipelines healthy: pipeline observability.

items.title: Pipeline observability
items.body:
## Seeing inside a running pipeline
A pipeline that runs automatically in production needs to be *watchable*, or you will not know when it silently breaks, and **pipeline observability** is recording what happens as the pipeline runs so you can see its health and debug failures. Like the observability you built for AI systems (AI-eng W18), it answers "what is the pipeline doing, is it healthy, and when something goes wrong, where and why?" For each pipeline run and each step, you want visibility into: did it succeed or fail, how long did it take, what did it produce, and what were the inputs, so that a failed nightly retraining is something you *see and diagnose*, not something you discover days later when the stale model causes problems.

## What to observe, and why each matters
Pipeline observability tracks several things, each catching a different kind of problem:
- **Status:** did each step and the overall run succeed or fail? This is the basic health signal, and an alert on failure is what turns "the pipeline broke silently three days ago" into "I was notified the moment it failed."
- **Duration and resource use:** how long did each step take, and how much compute/memory? A step that suddenly takes much longer (or runs out of memory) signals a problem, growing data, a regression, even before it fails outright, the same way latency and cost trends warn you in production AI.
- **Data quality / metrics at each step:** is the data flowing through each step *sane*, expected row counts, no surge in missing values, distributions in range? ML pipelines fail in a uniquely dangerous way, they can run "successfully" while producing *garbage* because the input data quietly broke, so checking data quality between steps catches the silent failures that status alone misses.
- **Lineage and outputs:** which data and code produced this run's outputs (the lineage from W13), so a bad result is traceable.
Together these let you trust an automated pipeline, because you can *see* it working and be *told* when it does not.

## The silent-failure danger that makes ML observability special
The reason pipeline observability matters more in ML than in ordinary software is the **silent failure**, and internalising this is the key lesson. A normal software pipeline that breaks usually *errors* (a crash, an exception) and you notice. An ML pipeline can complete every step "successfully", no errors, green status, and still produce a broken model, because the failure is in the *data* or the *result*, not the code: an upstream data source changed format and now half the features are null, but the pipeline dutifully trained on the garbage and deployed a model that quietly makes bad predictions. Status monitoring alone would show all green. This is why ML pipeline observability must watch the *data and the metrics*, not just whether steps ran: you check that each step's output is sane (row counts, distributions, null rates), and you check that the trained model's metrics did not regress (the eval-gate idea from AI-eng W17, here guarding the pipeline), so a silent data-quality break or a quality regression *raises an alarm* even though no code errored. The mature stance is to assume that "the pipeline ran successfully" does *not* mean "the pipeline produced a good model," and to build the data-quality and metric checks that close that gap, because in ML, the most dangerous failures are the ones that do not look like failures. Observability that watches data and results, not just execution, is what makes an automated ML pipeline genuinely trustworthy.

## Where this fits
You understand pipeline observability: monitoring status, duration, resource use, and especially *data quality and model metrics* at each step, with alerting, because ML pipelines fail silently, running "successfully" while producing garbage, and only data-and-result observability catches that. Tomorrow you assemble the week's pieces, DVC, DAG pipeline, orchestration, observability, into a complete reproducible pipeline and ship it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a versioned, automated ML pipeline
You assemble the week into a real, reproducible ML pipeline, taking a model from the track (FlightWise or another) out of the notebook and into engineered infrastructure:
- **DVC** versioning the dataset, so the model traces to the exact data, and a teammate can `dvc pull` the precise version.
- the workflow as a **DAG pipeline** (load, preprocess, train, evaluate) with **caching**, defined as **versioned code**, so re-runs only redo what changed and the pipeline lives in the repo.
- **orchestration** (even a simple scheduled run) and **observability** (status, plus a data-quality check between steps) appropriate to the project's scale.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "ML pipeline: DVC data versioning + cached DAG, workflow as code"
dvc push   # data to remote storage
git push
```

## The deliverable is reproducibility a stranger can verify
What makes this project demonstrate real ML engineering is **end-to-end reproducibility by someone else**: a teammate (or a reviewer, or future-you) can clone the repo, run `dvc pull` to get the exact data, run the pipeline, and reproduce your model *exactly*, no notebook archaeology, no "which data did I use?", no manual steps. That is the concrete proof of the week's whole point, ML as reproducible, versioned, automated software. Show it: the `.dvc` pointer files versioning gigabyte-scale data in a tiny git repo, the pipeline definition in code, the cache skipping unchanged steps on a re-run, and the data-quality check that would catch a silent break. Demonstrating that your ML is fully reproducible from a clone, data, code, pipeline, and result all versioned and automated, is exactly the engineering maturity that separates a production ML system from a notebook, and it is a strong, credible portfolio signal because most people's ML work is *not* reproducible this way.

## What the pipeline week established
Step back: you have moved ML out of the notebook and into engineered software. You can version data at scale (DVC), structure work as a reproducible cached DAG, define the workflow as version-controlled code, run it automatically with orchestration, and watch it with observability that catches ML's silent data failures. Combined with experiment tracking (W13) and GPU training (W14), your ML is now reproducible, scalable, automated, and observable, the system properties that production demands and that notebooks cannot provide. The throughline of the phase has been to *make everything a versioned, reproducible artifact*, code, data, models, experiments, workflow, and you have now built that for the data and the pipeline. This is the precise boundary where ML engineering diverges from data science, and you are now on the engineering side of it.

## Where this fits
You shipped a versioned, automated, reproducible ML pipeline that a stranger could clone and reproduce exactly, completing the move from notebooks to engineered ML software. One piece of the infrastructure phase remains: next week you make the *environment* itself reproducible with **containers and Docker**, freezing the Python, CUDA, and dependency stack so your training runs identically on any machine, the final guarantee of reproducibility that ties the whole phase together.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You add a new CSV file to your dataset directory and run dvc add data/. What happens and what gets committed to git? DVC computes the MD5 hash of the entire data directory, writes a data.dvc pointer file containing the hash and the remote storage path, and adds the data to the DVC cache (local). The actual data files are not committed to git, only the data.dvc file (a few hundred bytes). You git add data.dvc and git commit. When a teammate runs dvc pull, DVC reads the hash from data.dvc and downloads the exact files from remote storage. If the data changes, the hash changes, the pointer file changes, and git tracks that change.

weeks.title: Containers and Reproducibility, Dockerfile as a Lab Notebook
weeks.context:
Reproducibility in ML is harder than in regular software. Not because engineers are careless, but because ML training depends on many things that are easy to forget to version: the Python environment, the random seeds, the GPU driver version, the preprocessing order, the exact dataset slice. Docker solves the environment problem comprehensively: everything your training needs, Python, CUDA libraries, installed packages, environment variables, is declared in a Dockerfile, frozen into an image, and reproducible on any compatible machine.

A Dockerfile is a recipe. The FROM instruction specifies the base image, for ML, this is usually an official PyTorch or CUDA image. Each subsequent RUN instruction adds a layer. Layers are cached: if the first 5 instructions have not changed, Docker skips them and rebuilds only from the changed instruction. This caching is what makes iterative development with Docker practical.

Layer ordering matters for cache efficiency. The most stable layers go first. Dependencies (requirements.txt install) go before application code, because requirements change rarely and code changes often. If you put COPY . . before RUN pip install, every code change invalidates the pip install layer, costing minutes on rebuilds.

Multi-stage builds solve the size problem. The build stage installs compilers and build dependencies needed to compile packages. The runtime stage copies only the compiled artifacts, leaving the build tools behind. A training image built naively might be 8GB. A multi-stage build can shrink it to 3GB by excluding the build toolchain from the final image.

The Dockerfile as a lab notebook metaphor means: every environment decision (Python version, CUDA version, library version) is explicitly recorded in the Dockerfile and in version control. Anyone who has the Dockerfile can reproduce the exact environment. This is the gold standard for reproducibility that "works on my machine" can never achieve.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Why ML reproducibility is uniquely hard
You used Docker briefly to deploy FlightWise (W4); this week you understand it deeply as the tool that solves ML's hardest reproducibility problem: the *environment*. Reproducibility in ML is harder than in regular software, not because ML engineers are careless, but because ML training depends on a long list of things that are easy to forget to version: the exact Python environment, the random seeds, the **GPU driver and CUDA library versions**, the preprocessing order, the precise dataset slice. Any one of these differing between machines can change your results or break training entirely, the infamous "it trains on my machine but not on the server." **Docker** solves the environment piece comprehensively: everything your training needs, Python, CUDA, every package, environment variables, is declared in a Dockerfile, frozen into an image, and reproducible on any compatible machine.

## What Docker freezes, and why it matters for ML
A **container** packages your application *with its entire environment* into a single image that runs identically anywhere Docker runs, and for ML this is transformative because the environment is so fragile. The classic ML reproducibility nightmare is the **CUDA/driver stack**: deep learning depends on specific versions of CUDA libraries that must match your GPU driver and your PyTorch build, and getting this combination right is notoriously painful, a model that trains fine with one CUDA version can fail or behave differently with another. Docker freezes that entire stack, the CUDA libraries, the exact PyTorch version, every dependency, into the image, so "works in this container" means "works identically on any machine that can run the container," GPU stack and all. This is why ML teams ship training and serving in containers: it eliminates the environment as a source of irreproducibility and "works on my machine" failures, which in ML is one of the biggest sources of wasted time.

## The Dockerfile is your lab notebook
The week's framing, "Dockerfile as a lab notebook," captures the deeper value: a Dockerfile is a precise, executable record of exactly what environment your work requires, the modern equivalent of a scientist's lab notebook documenting their exact setup so an experiment can be reproduced. Where a lab notebook *describes* the conditions, a Dockerfile *recreates* them, run it and you get the identical environment, byte for byte. This makes the Dockerfile a first-class reproducibility artifact, versioned in your repo alongside the code, so the environment is no longer tribal knowledge ("you need CUDA 11.8 and these exact package versions") but executable, versioned code. You will learn Docker's fundamentals (images, layers, caching), multi-stage builds, volumes for data, docker-compose for local development, and how all of it serves reproducibility, completing the infrastructure phase's mission to make every part of ML a versioned, reproducible artifact.

## Where this fits
This week closes the ML Infrastructure phase by making the *environment* reproducible, the last and trickiest piece, joining versioned experiments (W13), scalable training (W14), and versioned data and pipelines (W15) so that *everything* about your ML, code, data, model, workflow, and now environment, is reproducible. It is the foundation for the Model Serving phase ahead, where you deploy models that must run reliably in production environments. Today's orientation: ML reproducibility is uniquely hard because of fragile environment dependencies (especially the CUDA/GPU stack), and Docker solves it by freezing the entire environment into a reproducible image defined by a Dockerfile. Tomorrow you learn Docker's fundamentals properly.

items.title: Docker fundamentals
items.body:
## Docker fundamentals: images, layers, containers
Three concepts are the whole foundation of Docker. An **image** is a frozen, complete environment (the OS libraries, Python, your packages, your code), built once and runnable anywhere. A **container** is a running instance of an image (you can run many containers from one image). And you build an image from a **Dockerfile**, a recipe of instructions:
```dockerfile
FROM pytorch/pytorch:2.1.0-cuda11.8-cudnn8-runtime   # base: PyTorch + CUDA, pre-built
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt                  # install dependencies (a layer)
COPY . .                                             # copy your code (a layer)
CMD ["python", "train.py"]                            # what runs by default
```
`FROM` picks a base image, and for ML this is usually an *official PyTorch or CUDA image* that already has the painful GPU stack set up correctly, so you build on a working foundation instead of assembling CUDA by hand. Each subsequent instruction adds to the image.

## Layers and caching: why build order matters
The key mechanism that makes Docker practical for iterative ML work is **layers and caching**. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a **layer**, and Docker **caches** layers: if the first five instructions have not changed since the last build, Docker reuses their cached layers and rebuilds only from the first *changed* instruction onward. This is exactly the pipeline-caching idea from last week, applied to image builds, and it is what makes developing with Docker fast rather than agonising (rebuilding from scratch every time would take many minutes). But it only helps if you **order the Dockerfile correctly**, and this is the single most important Docker skill: put the things that change *rarely* early and the things that change *often* late. Notice the example copies `requirements.txt` and installs dependencies *before* copying your code:
```text
GOOD order:  install deps (changes rarely) -> copy code (changes often)
  edit your code -> only the cheap "copy code" layer rebuilds; the slow "install deps" layer is CACHED
BAD order:   copy code -> install deps
  edit any code -> the slow dependency install re-runs every single time
```
Getting this ordering right, slow/stable steps first, fast/changing steps last, is the difference between a 5-second rebuild and a 5-minute one on every code change.

## Why containers are the reproducibility guarantee
The deeper reason Docker matters is that the image is a *complete, self-contained, frozen environment*, which is the strongest reproducibility guarantee available. Because the image bundles everything, the exact OS libraries, CUDA, Python, every package version, your code, there is nothing left to vary between machines: the same image runs the same way on your laptop, a teammate's machine, a cloud GPU server, and production, because they are all running the *identical* frozen environment, not "the same environment, hopefully." This eliminates the entire class of "works on my machine" failures that plague ML, where a different CUDA version or an un-pinned dependency silently changes behaviour. It also makes the environment *portable* (ship the image, run it anywhere) and *versioned* (images are tagged, so you can run last month's exact environment). For ML specifically, where the environment is both fragile and decisive for reproducibility, this guarantee is worth enormous effort, and Docker provides it almost for free once you understand images, layers, and caching. The Dockerfile, committed to your repo, becomes the executable, versioned definition of "the environment this works in," which is the lab-notebook promise made real.

## Where this fits
You understand Docker's fundamentals: images (frozen environments) built from Dockerfiles (recipes of cached layers) and run as containers, with the crucial skill of ordering instructions stable-first/changing-last so caching makes rebuilds fast. And you see why the self-contained image is the strongest reproducibility guarantee, eliminating "works on my machine." Tomorrow you learn multi-stage builds, which make ML images smaller and cleaner.

items.title: Multi-stage builds
items.body:
## The problem: ML images get huge
ML Docker images tend to be *enormous*, several gigabytes, because building a model needs a lot: compilers, build tools, large libraries, dataset-processing dependencies, much of which is needed only to *build* or *train*, not to *run* the final model. A bloated image is slow to build, slow to push and pull, slow to deploy, and carries unnecessary attack surface. **Multi-stage builds** solve this by using multiple `FROM` stages in one Dockerfile: a "builder" stage with all the heavy build tooling, and a lean "final" stage that copies *only* the finished artifacts it needs from the builder, leaving the bulk behind.
```dockerfile
FROM pytorch/pytorch:...  AS builder      # heavy: compilers, build deps
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt   # build everything here

FROM pytorch/pytorch:...-runtime           # lean final stage
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local   # copy ONLY what's needed
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "serve.py"]                  # the final image lacks the build bloat
```

## Why this makes images smaller and better
The idea behind multi-stage builds is that *build-time* needs and *run-time* needs are different, and the final image should contain only the latter. The builder stage can be as heavy as it must be, full of compilers, build dependencies, and intermediate files, because it is thrown away; only the artifacts you explicitly `COPY --from=builder` into the final stage survive, so the shipped image contains just the runtime essentials and your trained model, not the toolchain that produced them. The benefits are concrete and compounding: a **smaller image** is faster to push to a registry, faster to pull onto a server, faster to start (less to load), and cheaper to store; it has a **smaller attack surface** (fewer installed tools means fewer vulnerabilities, a security win that matters in production); and it is **cleaner** (the running container is not cluttered with build-time cruft). For ML, where images are already large from the deep-learning libraries, multi-stage builds are often the difference between a manageable image and an unwieldy multi-gigabyte one, and they are standard practice for any image headed to production.

## The principle: separate building from running
Multi-stage builds express a principle that recurs across software and is worth internalising: **separate the build environment from the runtime environment, and ship only what you need to run.** This is the same instinct as the "feature extractor plus head" separation in CNNs or the "build the model, then serve the model" split, the thing you *make* and the thing you *run* are different, and conflating them produces bloat and fragility. In Docker it means the final image is a minimal, purpose-built runtime, not a copy of your entire development setup. It pairs naturally with the layer-ordering discipline from yesterday (cache the slow stable steps) and good `.dockerignore` hygiene (do not copy data, git history, or caches into the image), all in service of images that are small, fast, secure, and reproducible. The mature stance is that a production image should contain the *minimum* needed to run, the runtime libraries, your code, the model, and nothing else, because every extra megabyte is slower deployment, more storage, and more attack surface, and multi-stage builds are the primary tool for achieving that minimalism without sacrificing the heavy tooling you need at build time. Lean images are not a nicety; they are part of operating ML reliably and securely at scale.

## Where this fits
You understand multi-stage builds: separate heavy builder stages from a lean final stage that copies only runtime artifacts, producing smaller, faster, more secure images, the standard practice for production ML containers. This expresses the principle of separating build from runtime and shipping only what you need. Tomorrow you handle how containers access data and persist outputs: volumes and bind mounts.

items.title: Volume mounts and bind mounts
items.body:
## Getting data in and results out of containers
A container is isolated by design, its filesystem is frozen in the image and disappears when the container stops, which raises an immediate ML problem: your *data* is too big to bake into the image, and your *outputs* (trained models, logs) would vanish when the container exits. **Volumes** and **bind mounts** solve this by connecting storage *outside* the container to a path *inside* it, so the container can read external data and write persistent results:
```text
bind mount:  mount a HOST directory into the container
  docker run -v /host/data:/app/data ...        # container sees host's /data at /app/data
  docker run -v /host/models:/app/models ...     # writes here persist on the host

volume:      Docker-managed persistent storage (better for production data)
  docker run -v mydata:/app/data ...
```

## Bind mounts vs volumes: when to use each
The two mechanisms serve different needs, and knowing which to reach for is the practical skill:
- **Bind mounts** map a specific *host directory* into the container, so the container directly sees files on your machine. They are ideal for **development**: mount your code directory in, and you can edit code on the host and have it immediately reflected in the running container without rebuilding the image, a fast iteration loop. They are also how you feed in a local dataset and pull out results during development.
- **Volumes** are storage that *Docker manages*, decoupled from any specific host path. They are preferred for **persistent data in production** because they are portable, managed by Docker, and not tied to your particular machine's directory layout, so they work cleanly across environments.
The rule of thumb: bind mounts for development (direct access to your host's code and data), volumes for production persistence (Docker-managed, portable). Either way, the point is the same, keep large data and important outputs *outside* the ephemeral container, connected via a mount.

## The principle: separate the (immutable) environment from the (mutable) data
The deeper idea volumes and mounts teach is a clean and important separation: **the container image is immutable and reproducible (the environment and code), while data and outputs are mutable and live outside it (mounted in).** This separation is exactly right for ML and reinforces the whole phase. The *image* stays a frozen, versioned, reproducible artifact, you do not bake a 50GB dataset or your changing model outputs into it, which would make it huge and tie a specific environment to specific data. Instead the image is the reproducible *environment*, and the *data* is versioned separately (by DVC, from W15) and mounted in at runtime, so you can run the same immutable image on different data versions, or persist outputs without altering the image. This composes beautifully with the rest of your infrastructure: DVC versions the data, Docker versions the environment, and mounts connect them at runtime, each handling what it is best at. It also keeps the reproducibility story clean, "this exact image, run on this exact DVC data version, produced this model" is a complete, reproducible statement precisely because the environment (image) and the data (mount) are versioned independently and combined explicitly. Conflating them, baking data into images, would break both the image's reusability and the data's independent versioning. Keeping the immutable environment and the mutable data separate, joined by mounts, is the architecture that makes containerised ML both reproducible and practical.

## Where this fits
You understand volumes and bind mounts: connecting external storage into isolated containers, bind mounts for development (live host code/data) and volumes for production persistence, keeping large data and outputs outside the ephemeral container. This expresses the key separation of immutable environment (image) from mutable data (mounted, DVC-versioned). Tomorrow you orchestrate multi-container local development with docker-compose.

items.title: docker-compose for local development
items.body:
## Multi-container setups: docker-compose
Real ML systems are rarely one container, training might need a database, serving might need a model server plus a cache plus a monitoring tool, and running several containers by hand (starting each, wiring up their networking, passing the right settings) is tedious and error-prone. **docker-compose** solves this: you declare your whole multi-container setup in one `docker-compose.yml` file, and a single command starts everything, correctly networked together:
```yaml
services:
  trainer:
    build: .
    volumes: ["./data:/app/data"]
  mlflow:
    image: ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow
    ports: ["5000:5000"]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
# `docker compose up`  -> starts all three, networked so they can talk by name
```
One file, one command, and your entire local stack, trainer, experiment tracker, database, comes up consistently every time.

## Why compose is the right tool for local development
docker-compose's sweet spot is **local development and testing of multi-service systems**, and it earns that role for concrete reasons. It makes the whole environment **reproducible and shareable**: the `docker-compose.yml` is versioned in your repo, so a teammate clones it and runs `docker compose up` to get the *identical* multi-container setup, no "install Postgres, then set up MLflow, then configure the networking" tribal-knowledge onboarding, the entire stack is declared as code (the workflow-as-code principle from W15, applied to your local environment). It handles the **networking** automatically (services can reach each other by name, `trainer` can talk to `mlflow` and `db` without you wiring up IPs), which is otherwise fiddly. And it gives a clean **lifecycle**: `up` to start everything, `down` to tear it all down cleanly, so you can spin your full dev environment up and down at will without residue. For developing an ML system that has multiple moving parts, this turns a painful manual setup into a single declarative file and one command.

## Compose for development, orchestrators for production scale
The important judgement is knowing compose's boundary: it is excellent for **local development and small single-machine deployments**, and it is *not* the tool for large-scale production orchestration, that is where Kubernetes (and the ML orchestrators from W15) take over. The distinction matters so you reach for the right tool: docker-compose runs your containers on *one machine* with simple coordination, perfect for developing and testing your ML system locally with all its services, or running a modest deployment; **Kubernetes** orchestrates containers across *many machines* at production scale, handling auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, and the operational demands of serving real traffic, which is overkill (and significant operational burden) for local development. So the practical path is to use docker-compose to develop and test your multi-container ML system locally, where its simplicity and reproducibility shine, and graduate to Kubernetes only when you need production-scale orchestration across a cluster, the same don't-over-engineer judgement from the orchestrators lesson, applied to containers. Recognising that compose and Kubernetes solve the *same shape* of problem (run and coordinate multiple containers) at *different scales* (one machine vs a cluster) lets you choose deliberately, and for most of your development work, compose is exactly right and Kubernetes would be a heavy distraction. Use the simple tool until the scale genuinely demands the complex one.

## Where this fits
You understand docker-compose: declaring a multi-container ML stack in one versioned file that starts with a single command, fully networked, ideal for reproducible local development and small deployments, while Kubernetes handles production-scale cluster orchestration. This completes your container tooling. Tomorrow you bring the week together around its central theme, full ML reproducibility, before shipping.

items.title: Reproducibility
items.body:
## Reproducibility: pulling the whole thread together
This lesson steps back to the theme of the entire week and much of the phase: **full ML reproducibility**, the ability to recreate any result exactly, and Docker's place as the piece that completes it. Recall *why* ML reproducibility is uniquely hard, it depends on many fragile, easily-forgotten things: the Python environment, the random seeds, the GPU driver and CUDA versions, the preprocessing order, the exact dataset slice, the model code. Reproducing a result requires controlling *all* of them, and missing any one breaks it. The phase has built a tool for each: experiment tracking and seeding (W13) pin the config, seeds, and metrics; DVC (W15) pins the data; workflow-as-code (W15) pins the pipeline; and Docker (this week) pins the *environment*, the Python, CUDA, and dependency stack that is the hardest piece to control any other way.

## The complete reproducibility stack
Putting it together, full ML reproducibility is achieved when *every* input to a result is a versioned, pinned artifact, and you can now name the complete stack:
```text
to reproduce a result EXACTLY, version ALL of:
  code         -> git commit
  data         -> DVC version
  environment  -> Docker image (Python, CUDA, all deps)   <-- this week
  config+seed  -> experiment tracker (W13)
  pipeline     -> workflow as code (W15)
```
When all five are pinned, "reproduce this model" has a complete, executable answer: check out this git commit, `dvc pull` this data version, run this Docker image, with this config and seed, through this pipeline, and you get the identical result, on any machine, any time. This is the difference between a result you *hope* you can reproduce and one you *know* you can, and it is exactly what production ML, scientific rigour, regulatory audits, and reliable collaboration require. Docker is the keystone because the environment, especially the CUDA/GPU stack, is the piece most likely to silently differ between machines and the hardest to pin without containerisation, so freezing it into an image is what makes the *whole* reproducibility chain solid rather than mostly-solid.

## Why this is the heart of ML engineering
The deepest takeaway, fitting for the final content lesson of the infrastructure phase, is that **reproducibility is not a nice-to-have, it is the foundation that makes ML an engineering discipline rather than a craft.** A result you cannot reproduce is a result you cannot trust, debug, improve, audit, or deploy with confidence, it is a lucky outcome, not an engineered one. Everything that makes ML *reliable* depends on reproducibility: you can only improve a model methodically if you can reproduce the baseline; you can only debug a regression if you can reproduce both versions; you can only deploy responsibly if you can recreate exactly what you are deploying; you can only collaborate if teammates can reproduce each other's work; and you can only satisfy an audit if you can show precisely how a model was built. This is why the entire ML Infrastructure phase, experiment tracking, GPU training, pipelines, and containers, ultimately serves reproducibility, and why it is the boundary between data science (a model proven possible) and ML engineering (a model reliably and repeatably produced). Docker completing the environment piece is what makes the reproducibility *total*: with code, data, environment, config, and pipeline all versioned, nothing about your result is left to chance or to the vagaries of a particular machine. Mastering this, treating reproducibility as the non-negotiable foundation and having the tools to achieve it completely, is what makes you an ML engineer rather than someone who can train models.

## Where this fits
You understand full ML reproducibility as the unifying goal of the infrastructure phase: version *everything*, code (git), data (DVC), environment (Docker), config and seed (tracking), and pipeline (workflow-as-code), with Docker as the keystone that pins the fragile environment, making results exactly recreatable on any machine. This is the foundation of ML as engineering. Tomorrow you assemble the fully reproducible, containerised setup and ship it, closing the phase.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a fully reproducible, containerised ML project
You assemble the week (and the phase) into a completely reproducible ML project, where the environment is frozen and every input is versioned:
- a **Dockerfile** (well-ordered layers, multi-stage for a lean image) freezing the exact environment, Python, CUDA, all dependencies, so training runs identically anywhere.
- **data mounted in** (DVC-versioned, from W15) rather than baked into the image, keeping environment and data versioned separately.
- ideally a **docker-compose** setup bringing up the training/tracking stack with one command.
- the complete reproducibility chain documented: code (git), data (DVC), environment (Docker), config and seed (tracking), pipeline (workflow-as-code).
```bash
docker build -t flightwise-train .
docker run --gpus all -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data flightwise-train
git add Dockerfile docker-compose.yml && git commit -m "Containerized, fully reproducible ML environment"
```

## The deliverable is "runs identically anywhere"
The proof of this project is that *anyone, on any compatible machine, can reproduce your training exactly* by building and running your container, no environment setup, no CUDA-version debugging, no "it works on my machine." Demonstrate the complete chain: a stranger clones the repo, `dvc pull`s the data, `docker build`s the image, and `docker run`s it to get your exact model, with the Dockerfile guaranteeing the identical Python/CUDA/dependency stack regardless of what is installed on their machine. This is the strongest form of reproducibility, the environment itself is frozen and shippable, and it is exactly what production ML and serious collaboration require. Showing a containerised, fully-versioned ML project, where the README documents how code, data, environment, config, and pipeline are *all* pinned, is a standout demonstration of ML-engineering maturity, because it proves you can make ML *reliably reproducible*, which is the discipline most ML work conspicuously lacks.

## What the ML Infrastructure phase delivered
Step back across the whole phase: you have transformed how ML work is done, from ad-hoc notebooks to engineered, reproducible systems. You can track and reproduce every experiment (W13), train efficiently and at scale on GPUs (W14), version data and automate workflows as code (W15), and freeze the entire environment for total reproducibility (W16). The unifying achievement is **complete reproducibility**: every input to every result, code, data, environment, config, pipeline, is now a versioned, pinned artifact, so any result is exactly recreatable, debuggable, improvable, and auditable. This is the infrastructure that turns model-building into ML *engineering*, and it is the foundation the production phases stand on, you cannot serve, monitor, or continuously improve models you cannot reliably reproduce. You have built the systems backbone of professional ML.

## Where this fits
You shipped a fully containerised, reproducible ML project and completed the ML Infrastructure phase: tracked experiments, scalable GPU training, versioned data and pipelines, and a frozen reproducible environment, the complete systems backbone of professional ML. Next comes the **Model Serving phase** (W17-20), where you take models into production for real users: serving them as reliable endpoints, monitoring them for the silent failures unique to ML, A/B testing them with statistical rigour, and building recommender systems, turning your reproducible models into live products that serve predictions at scale.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You want to train your model in a Docker container with GPU access. What additional configuration is required beyond a standard CPU container? You need the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed on the host machine. The docker run command requires the --gpus flag: `docker run --gpus all my-training-image`. Inside the container, CUDA-capable GPU is available to PyTorch. The base image must match the CUDA version installed on the host: if the host runs CUDA 12.1, the base image should be pytorch/pytorch:2.1.0-cuda12.1-cudnn8-runtime or similar. Version mismatch between host CUDA driver and container CUDA toolkit is the most common GPU-in-Docker failure.

weeks.title: Model Serving, From Notebook to Production Endpoint
weeks.context:
Training a model is the beginning. Getting it to serve predictions reliably to real users, at low latency, at scale, with good error handling, is the engineering challenge that occupies most of a production ML engineer's time. Model serving involves architectural decisions that are not visible in the model itself: synchronous versus asynchronous, single-instance versus distributed, online versus batch, request-level versus session-level state.

FastAPI is the current standard for Python model serving. It is async-first, has automatic OpenAPI documentation, validates request and response schemas through Pydantic, and handles concurrent requests efficiently. For most model serving use cases, one model, moderate traffic, FastAPI with uvicorn is the correct starting point. The limitations appear when your model is slow (long GPU inference) or when you need dynamic batching.

Dynamic batching is the technique that makes GPU model serving efficient. GPUs are parallelism engines, they perform far more efficiently on batched inputs than on one sample at a time. But users send requests one at a time. Dynamic batching collects concurrent requests into a batch, runs one GPU forward pass for the entire batch, and returns results to each requester. At low traffic, a short time window collects whatever concurrent requests arrive. At high traffic, the window fills instantly with a full batch. The net effect: GPU utilisation is much higher and cost per request is much lower.

Serving patterns: synchronous request/response is the simplest, client sends a request, waits, gets a response. Appropriate when inference latency is under 1 second and users can tolerate waiting. Async with queue is better for slow inference or batch processing, client submits a job and gets a job ID, then polls or receives a webhook when complete. Batch inference runs at scheduled times on accumulated data without any real-time user interaction.

TorchServe (for PyTorch) and Triton Inference Server (for multiple frameworks including ONNX) are production serving frameworks that handle dynamic batching, GPU memory management, model versioning, and health checks at a level that hand-built FastAPI servers cannot match at scale. Knowing when you have outgrown FastAPI and need one of these frameworks is an important judgment call.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Training is the beginning; serving is the job
You trained FlightWise and wrapped it in a simple Flask API back in W4. This week you take serving seriously, because getting a model to serve predictions *reliably*, at low latency, at scale, with proper error handling, is the engineering challenge that occupies most of a production ML engineer's time. Training a model is the start; making it a dependable production service is where the real work lives, and it involves architectural decisions that are invisible in the model itself: synchronous versus asynchronous, single-instance versus distributed, online versus batch, request-level versus session state. This week you make those decisions deliberately and learn the tools, FastAPI, dynamic batching, TensorRT, Triton, that turn a model into a production-grade endpoint.

## Serving is architecture, not just a wrapper
The key shift this week is recognising that *how* you serve a model is an architecture decision with real trade-offs, not an afterthought. The same trained model can be served in fundamentally different ways depending on the requirements, and choosing wrong makes the service slow, expensive, or unreliable:
- **Synchronous vs asynchronous:** does the caller wait for the prediction (a real-time API), or submit a job and collect the result later (heavy batch work)?
- **Online vs batch:** do you predict one request at a time as it arrives (online, low-latency), or score millions of records in a scheduled run (batch, high-throughput)?
- **Single-instance vs distributed:** does one server handle the load, or do you need many behind a load balancer?
These are the same kinds of serving decisions you met in the AI-engineering deployment week, now for your own trained models, and the right answer depends on the latency, throughput, and cost the use case demands.

## FastAPI: the right starting point
**FastAPI** is the current standard for Python model serving, and for good reason: it is **async-first** (handles concurrent requests efficiently), generates **automatic API documentation** (OpenAPI), and **validates requests and responses** through Pydantic schemas, the same structured-validation idea from the AI-engineering track, here guarding your model's inputs. For most serving needs, one model, moderate traffic, FastAPI with the uvicorn server is the correct, simple starting point, a notable upgrade from the bare Flask of W4 (async, validation, and docs built in). Its limits appear in two situations the rest of the week addresses: when your model is **slow** (long GPU inference) and when you need **dynamic batching** to use a GPU efficiently. Knowing FastAPI is the right default, *and* knowing exactly when you outgrow it, is the practical framing of the week: start simple, escalate to specialised serving infrastructure only when the model's speed or scale demands it.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Model Serving phase** (W17-20), where your reproducible, trained models become live products: served reliably (this week), monitored for silent failure (W18), A/B tested for real-world value (W19), and extended to personalisation (W20). It builds directly on the W4 Flask deployment and the AI-engineering deployment week, now with the depth that production model serving demands. Today's orientation: serving is an architecture decision (sync/async, online/batch, single/distributed), FastAPI is the right default, and you escalate to specialised tools when the model is slow or needs batching. Tomorrow you go deeper into those serving patterns.

items.title: Serving patterns
items.body:
## The serving patterns, and choosing among them
"Serve the model" is not one thing, it is a choice among patterns, and the right one depends on your latency, throughput, and cost needs. The main axes:
- **Online (real-time) serving:** predict one request at a time, as it arrives, with low latency, an API that answers in milliseconds. This is FlightWise's `/predict`: a user (or service) needs an answer *now*. Optimised for latency.
- **Batch (offline) serving:** score a large set of records all at once, on a schedule, where no one is waiting on any single prediction, recompute every user's churn score nightly. Optimised for throughput, not latency.
- **Streaming serving:** predict on a continuous stream of incoming events, between online and batch, for things like real-time fraud scoring on a transaction feed.
The same model can serve in any of these modes; the pattern is dictated by *how the predictions are consumed*, not by the model.

## Match the pattern to how predictions are used
The skill is reading the use case to pick the pattern, because choosing wrong wastes resources or fails requirements. If predictions are needed **interactively** (a user clicks and waits, a service calls and blocks), you need **online** serving with low latency, and batch would be useless (the answer arrives too late). If predictions are needed for **many records with no urgency** (a nightly report, pre-computing recommendations for every user), **batch** is far more efficient, processing everything in one optimised run is cheaper and simpler than a stream of online calls, and online serving would be wasteful overkill. A revealing pattern is **pre-computation**: if the set of possible inputs is known and bounded (recommendations for your existing users), you can *batch*-compute all the predictions ahead of time and serve them from a fast lookup, getting online-latency responses without online-inference cost, the right architecture is sometimes to not infer at request time at all. So you ask: who consumes the prediction, how fast do they need it, and how many are there? The answers point to online (interactive, low-latency), batch (bulk, no urgency), or pre-computed (bounded inputs, served from a cache), and getting this right is a bigger lever on cost and latency than any model optimisation.

## State: another dimension of the decision
A further serving distinction is **request-level vs session-level state**, which shapes the architecture. Most model serving is **stateless**: each request is independent and carries everything the model needs (FlightWise's `/predict` takes a flight and returns a probability, remembering nothing), which is the simplest and most scalable design, because any server can handle any request and you scale by just adding servers (the stateless property from W4). Some applications need **state across requests**, a session, a sequence of user actions, accumulated context, which is more complex because the serving system must track and route state (which server holds this session's data?), constraining how you scale. The guidance is to **prefer stateless serving** wherever possible, because it is dramatically simpler to scale and operate, and to introduce session state only when the use case genuinely requires remembering across requests, the same simplicity discipline from the rest of the track. Recognising the serving pattern (online/batch/streaming, stateless/stateful) that fits your use case is the foundational architecture decision of model serving, and it is mostly determined by *how predictions are consumed*, which is why you analyse that before writing any serving code.

## Where this fits
You understand the serving patterns, online (interactive, low-latency), batch (bulk, efficient), streaming, and pre-computation, plus the stateless-vs-stateful choice, and that the right pattern is dictated by how predictions are consumed. This architecture decision is the biggest lever on serving cost and latency. Tomorrow you handle the specific challenge of serving *slow* models efficiently on a GPU: dynamic batching.

items.title: Dynamic batching
items.body:
## The GPU serving problem, and dynamic batching
Serving a deep learning model on a GPU has a specific efficiency problem: a GPU is fast *per batch* but processing requests **one at a time** wastes most of its parallel capacity, you fire up thousands of cores to process a single input, then again for the next. Yet online serving receives requests one at a time, as users send them. **Dynamic batching** resolves this tension: the serving system *waits a few milliseconds* to collect several incoming requests, groups them into a batch, runs them through the GPU together in one efficient pass, and returns each result to its caller.
```text
without batching:  req1 -> GPU (wasteful), req2 -> GPU (wasteful), ...
dynamic batching:  collect req1,req2,req3 for ~5ms -> ONE GPU pass -> split results back
```
This gives near-batch GPU efficiency while still serving individual online requests.

## The latency/throughput trade it manages
Dynamic batching is a deliberate trade between **latency and throughput**, and understanding it is the point. Waiting to collect a batch adds a *small latency* to each request (it waits up to a few milliseconds for batch-mates), but it dramatically increases *throughput* (the GPU does far more useful work per unit time by processing many requests at once) and thus lowers cost per prediction (you need fewer GPUs for the same load). You tune two knobs, the **maximum wait time** (how long to wait for a batch to fill) and the **maximum batch size**, to balance the trade for your needs: a latency-critical service uses a tiny wait window (sacrificing some batching efficiency for speed), while a throughput-oriented service waits longer to fill bigger batches. The key insight is that dynamic batching lets you get *most* of the GPU's batch efficiency in an *online* (one-request-at-a-time) setting, which would otherwise be impossible, at the cost of a few milliseconds of added latency, usually a great trade for GPU-served models. This is exactly the kind of serving-infrastructure technique FastAPI alone does not give you, and it is why GPU model serving often needs the specialised servers (Triton) you will meet this week.

## Why this matters: GPU serving economics
The reason dynamic batching is a headline technique is **cost**: GPUs are expensive (the W14 lesson), and serving them inefficiently, one request per GPU pass, means you need many more GPUs (and dollars) to handle your traffic than you should. Dynamic batching can increase a GPU's serving throughput several-fold, directly cutting the number of GPUs and the cost to serve a given load, the inference-side echo of the training-efficiency-is-cost-efficiency lesson from W14. It is the single most important technique for making GPU model serving economical, which is why production deep-learning serving systems are built around it. For a CPU-served classical model (like FlightWise's XGBoost), batching matters less, but for any GPU-served deep model at real traffic, dynamic batching is often the difference between an affordable service and a ruinously expensive one. Recognising when you need it, GPU model, online serving, meaningful traffic, and that it is a latency-for-throughput trade you tune, is the practical takeaway, and it sets up *why* the specialised inference servers (Triton, next) exist: they provide dynamic batching and more as production infrastructure, so you do not hand-build it.

## Where this fits
You understand dynamic batching: collecting incoming requests into batches for efficient GPU inference, trading a few milliseconds of latency for several-fold throughput (and thus much lower cost per prediction), tuned via wait-time and batch-size. This is the core technique that makes GPU serving economical. Tomorrow you learn TensorRT, which speeds up the model itself before it even reaches the serving layer.
