items.title: TensorRT
items.body:
## Making the model itself faster: TensorRT
Dynamic batching makes the *serving* efficient; **TensorRT** (and similar tools) makes the *model* itself faster, by optimising it for inference on the target hardware. A model as trained is not optimised for fast prediction, it carries training-time overhead and runs operations naively, and inference-optimisation compilers like TensorRT (NVIDIA's, for their GPUs) rewrite the model into a highly efficient form for serving:
```text
trained model  --TensorRT optimisation-->  optimised inference engine
  (techniques: layer fusion, precision reduction, kernel selection for the GPU)
  -> often 2-5x faster inference, same predictions
```
You convert the trained model once, and the optimised version serves predictions substantially faster, with no change to *what* it predicts, just *how fast*.

## What inference optimisation actually does
TensorRT's speedups come from a handful of techniques that are worth understanding because they reveal where inference time goes:
- **Layer fusion:** combine several consecutive operations into one (a convolution, a bias add, and an activation become a single fused operation), reducing overhead and memory traffic between steps.
- **Precision reduction:** run the model in lower precision (float16 or int8 via quantization) where accuracy permits, the mixed-precision and quantization ideas from W14, now applied to serving, fewer bits means faster math and less memory.
- **Kernel auto-tuning:** pick the fastest GPU implementation of each operation for the specific GPU you are serving on, since the optimal way to run an operation depends on the hardware.
- **Graph optimisation:** prune and simplify the computation graph, removing operations only needed for training.
The result is the *same model* (same architecture, same learned weights, essentially the same predictions) running 2-5x faster at inference, which directly cuts latency and serving cost.

## The trade-offs, and when it is worth it
Inference optimisation is powerful but not free, and knowing the trade-offs keeps you from over-applying it. The costs: it adds a **conversion/compilation step** to your deployment pipeline (you must convert and validate the optimised model), it can be **hardware-specific** (a TensorRT engine is tuned for a particular GPU, reducing portability), and aggressive **precision reduction** (especially int8 quantization) can slightly change predictions, so you must *validate* that the optimised model still meets your accuracy bar, the same "confirm quality survived the optimisation" discipline from the AI-engineering cost week. So you reach for inference optimisation when serving performance genuinely matters, high traffic where latency or GPU cost is significant, real-time requirements a naive model cannot meet, and you skip it when the model is already fast enough or traffic is low (the conversion complexity is not worth it for a low-traffic service). The judgement mirrors the whole track's efficiency theme: optimise the model for inference when the latency or cost payoff justifies the added pipeline complexity and the validation effort, and confirm the optimised model still predicts correctly. For a heavily-served GPU model, TensorRT-style optimisation combined with dynamic batching can cut serving cost dramatically; for a lightly-used one, it is premature optimisation.

## Where this fits
You understand inference optimisation with TensorRT: rewriting the trained model (layer fusion, precision reduction, hardware-tuned kernels) for 2-5x faster serving with validated-equivalent predictions, worth it when latency or GPU cost matters, at the cost of a hardware-specific conversion step. Model-level speedup (TensorRT) plus serving-level batching (dynamic batching) are the two halves of efficient GPU serving. Tomorrow you meet Triton, the production server that provides both as infrastructure.

items.title: Triton Inference Server
items.body:
## Production inference at scale: Triton Inference Server
FastAPI is great for serving one model at moderate traffic, but production model serving at scale, multiple models, GPU efficiency, dynamic batching, high throughput, needs purpose-built infrastructure, and **Triton Inference Server** (NVIDIA's) is the standard. Triton is a dedicated model-serving system that provides, as built-in infrastructure, the things you would otherwise hand-build: **dynamic batching** (D3), support for **multiple models and frameworks** at once (PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX, TensorRT models side by side), **GPU sharing** across models, **concurrent model execution**, and serving metrics. You give Triton your models and a config, and it handles efficient, scalable inference serving for you.

## Why a specialised server beats rolling your own
The reason production teams use Triton (or similar, like TorchServe, KServe) rather than scaling up a FastAPI app is that efficient serving infrastructure is a large, hard problem you do not want to rebuild. Hand-rolling dynamic batching, multi-model management, GPU memory sharing, concurrent execution, and serving metrics in your own FastAPI code would be a major engineering project, error-prone and never as optimised as the dedicated server, exactly the build-vs-buy logic that favoured experiment trackers and orchestrators earlier. Triton provides all of it, tuned and battle-tested, so you focus on *your* models and the serving config rather than reinventing the serving engine. It also unifies serving: instead of a separate bespoke service per model, one Triton instance serves many models across frameworks efficiently on shared GPUs, which is both simpler to operate and far more cost-efficient at scale (better GPU utilisation across models). For a production ML platform serving many models to real traffic, this consolidation and efficiency is the whole point.

## When to use FastAPI and when to reach for Triton
The practical judgement, consistent with the track's simplicity discipline, is to match the serving infrastructure to your actual scale and not over-build. **FastAPI (with uvicorn)** is the right choice for a single model, moderate traffic, CPU or simple GPU inference, it is simple, fast to set up, and entirely sufficient, and reaching for Triton here would be heavy over-engineering (Triton is itself infrastructure to learn and operate). **Triton** (or another dedicated inference server) becomes the right choice when you genuinely need its capabilities: serving *multiple* models, needing dynamic batching for GPU efficiency at meaningful traffic, requiring high throughput, or running a serving *platform* for a team. The signal to graduate is concrete, your FastAPI serving is hitting GPU-efficiency or throughput limits, or you are managing many models, exactly the limits this week's D1 said FastAPI would eventually hit (slow models, dynamic batching needs). So the path is: start with FastAPI, and adopt Triton when the model speed, the GPU economics, or the number of models genuinely demands production serving infrastructure. Knowing both, and *when* to move from one to the other, is the serving-architecture judgement, the same start-simple-escalate-deliberately pattern as orchestrators (W15) and Kubernetes (W16).

## Where this fits
You understand Triton Inference Server: production infrastructure providing dynamic batching, multi-model multi-framework serving, and GPU efficiency out of the box, adopted when scale (multiple models, GPU throughput, high traffic) outgrows FastAPI's simple sufficiency. You can now choose serving infrastructure deliberately by scale. Tomorrow you handle a serving challenge that affects everyone: cold starts versus warm instances.

items.title: Cold start vs warm
items.body:
## The cold-start problem in serving
A serving challenge that bites in practice: the **cold start**. When a serving instance starts up, or scales from zero, or handles its first request after being idle, the *first* request is slow, because the system must do expensive one-time work before it can predict: load the (possibly large) model into memory, initialise the framework and GPU context, warm up caches. After that, subsequent requests on the now-**warm** instance are fast. The gap can be dramatic, the first request takes seconds (loading a multi-gigabyte model onto a GPU) while warm requests take milliseconds, and that slow first request is a real user experience and reliability problem.
```text
cold instance:  request 1 -> [load model, init GPU, warm caches] -> SLOW (seconds)
warm instance:  request 2,3,4... -> model already loaded -> FAST (ms)
```

## Why cold starts happen and where they hurt
Cold starts are the price of *not* keeping a serving instance permanently loaded and ready, and they appear precisely in the architectures that save money by scaling down. **Serverless / scale-to-zero** serving (which you saw cause cold starts in the AI-engineering deployment week, and which keeps FORGE's own Neon database cold) shuts instances down when idle to avoid paying for them, so the next request after idle pays the cold-start penalty, you traded standing cost for first-request latency. **Autoscaling** has the same issue: when traffic spikes and the system spins up *new* instances to handle it, those new instances are cold, so exactly when load is highest, some requests hit slow cold starts. And **large models** make it worse, the bigger the model, the longer it takes to load, so the cold-start penalty grows with model size. So cold starts hurt most in cost-optimised, elastic deployments serving large models, which is a very common production situation, and ignoring them means a fraction of users (the unlucky ones hitting a cold instance) get a badly slow experience.

## Managing the cold-start vs cost trade
The fix is a deliberate trade between **always-warm cost** and **cold-start latency**, and the techniques span that trade:
- **Keep instances warm:** run a minimum number of always-on instances (never scale fully to zero), or send periodic "keep-alive" requests so an instance never goes idle long enough to go cold. This eliminates cold starts at the cost of paying for idle capacity, the right choice when latency matters and you can afford the standing cost.
- **Pre-warm proactively:** when autoscaling, spin up and *warm* new instances (load the model, run a dummy inference) *before* routing real traffic to them, so users never hit a cold one.
- **Speed up the cold start itself:** make the model load faster (smaller/optimised model, faster storage for the model file, lazy-loading only what is needed), shrinking the penalty even when it occurs.
- **Accept it where appropriate:** for a low-traffic internal tool, scale-to-zero with occasional cold starts is a fine cost saving, the penalty rarely hits and rarely matters.
The judgement is to decide how much cold-start latency your use case can tolerate and spend accordingly, always-warm for latency-critical user-facing services, scale-to-zero for cost-sensitive low-traffic ones, and pre-warming for spiky autoscaled traffic. This is the same standing-cost-vs-responsiveness trade that runs through serving, made concrete, and handling it well is what keeps a cost-efficient elastic deployment from delivering occasional terrible latency.

## Where this fits
You understand the cold-start problem: the slow first request when an instance loads the model and initialises, hitting scale-to-zero, autoscaling, and large-model deployments, and the techniques to manage the cold-start-vs-cost trade (keep warm, pre-warm, speed the load, or accept it). Tomorrow you assemble the week's serving knowledge and ship a production-grade endpoint.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a production-grade serving endpoint
You assemble the week into a serving setup that is a real upgrade from the W4 Flask API, demonstrating production serving judgement:
- a **FastAPI** service (async, Pydantic-validated, auto-documented) serving your model, with the serving pattern (online/batch) chosen for the use case.
- the **efficiency techniques** appropriate to your model, dynamic batching and/or inference optimisation (TensorRT) if it is a GPU deep model, or noting why they are unnecessary for a CPU classical model.
- **cold-start handling** suited to the deployment (keep-warm vs accept), and proper error handling and validation.
- a clear write-up of the serving *architecture decisions* and why.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Production model serving: FastAPI + serving-architecture decisions"
git push
```

## The deliverable is architecture judgement, not just a running endpoint
What makes this project demonstrate production-serving competence is the *reasoning* about architecture, not just that the endpoint responds. The strongest artifact explains the decisions: "this is online serving because predictions are interactive; it is stateless so it scales horizontally; I used FastAPI because it is a single model at moderate traffic (Triton would be over-engineering here); the model is CPU XGBoost so dynamic batching is unnecessary; I keep one instance warm because the use case is latency-sensitive." That decision narrative, showing you chose each serving pattern and tool *deliberately* for the requirements, and knew when *not* to reach for the heavy infrastructure, is exactly the production judgement that distinguishes an ML engineer from someone who can only wrap a model in a Flask route. Pair it with the operational basics, validation, error handling, latency measurement, to show the endpoint is genuinely production-ready, reliable and observable, not just functional.

## What model serving established
Step back: you can now take a trained model and serve it as a real production service, with the architecture judgement that the job actually requires. You understand serving as a *decision* (online/batch/streaming, stateless/stateful, FastAPI/Triton) driven by how predictions are consumed and at what scale; you know the efficiency techniques (dynamic batching, inference optimisation) that make GPU serving economical and *when* they are warranted; and you can handle the operational realities (cold starts, validation, error handling) that separate a robust endpoint from a fragile one. This is the engineering that occupies most of a production ML engineer's time, and it turns your reproducible trained models (from the infrastructure phase) into live, reliable products. But a deployed model is not done, it starts degrading the moment it launches, which is exactly what next week addresses.

## Where this fits
You shipped a production-grade serving endpoint with deliberate architecture decisions, the upgrade from a toy Flask wrapper to real serving engineering. Your model is now live and reliable. Next week confronts the uncomfortable truth that a deployed model *degrades over time as the world changes*, **model monitoring**: detecting the silent failures, input drift, concept drift, that quietly destroy a model's accuracy in production, before your users discover them for you.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You serve your PyTorch model with FastAPI. Each request takes 200ms (model inference). Your server receives 20 requests per second. What happens? Each request takes 200ms and FastAPI with a single uvicorn worker processes them sequentially in the async loop. At 20 requests/second, the server falls 4 seconds behind every second, requests queue and latency grows without bound. Fix: run with multiple workers: `uvicorn main:app --workers 4`. Four workers can handle 4 * (1000/200) = 20 requests/second in parallel. Alternatively, move inference to a background thread with asyncio.to_thread() so the async event loop is not blocked. For GPU inference, add dynamic batching.

weeks.title: Model Monitoring, Catching the Silent Failures
weeks.context:
A model deployed to production starts degrading the moment it launches. Not because of bugs, but because the world changes. The distribution of inputs shifts. The relationship between inputs and outputs changes. The ground truth labels collected over time reveal that the model's predictions are no longer accurate. Without monitoring, this degradation is invisible until it is severe enough for users or stakeholders to notice.

Input drift is the most common failure mode. The distribution of the model's input features at deployment time differs from the distribution at training time. A model trained on pre-pandemic flight patterns fails on post-pandemic patterns. A loan model trained on 2019 economic conditions fails in 2022. Detecting drift requires statistical tests: KL divergence, Wasserstein distance, Population Stability Index (PSI), or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Each measures, in different ways, how different the current input distribution is from the reference (training) distribution.

Concept drift is more dangerous and harder to detect. The input distribution may be stable, but the relationship between inputs and outputs has changed. Routes that were on-time reliably now have delays due to new airline policies. High-income customers who were low default risk now exhibit different patterns. Detecting concept drift requires ground truth labels, you must wait for the outcome (flight actually late or not, loan actually defaulted or not) and compare model predictions against it. This delay between prediction and ground truth is often significant (weeks or months).

Performance drift is what you see in metrics: accuracy, ROC AUC, precision, recall falling over time on the slice of predictions where you have ground truth labels. It is a symptom of either input drift or concept drift. Measuring it requires a continuous labelling pipeline, some mechanism to collect ground truth for recent predictions.

Evidently AI is a Python library for monitoring ML models. It produces HTML reports and JSON metrics for data drift, concept drift, and model performance. It can be integrated into batch monitoring jobs (run nightly on recent predictions) or into real-time serving (compute statistics per request window).

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## A deployed model starts dying the day it launches
Here is the uncomfortable truth of production ML: a model deployed to production **begins degrading the moment it launches**, not because of bugs in your code, but because the world changes. The distribution of inputs shifts, the relationship between inputs and outputs changes, and over time the model's predictions drift away from accurate. A model is a snapshot of patterns at training time, and reality keeps moving after that snapshot. **Model monitoring** is the practice of detecting this degradation, and the central, dangerous fact is that without monitoring it is **invisible**: the model keeps returning confident predictions, the service shows all green, and nothing errors, while the predictions quietly get worse, until they are bad enough that users or stakeholders notice, which is the worst possible way to find out.

## Why models degrade: the world is not stationary
Unlike ordinary software, which keeps working until you change it, a model can break with *no change to your code at all*, because its correctness depends on the world matching its training data, and the world does not hold still. Two forces drive the decay, and naming them frames the week:
- **Input drift (data drift):** the distribution of the *inputs* the model sees in production diverges from what it trained on. A delay model trained on pre-pandemic flight patterns meets post-pandemic patterns; a loan model trained on 2019 economic conditions meets 2022. The inputs moved.
- **Concept drift:** the *relationship* between inputs and outputs changes, the same input now implies a different outcome, because the underlying dynamics shifted (a feature that predicted default in 2019 means something different after an economic shock).
Both silently erode accuracy, and both are about the world moving away from the training snapshot, which is why a model that was accurate at launch is not guaranteed to stay accurate, and why "we deployed it and it works" is a statement with an expiry date.

## The defining property: these are silent failures
The reason monitoring is a whole discipline, and the theme of the week, is that model degradation is a **silent failure**, you saw this danger for pipelines in W15, and it is even sharper for deployed models. A crashed server alerts you; a model whose accuracy slid from 0.85 to 0.65 does not, it returns predictions in exactly the same format, just wronger, with no error, no exception, no signal in any standard system monitor. The model looks healthy by every conventional measure (it is up, it is fast, it responds) while being increasingly *wrong*, and that gap between "looks fine" and "is fine" is precisely what model monitoring exists to close. So monitoring a model is not like monitoring a web service (is it up? is it fast?), it is about watching whether the model is still *correct*, by tracking the inputs (for drift), the predictions, and, where possible, the eventual ground truth, so that degradation raises an alarm long before users feel it. This week you build that, the early-warning system for the silent decay that every production model eventually suffers.

## Where this fits
This week is the second pillar of the Model Serving phase: W17 got the model serving reliably; W18 keeps it *correct* over time by detecting the drift and degradation that silently erode it. It mirrors the AI-engineering observability and drift lessons (W18 there), now for classical/deep ML models with the statistical drift tests they require. Today's orientation: deployed models degrade as the world shifts (input drift, concept drift), and this degradation is a *silent failure* invisible to normal monitoring, so you need ML-specific monitoring to catch it. Tomorrow you catalogue exactly what can go wrong in production.

items.title: What can go wrong in production
items.body:
## A catalogue of production failures
To monitor a model well, you need to know what you are watching *for*, so today you catalogue the ways a production model fails, beyond the obvious code bugs. The major categories:
- **Input drift (data drift):** production inputs no longer match the training distribution, the model is being asked about a world it was not trained on.
- **Concept drift:** the input-output relationship itself changed (tomorrow's topic).
- **Data quality breaks:** an upstream change feeds the model malformed inputs, a feature that is suddenly all nulls, a unit change (dollars to cents), a reordered or renamed column, so the model receives garbage and predicts garbage.
- **Outliers / out-of-distribution inputs:** individual requests unlike anything in training, where the model's prediction is unreliable but confident (D5's topic).
- **Performance/serving issues:** latency creep, errors, the operational problems from W17.
Each fails differently and needs a different signal, and most of them, crucially, produce *no error*, just wrong or unreliable predictions.

## Watching inputs when you cannot watch accuracy
The deep challenge of model monitoring, and the reason input drift gets so much attention, is that **you usually cannot measure accuracy in real time**, because the ground truth arrives late or never. When FlightWise predicts a flight will be late, you only learn if it *was* late hours later (and you may never systematically collect it); a loan default model's "correct answer" arrives months or years after the prediction. So you cannot just watch live accuracy the way you watched test AUC, the labels are not there yet. This is why monitoring leans heavily on **input drift detection**: you *can* observe the inputs immediately (you see every request), so you watch whether the input distribution is shifting away from training, as a *leading indicator* of likely accuracy loss. The logic is that if the inputs now look very different from what the model trained on, its predictions are probably less reliable, even before you can confirm it with labels. Watching the inputs is your early warning precisely because the inputs are observable now and the accuracy is not, which makes input drift the workhorse of model monitoring.

## Detecting drift: statistical distance tests
Input drift detection is fundamentally a statistical question, how different is the current input distribution from the training distribution?, and several tests measure that distance, each in its own way:
- **Population Stability Index (PSI):** a widely-used industry measure of how much a feature's distribution has shifted, with rule-of-thumb thresholds (small = stable, large = significant drift).
- **Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test:** a statistical test of whether two samples come from the same distribution, good for continuous features.
- **KL divergence / Wasserstein distance:** information-theoretic and distributional measures of how far one distribution is from another.
You compute these per feature, comparing the recent production data against the training (reference) distribution, and a feature whose drift metric crosses a threshold flags as "this input has shifted meaningfully." The practical workflow is to track these drift scores continuously and **alert** when they exceed thresholds, so a meaningful shift in the inputs raises a flag (and prompts investigation or retraining) *before* the accuracy loss becomes visible to users. You do not need to derive the statistics; you need to understand that these tests quantify "how different is now from training," that you run them per feature on a schedule, and that a crossed threshold is an early warning of likely degradation.

## Where this fits
You can catalogue what goes wrong in production, input drift, concept drift, data-quality breaks, outliers, serving issues, and you understand why monitoring leans on *input drift detection* (you can observe inputs immediately but not accuracy), using statistical distance tests (PSI, KS, KL/Wasserstein) per feature to flag meaningful shifts as an early warning. Tomorrow you handle the subtler, harder failure: concept drift, where the relationship itself changes.

items.title: Concept drift
items.body:
## The harder failure: concept drift
Input drift is the inputs changing; **concept drift** is the *relationship* between inputs and outputs changing, the same input now implies a different outcome, and it is both subtler and harder to detect. The model learned a mapping from features to target at training time, and concept drift means that mapping is no longer correct, even if the inputs look the same. An example makes it concrete: a fraud model learns the patterns of fraud in 2022, but fraudsters change tactics in 2023, so the *same* transaction features now indicate something different, the concept of "what fraud looks like" drifted, and the model's learned relationship is stale. Crucially, this can happen with *no* input drift at all: the inputs may be distributed exactly as before, but what they *mean* for the target has shifted, so input-drift detection alone misses it.

## Why concept drift is hard to catch
Concept drift is the most insidious failure because detecting it usually *requires the ground truth*, which is exactly what you often lack in real time. Input drift you can spot by watching inputs alone (D2); but to know the input-output *relationship* changed, you generally need to compare predictions against actual outcomes, and see that the model is now wrong more often, which means you need labels. When labels arrive late or never, concept drift can progress undetected for a long time, the model is quietly making the *wrong* prediction for inputs that look perfectly normal, with no input-drift signal to warn you. This is why concept drift is the failure that most often surprises teams: nothing in the inputs looked wrong, yet the model decayed, because the world's rules changed underneath it. The forms it takes also vary, gradual drift (slow change over months), sudden drift (an abrupt shift, like a pandemic or a regulation change), or recurring/seasonal drift, and each calls for different vigilance.

## Detecting and responding to concept drift
Given that concept drift usually needs labels, the strategies for catching it center on *getting* ground truth, even partially, and watching the model's real correctness:
- **Track performance as labels arrive:** even when ground truth is delayed, it usually *does* come eventually (you learn whether the flight was late, whether the loan defaulted), so you log predictions and, when the true outcome arrives, compute the model's actual accuracy over time, a falling accuracy trend is the direct signal of concept drift (or any degradation).
- **Collect labels deliberately:** sample some predictions for human labelling, or set up feedback loops (user corrections, downstream outcomes), to get a steady, if partial, stream of ground truth for monitoring.
- **Watch proxy signals:** monitor the *prediction* distribution and downstream business metrics, if the model's output distribution shifts oddly or a business KPI tied to the model degrades, it can hint at concept drift even before labels confirm it.
The fundamental response to confirmed drift, input or concept, is **retraining** on recent data, so the model relearns the current patterns and relationships, which is why monitoring and retraining are partners: monitoring detects when the model has gone stale, and retraining refreshes it. The mature stance is to assume *every* production model will eventually drift and to build the monitoring (input drift as early warning, accuracy tracking as confirmation) and the retraining process *before* the degradation bites, rather than discovering staleness from angry users. Concept drift, the silent change in what the data means, is the deepest reason a model is never "done" once deployed.

## Where this fits
You understand concept drift, the input-output relationship changing so the model's learned mapping goes stale, which can occur with no input drift and usually requires ground truth to detect, caught by tracking actual accuracy as labels arrive and by proxy signals, and addressed by retraining. Tomorrow you handle the metrics you *can* watch in real time to monitor a live model: online metrics.

items.title: Online metrics
items.body:
## What you can measure right now: online metrics
Accuracy needs labels you may not have yet, but plenty *is* observable in real time, and **online metrics** are the signals you monitor continuously on a live model. They split into what you can always see and what you can sometimes confirm:
- **Always observable (no labels needed):** the **input distributions** (for drift, D2), the **prediction distribution** (what fraction of flights is the model calling "late" this week, and is that shifting?), and **operational metrics** (latency, throughput, error rate, the W17 serving health).
- **Observable when labels arrive:** the actual **accuracy / AUC / precision-recall** over time, computed as ground truth comes in (D3), the direct correctness signal, just delayed.
A monitoring dashboard tracks all of these together, so you watch the model's inputs, outputs, performance, and (eventually) its real accuracy, the same multi-signal observability you built for AI systems in the AI-engineering track, now for a deployed ML model.

## The prediction distribution is a free early warning
A particularly useful and often-overlooked signal is the **prediction distribution**, what the model is actually outputting, because it needs no labels and reacts immediately. If FlightWise normally predicts ~18% of flights late and that suddenly jumps to 40% or drops to 5%, *something changed*, the inputs drifted, a data-quality break fed it garbage, or the world shifted, and you see it instantly in the output distribution, before any ground truth could confirm a problem. This makes the prediction distribution a cheap, real-time early-warning signal that complements input-drift detection: input drift watches what goes *in*, prediction monitoring watches what comes *out*, and a sharp change in either is a flag to investigate. It also catches failures that input monitoring might miss, a subtle data-quality break that shifts predictions even if each input feature looks individually plausible. Watching the prediction distribution is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort monitoring practices, and it works on every model regardless of label availability.

## Building the monitoring system: track, threshold, alert
The practical shape of online monitoring is the same as any good observability, **track, threshold, alert**, applied to these ML-specific signals. You continuously *track* the input distributions, prediction distribution, operational metrics, and (as labels arrive) accuracy, into a monitoring store and dashboard; you set *thresholds* for what counts as a meaningful problem (drift score above X, prediction rate shifted by more than Y, accuracy below the bar); and you *alert* when a threshold is crossed so a human investigates, rather than discovering the issue from users. The discipline that makes this work is the same as the AI-engineering drift lesson: tune thresholds so alerts mean something real (a flood of false alarms gets muted, and a muted monitor protects nothing), and watch *trends* over time, not single noisy points. The goal is an early-warning system where a drifting model, a data-quality break, or a falling accuracy *raises a flag while it is still small*, giving you time to investigate and retrain before users are affected. This turns the silent failure into a visible, alertable signal, which is the entire point of monitoring, and it is the operational backbone that keeps a deployed model trustworthy over its life, not just at launch.

## Where this fits
You understand online metrics: continuously tracking input distributions, the prediction distribution (a free, immediate early warning), operational health, and delayed accuracy, with a track-threshold-alert system tuned so flags mean real problems. This is the real-time early-warning backbone of model monitoring. Tomorrow you handle a per-request concern: detecting individual outlier inputs at serving time.

items.title: Outlier detection at serving time
items.body:
## Per-request safety: outlier detection at serving time
Distribution monitoring (D2-D4) watches the *aggregate* of inputs over time; **outlier detection at serving time** watches *each individual request* as it arrives, flagging inputs that are unlike anything the model trained on. This matters because a single out-of-distribution (OOD) input, a request whose feature values fall far outside the training data, gets a prediction from the model that is **unreliable but delivered with full confidence**, and acting on that confident-but-meaningless prediction can cause real harm. So at serving time, you check whether each incoming request is "normal" (within the realm the model can handle) or an outlier the model is not qualified to predict on, and you handle the outliers specially rather than blindly trusting the prediction.

## Why a confident prediction on a weird input is dangerous
The core danger here is that a model **always returns a prediction**, no matter how strange the input, and it does not know what it does not know. Feed FlightWise a flight with a departure hour of 47 or a route it never saw, and it will not error, it will compute *some* probability and return it with the same apparent confidence as any normal prediction, even though that prediction is essentially meaningless because the input is outside its training experience. This is the model-level version of the "garbage in, confident garbage out" problem, and it is dangerous precisely because there is no signal in the prediction itself that it should not be trusted. The W17 input validation catches *malformed* inputs (wrong type, out of range), but outlier detection catches a subtler case: inputs that are *valid* but *unusual*, each feature individually plausible, yet the combination unlike anything in training, where the model is technically able to predict but should not be relied upon. Detecting these OOD inputs at serving time, and treating their predictions with appropriate caution, is how you stop the model from confidently advising on cases it has no basis to judge.

## How to detect and handle outliers
Detecting OOD inputs reuses the unsupervised tools from W7, now at serving time per request, and handling them is a judgement about risk:
- **Detect:** score each input's "unusualness," distance from the training data's typical region (a point far from all training clusters), reconstruction error from an autoencoder trained on normal data, or a model's own uncertainty estimate. A high score flags an outlier.
- **Handle:** decide what to do with a flagged outlier rather than silently trusting it, depending on the stakes. Options include **flagging the prediction as low-confidence** (so downstream systems or users know to treat it cautiously), **routing to a human** for review (in high-stakes domains like lending or medicine, an unusual case deserves a person), **falling back** to a safe default, or at minimum **logging** the outlier for investigation (a stream of outliers may itself signal drift). 
The principle is that the model should be *honest about its limits*: when it receives an input it has no real basis to judge, the system should recognise that and respond accordingly, not launder an unreliable guess as a confident prediction. This is especially vital in high-stakes applications, where a confident wrong prediction on a weird case can cause real damage, and it complements the aggregate drift monitoring: drift detection catches the *population* shifting, outlier detection catches the *individual* request that is off, and together they keep the model from being trusted where it should not be. Knowing what the model does not know is one of the most important and underappreciated parts of trustworthy ML serving.

## Where this fits
You understand outlier/OOD detection at serving time: flagging individual inputs unlike the training data, because the model returns confident-but-unreliable predictions on them, and handling flagged cases with low-confidence labels, human review, fallbacks, or logging, so the model is honest about its limits. This per-request safety complements aggregate drift monitoring. Tomorrow you survey the tools that provide model monitoring as infrastructure.

items.title: Tools
items.body:
## Monitoring as infrastructure: the tools
You could build model monitoring from scratch, computing drift statistics, tracking prediction distributions, storing and dashboarding metrics, but as with experiment tracking and serving, dedicated **tools** provide it as infrastructure so you do not reinvent it. The model-monitoring landscape includes purpose-built platforms (Evidently, Arize, WhyLabs, Fiddler, NannyML, and others) that specialise in exactly this: they compute drift metrics (PSI, KS, and the rest) for you, track input and prediction distributions, monitor performance as labels arrive, detect outliers, and provide dashboards and alerting tuned for ML monitoring. You instrument your serving to send it the inputs, predictions, and (when available) labels, and the platform handles the drift detection, visualisation, and alerting.

## What the dedicated tools give you
The value of a specialised model-monitoring tool over hand-rolled scripts or generic dashboards is that it understands ML monitoring's specific shape, the same "AI-native" advantage you saw with observability platforms in AI-engineering. A model-monitoring platform knows what *drift* is and computes the right statistical tests per feature out of the box; it knows to compare production against a *reference* (training) distribution; it handles the *delayed-label* reality (tracking predictions now, joining accuracy later when ground truth arrives); it detects outliers; and it renders ML-meaningful views (per-feature drift, prediction distribution over time, accuracy as labels come in) rather than generic metric graphs. Building all of this correctly, especially the statistical drift tests and the delayed-label accuracy tracking, is real work the tools have already done and battle-tested, so you instrument and configure rather than implement. This lets you get robust monitoring quickly and focus on *responding* to what it shows (investigating drift, deciding when to retrain) rather than on building the detection machinery.

## Choosing and using monitoring tools wisely
The familiar judgement applies: match the tooling to your needs, and integrate monitoring into your broader ML operations rather than treating it as a bolt-on. For a learning project or a simple model, a lightweight open-source library (like Evidently) that generates drift reports may be entirely sufficient, and a full enterprise monitoring platform would be over-engineering. For a production model serving real users with real consequences, a more complete monitoring platform with continuous tracking, alerting, and dashboards earns its place, especially in regulated or high-stakes domains where undetected drift is costly. The hosted-vs-self-hosted choice recurs here too (send your production data to a vendor, or self-host for privacy), the same trade you have navigated throughout. The most important point is that monitoring must **connect to action**: a drift alert is only valuable if it triggers a response, investigation, and retraining, so you wire monitoring into your operations (alerts reach the right people, drift triggers a retraining workflow) rather than letting it produce dashboards nobody acts on. Monitoring tooling provides the detection; your job is to ensure the detected problems lead to fixes, closing the loop from "the model is drifting" to "the model has been retrained," which is what actually keeps a production model accurate over its life.

## Where this fits
You know the model-monitoring tool landscape (Evidently, Arize, WhyLabs, and others) and what dedicated platforms give you, ML-aware drift detection, delayed-label accuracy tracking, outlier detection, and alerting as infrastructure, chosen by scale and wired to *action* (alerts that trigger investigation and retraining). Tomorrow you assemble the week's monitoring into a complete system and ship it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a monitored production model
You assemble the week into a monitoring system around a deployed model (FlightWise from W17), turning the silent failure into a visible, alertable one:
- **input drift detection** (statistical tests per feature against the training reference) as the leading early-warning signal.
- **online metrics**: tracked input and prediction distributions, operational health, and accuracy computed as labels arrive (concept-drift detection).
- **outlier detection at serving time** flagging OOD requests for cautious handling.
- a **dashboard and alerting** (via a tool like Evidently, or built) that flags meaningful drift or degradation, wired to a retraining response.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Model monitoring: drift detection + online metrics + outlier flags + alerting"
git push
```

## The deliverable: catching degradation before users do
The proof of this project is that it **catches a degradation before users would**, which you can demonstrate directly: feed the monitored model a batch of *drifted* inputs (post-pandemic flight patterns, or simply data shifted from the training distribution) and show the monitoring system *detecting and alerting* on the drift, the input-drift score crossing threshold, the prediction distribution shifting, an alert firing, all before any accuracy report could confirm the problem. That demonstration, the silent failure made loud, the model's degradation surfaced as an early warning rather than discovered from angry users, is the entire point of the week and the strongest thing the project can show. Pair it with the full monitoring view (input distributions, prediction distribution, accuracy-over-time as labels arrive, outlier flags) and the alert-to-retraining loop, to prove you built not just detection but a complete early-warning system wired to action. Most ML projects deploy a model and forget it; demonstrating that you *monitor* it for the inevitable drift is exactly the production maturity that distinguishes an ML engineer.

## What model monitoring established
Step back: you have confronted and solved production ML's defining problem, that a deployed model silently degrades as the world changes, and most monitoring misses it because the model looks healthy while being wrong. You can now detect input drift (the observable early warning), concept drift (the relationship changing, caught via accuracy as labels arrive), data-quality breaks, and outlier inputs, with online metrics, the prediction distribution as a free signal, and tooling wired to alerts and retraining. The deep lesson is that **deploying a model is not the finish line, it is the start of an ongoing responsibility** to keep it correct, because correctness decays, and only monitoring makes that decay visible in time to act. This is what makes a model a *maintained* production asset rather than a deployed-and-forgotten liability, and it is the operational core of trustworthy ML.

## Where this fits
You shipped a monitored model that catches drift and degradation before users do, turning the silent failure into an early warning wired to retraining, the operational core of keeping a production model correct over time. With models served (W17) and monitored (W18), next week asks the sharper question: when you have a new model that scores better offline, is it *actually* better for real users? **A/B testing models** gives you statistically valid evidence about which model produces better real-world outcomes, because, as you will see, offline metrics alone cannot tell you.

weeks.title: A/B Testing Models, Statistical Truth, Production Edition
weeks.context:
You cannot trust offline metrics to predict online performance. A model that achieves 0.79 ROC AUC on a held-out test set may or may not be better than the production model for real users making real decisions. The gap between offline and online performance comes from distribution shift, user behaviour differences, and the fact that your test set was sampled from the same distribution as your training data. A/B testing is the method that generates statistically valid evidence about which model produces better outcomes in the real world.

The question of statistical significance in model A/B testing is more complex than in web A/B testing. Web A/B tests measure binary outcomes (clicked or not). Model A/B tests often measure continuous outcomes (quality score, revenue per prediction) or rare events (default rate, fraud rate). The statistical tests differ, the sample sizes required differ, and the time to significance differs.

Sample size calculation comes before the experiment. You need to specify: the minimum detectable effect (MDE, the smallest improvement worth detecting), the current baseline metric value, the desired statistical power (typically 80%), and the significance level (typically 5%). With these inputs, a power analysis tells you how many samples you need per variant. Running an underpowered experiment produces inconclusive results even if your hypothesis is correct.

Guardrail metrics are the metrics you monitor to prevent harm. If your primary metric is ROC AUC but you are also tracking user complaint rate, you need a guardrail that stops the experiment if complaint rate increases significantly. This prevents a scenario where one model scores better on your primary metric but harms users in a way you did not anticipate.

The challenge specific to model A/B testing: model updates from the provider mid-experiment. If you are using GPT-4o and OpenAI silently updates the model version during your 4-week experiment, both variant A (old prompt) and variant B (new prompt) might be affected differently. Log the model version with every prediction so you can account for this in analysis.

concept_check.q: You want to detect a 3% relative improvement in ROC AUC (from 0.74 to 0.762). Your daily traffic is 500 scored requests. How long will the experiment need to run? Use a power calculator: with alpha=0?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You run a two-week A/B test. At day 5, the results look conclusive: variant B is significantly better (p=0.02). Your manager wants to ship B immediately. Should you? No. Looking at the results before?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You run the A/B test and get p=0.07. Is there no difference between the models? A p-value of 0.07 means you cannot confidently reject the null hypothesis at the 5% significance level. It does not mean?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## The gap between offline metrics and real value
You have trusted held-out test metrics all track, and they are essential, but this week confronts their limit: **you cannot trust offline metrics to predict online performance.** A model that scores 0.79 AUC on a held-out test set *may or may not* be better, for real users making real decisions, than the model currently in production. The gap is real and it has causes: your test set was sampled from the *same* distribution as your training data (so it may not reflect live conditions), real users behave differently than the historical data suggests, and distribution shift between when you trained and when you serve means offline performance does not cleanly transfer to online outcomes. **A/B testing** is the method that generates statistically valid evidence about which model produces better outcomes *in the real world*, with actual users, which is the only verdict that ultimately matters.

## Why a better offline score is not a better model
It is worth sitting with *why* a higher test AUC does not guarantee a better production model, because it is counterintuitive after weeks of optimising offline metrics. First, the **test set is not the world**: it was drawn from your training distribution, so a model that scores higher on it may simply fit that historical distribution better, not the live one users actually generate. Second, **the metric is not the outcome**: AUC measures ranking quality, but the *business* cares about real outcomes, revenue, user satisfaction, decisions made, and a model with higher AUC might not move those, or might even hurt them (a "better" recommender by offline accuracy might show less diverse items and reduce engagement). Third, **users react to the model**: in production the model influences behaviour (people respond to its predictions/recommendations), a feedback loop that no static offline test can capture. So offline metrics are a necessary *filter* (a model that fails offline is not worth deploying) but not a *sufficient* verdict (passing offline does not prove it helps in production). The only way to know if a model genuinely produces better real-world outcomes is to test it on real users, which is A/B testing.

## What A/B testing does
A/B testing answers the real question, "does model B produce better outcomes than model A for real users?", by running a controlled experiment in production: you split live traffic, send some users to the current model (A, the control) and some to the new model (B, the treatment), and compare the *real outcomes* they produce, with **statistical rigour** to know whether any difference is genuine or just noise. The output is statistically valid evidence, "model B increased the outcome we care about by X%, and we are confident this is real, not chance", which is exactly the basis on which you should decide to roll out a new model. This week you learn to do it properly: why offline is not enough (the foundation), the statistical tests that make the comparison valid, Bayesian alternatives, experimentation platforms, and holdouts. The throughline is that **deciding to deploy a new model is an experiment, and it deserves the rigour of one**, not a leap of faith from an offline score.

## Where this fits
This week is the third pillar of the Model Serving phase: W17 served the model, W18 monitored it, and W19 answers whether a *new* model is genuinely better for real users before you roll it out. It connects to the AI-engineering A/B-testing-for-AI lesson, now with the statistical depth ML model comparison requires. Today's orientation: offline metrics cannot prove a model is better in the real world, so A/B testing generates statistically valid evidence from real users, and deploying a new model deserves to be treated as the experiment it is. Tomorrow you go deeper into exactly why offline metrics fall short.

days.title: Why offline metrics aren't enough
days.summary: Focus: Why offline metrics aren't enough

items.title: Why offline metrics aren't enough
items.body:
## Why offline metrics are necessary but not sufficient
Today examines the central premise carefully, because getting it right shapes how you ship every model. Offline metrics (test-set AUC, accuracy) are **necessary**: a model that performs poorly on held-out data is not worth deploying, so offline evaluation is the essential first filter, do not A/B test a model that fails offline. But they are **not sufficient** to conclude a model is better in production, and naming the specific reasons makes the gap concrete:
- **Distribution shift:** your test set came from the training distribution, but production data can differ (the drift from W18), so offline performance may not hold live.
- **Metric-outcome mismatch:** offline metrics measure statistical quality (AUC, accuracy), but the business cares about *outcomes* (revenue, retention, decisions), and these do not move in lockstep, a model can win on AUC and lose on the outcome that matters.
- **User feedback effects:** in production, users *react* to the model's outputs, creating dynamics no static test captures.
So offline metrics tell you a model is *plausible*, not that it is *better* for real users.

## The offline-online gap is the heart of it
The single most important idea this week is the **offline-online gap**: the difference between how a model performs on your test set and how it performs in production, and the recognition that this gap can be large, even inverting which model is "better." A model with higher test AUC can produce *worse* business outcomes, and a model with slightly lower offline metrics can perform *better* live, because offline and online measure different things under different conditions. Concrete example: two recommenders, model B has higher offline accuracy (it predicts what users already clicked), but model A, with slightly lower offline accuracy, recommends more diverse items that users actually engage with more, so A wins online despite losing offline. The offline metric rewarded predicting the past; the online outcome rewarded driving future engagement, and they disagreed. Internalising that this gap exists, and can be large enough to reverse your decision, is what motivates A/B testing: you cannot close the gap by thinking harder about offline metrics; you can only measure across it by testing in production. The teams that ship confidently are the ones who treat the offline score as a hypothesis and the A/B test as the verdict.

## What this means for how you ship models
The practical consequence is a two-stage shipping discipline that respects both kinds of evidence. **Offline first, as a filter:** use held-out metrics (and your W13 experiment tracking) to develop, compare, and select candidate models, only the ones that clearly pass offline are worth the cost of a production test. **Online second, as the verdict:** A/B test the offline-winning candidate against the current production model on real users, and let the *online* outcome decide whether to roll it out. This respects that offline evaluation is cheap and fast (so you do most of your iteration there) while online evaluation is the true measure (so the final decision rests on it). It also means you must define, *before* the test, what *online* outcome you are optimising, the real metric (engagement, revenue, decision quality) that the model is meant to improve, not just AUC, so the A/B test measures what actually matters. This is the same "define success measurably before you start" discipline from the AI-engineering capstone, applied to model rollout. The mature ML engineer never deploys a new model on offline metrics alone, nor wastes A/B tests on models that fail offline, but uses offline to filter and online to decide.

## Where this fits
You understand why offline metrics are necessary but not sufficient, distribution shift, metric-outcome mismatch, and user-feedback effects create an offline-online gap that can reverse which model is better, so you filter with offline metrics and decide with online A/B tests against a pre-defined real outcome. Tomorrow you learn the statistical machinery that makes an A/B comparison valid: two-sample tests.

items.title: Two-sample tests
items.body:
## Making the comparison valid: two-sample tests
An A/B test splits users between model A and model B and compares their outcomes, but you cannot just look at "B's average was higher" and declare B the winner, because of **noise**: random variation means B's group could look better by chance even if the models are identical. **Two-sample statistical tests** tell you whether an observed difference between the two groups is *real* (statistically significant) or could easily be random. The test answers: "given the variation in the data, how likely is a difference this big if the two models were actually the same?", and only if that is unlikely do you conclude B is genuinely better.
```text
A (control):   outcomes from users on the current model
B (treatment): outcomes from users on the new model
two-sample test -> is B's difference REAL, or could it be chance?
```

## ML A/B tests are harder than web A/B tests
A crucial point that makes this week non-trivial: model A/B testing is statistically *harder* than the classic web A/B test, and knowing why tells you which test to use. Web A/B tests usually measure a **binary** outcome (clicked or not), with well-known statistics and modest sample-size needs. Model A/B tests often measure **continuous** outcomes (a quality score, revenue per prediction) or **rare events** (default rate, fraud rate), and these change everything:
- **Continuous outcomes** need different tests (comparing *means*, e.g. a t-test, with attention to the variance) than binary ones, and the high variance of quality scores means you need more data to detect a difference.
- **Rare events** (a 1% default rate) need *large* samples to measure reliably, you need many observations to see enough of the rare event to compare rates with confidence, so the test can take a long time to reach a verdict.
So you must match the statistical test to the *kind* of outcome you are measuring (binary, continuous, or rare-event), and recognise that ML outcomes often demand larger samples and longer tests than web experiments, which is a practical constraint on how fast you can validate a model.

## Sample size, significance, and the discipline of honest testing
Two-sample testing comes with disciplines that protect you from fooling yourself, the same rigour as any experiment. **Sample size:** you need enough observations for the test to reliably detect a difference of the size you care about, too few and a real improvement is lost in noise (and a result is meaningless), so you estimate the required sample size *before* running (based on the effect size you want to detect and the outcome's variability) and run until you reach it. **Statistical significance:** you set a threshold (commonly p < 0.05) for how unlikely a chance result must be before you believe the difference is real, and only conclude B wins if the test clears it. And critically, **do not peek and stop early:** repeatedly checking the test and stopping the moment it looks significant dramatically inflates false positives (you will eventually see noise that looks like a win), so you decide the sample size and duration up front and wait for it, rather than calling the test the first time B looks ahead. These disciplines, adequate sample size, a pre-set significance threshold, and no early peeking, are what make an A/B test *valid* rather than a way to rationalise a decision you already wanted, and they are exactly where naive A/B testing goes wrong. The statistical rigour is not pedantry; it is what makes the test's verdict trustworthy.

## Where this fits
You understand two-sample tests for A/B comparison: determining whether a difference between models is real or chance, with the recognition that ML outcomes (continuous, rare-event) are statistically harder than binary web tests and need matched tests and larger samples, plus the disciplines (pre-set sample size, significance threshold, no early peeking) that keep the test honest. Tomorrow you meet a different statistical framework that addresses some of these pain points: Bayesian A/B testing.

items.title: Bayesian A/B testing
items.body:
## A different lens: Bayesian A/B testing
The two-sample (frequentist) approach answers "is this difference statistically significant?" with p-values and fixed sample sizes. **Bayesian A/B testing** reframes the question into one that is often more directly useful: instead of "is the difference significant?", it answers **"what is the probability that B is better than A, and by how much?"** It does this by maintaining probability distributions over each model's true performance and updating them as data arrives, yielding statements like "there is a 95% probability that B is better than A, and the most likely improvement is 3%." For a decision-maker, that is a more natural and actionable answer than a p-value, it speaks directly to the choice you actually face (should I roll out B?).

## Why the Bayesian framing helps in practice
Bayesian A/B testing has practical advantages that matter for model rollout, which is why many modern experimentation platforms use it:
- **Directly interpretable results:** "95% probability B is better, expected lift 3%" is something a stakeholder immediately understands and can act on, where "p = 0.04" requires statistical translation and is famously easy to misinterpret.
- **More graceful with continuous monitoring:** the rigid frequentist "do not peek" rule (D3) exists because repeated checking inflates false positives; Bayesian methods handle ongoing monitoring more naturally, you can update your belief as data flows in and reason about the current probability, which fits the reality of watching an experiment, though you still need discipline not to stop on noise.
- **Incorporates magnitude and uncertainty:** it tells you not just *whether* B is better but *by how much* and *how sure* you are, which supports better decisions (a 0.5% improvement that is "probably real" may not be worth a rollout's risk, while a likely 5% gain is).
- **Handles small samples and priors:** it can incorporate prior knowledge and gives sensible answers even with limited data, degrading gracefully rather than just saying "not significant."

## Frequentist vs Bayesian: not a war, a choice of framing
The honest takeaway is that frequentist (two-sample tests) and Bayesian A/B testing are two valid frameworks answering slightly different questions, and you should understand both rather than dogmatically pick a side. Frequentist testing is the long-standing standard, well-understood, and what many organisations and tools use; its discipline (fixed sample size, significance threshold) is rigorous and widely accepted. Bayesian testing offers more directly interpretable, decision-friendly outputs and handles monitoring and magnitude more naturally, which is why it has grown popular in modern experimentation platforms. In practice you often will not implement either from scratch, the platforms (tomorrow) provide them, but understanding *what each tells you* lets you read and trust their results: a frequentist result says "the difference is unlikely to be chance," a Bayesian result says "here is the probability B is better and by how much." For making a *rollout decision*, the Bayesian framing is frequently more useful because it directly quantifies the decision-relevant question, but the rigour and acceptance of frequentist testing keep it the default in many settings. Knowing both, and that they are complementary lenses on the same underlying question (is B really better?), is the statistical literacy that lets you run and interpret model A/B tests competently. The point is never the framework for its own sake; it is making a *valid, well-founded decision* about whether to roll out a model.

## Where this fits
You understand Bayesian A/B testing as a complementary framework that answers "what is the probability B is better, and by how much?", with more directly interpretable, decision-friendly, monitoring-friendly results than p-values, and you can read both frequentist and Bayesian results to make a sound rollout decision. Tomorrow you see the platforms that provide all this experimentation machinery as infrastructure.

items.title: Experimentation platforms
items.body:
## Experimentation platforms: A/B testing as infrastructure
Running A/B tests properly, splitting traffic correctly, assigning users consistently, collecting outcomes, computing valid statistics, managing many concurrent experiments, is a substantial system, and **experimentation platforms** (in-house ones at big tech companies, and tools/services like Optimizely, GrowthBook, Statsig, LaunchDarkly's experimentation, and others) provide it as infrastructure. A platform handles the machinery: consistent **traffic assignment** (each user reliably gets the same variant), **experiment management** (define, launch, monitor, and stop experiments), correct **statistical analysis** (frequentist or Bayesian, computed properly), and **guardrails** (watching that a variant is not harming key metrics). You define the experiment and the metrics; the platform runs it rigorously.

## What the platform gets right that ad-hoc testing gets wrong
The reason to use a platform rather than hand-rolling A/B tests is that there are many subtle ways to run an experiment *wrong*, and the platform encodes the correct handling of each, exactly the value of dedicated infrastructure seen throughout the track. Consistent assignment: a user must get the *same* variant on every visit (flipping them between A and B mid-experiment corrupts the data), which requires careful, sticky, hashed assignment the platform manages. Correct randomisation: traffic must be split without bias (no systematic difference between groups except the model), which is easy to botch by hand. Proper statistics: the platform applies the right test for the outcome type and guards against the early-peeking and multiple-comparison traps from D3 (running many experiments inflates false positives unless corrected). Guardrail metrics: the platform watches that the new variant is not quietly tanking a critical business metric even if it improves the target one, automatically stopping a harmful experiment. Hand-rolling all of this correctly is hard and error-prone, and a botched A/B test gives a *confidently wrong* answer (worse than no test, because you trust it), so the platform's rigor is exactly what makes the experiment's verdict trustworthy.

## Using platforms well, and the gradual-rollout pattern
The practical guidance is to use an experimentation platform for any serious model A/B testing (do not hand-roll the statistics and assignment for a decision that matters), while matching the tool to your scale, a simple open-source experimentation tool for a small setup, a full platform for an organisation running many experiments. A pattern these platforms enable, and that is the safe way to actually roll out a model, is the **gradual rollout** combined with A/B testing: rather than flipping all traffic to the new model at once, you ramp it up, send 1% of traffic to model B, watch the metrics and guardrails, then 5%, 20%, 50%, and finally 100%, stopping or rolling back instantly if anything degrades. This limits the blast radius of a bad model (only a small fraction of users are affected if B is worse), gathers A/B evidence as you go, and is the standard safe-deployment practice for ML in production (the same canary/gradual-rollout idea from deployment engineering, here driven by experiment results). So the platform does not just measure the A/B test; it operationalises a safe, evidence-driven rollout. The takeaway is that A/B testing and rollout are infrastructure-supported processes, and using that infrastructure (platforms, gradual rollouts, guardrails) is how you ship new models safely and on real evidence, rather than via a risky all-at-once switch justified by an offline score.

## Where this fits
You understand experimentation platforms: infrastructure providing consistent traffic assignment, correct statistics, guardrails, and experiment management, plus the gradual-rollout pattern (ramp traffic 1%-5%-50%-100% with guardrails) that ships new models safely on A/B evidence. Tomorrow you learn holdouts, the technique for measuring the cumulative, long-term value of your models.

items.title: Holdouts
items.body:
## Measuring long-term, cumulative value: holdouts
A/B tests measure a single experiment over a defined window, but some effects only show up over the *long term* and *across many model changes*, and **holdouts** are the technique for measuring those. A holdout is a small group of users **permanently** (or for a long period) kept on a baseline, e.g. the old model, or no personalisation at all, while everyone else gets your continuously-improving models, so by comparing the holdout group against everyone else you measure the *cumulative* value of all your model work over time, not just one experiment's incremental gain.
```text
99% of users:  receive your evolving, improving models (many A/B-tested changes)
1% holdout:    kept on the baseline, long-term
compare them  -> the TOTAL, cumulative value of all your ML work
```

## Why individual A/B tests miss the long-term picture
Holdouts exist because a series of individual A/B tests can each show a small win while *missing or overstating* the true long-term, aggregate impact, and understanding this gap is the insight. Three problems holdouts address: First, **small wins compound or wash out** in ways single tests do not capture, ten experiments each showing +1% might sum to +10%, or might overlap and deliver far less, and only a long-term holdout measures the *actual* cumulative effect of all of them together. Second, **novelty and long-term effects differ from short-term ones**: a model change might boost a metric briefly (users react to novelty) but fade, or conversely build value slowly, and a short A/B test sees only the immediate effect, while a holdout reveals the sustained one. Third, **drift in the baseline**: without a held-out baseline, you lose track of how far you have actually come, the holdout is a stable reference point showing the total distance between "all our ML" and "the baseline." So holdouts answer a question individual A/B tests cannot: *across everything we have shipped, over the long run, how much value has our ML work actually created?*, which is the question leadership and you ultimately care about.

## The cost of holdouts, and using them wisely
Holdouts have a real, honest cost that you weigh deliberately: the holdout users receive a *worse* (baseline) experience, so you are deliberately giving a fraction of users an inferior product to measure your cumulative impact, which has a direct cost in their outcomes (lost revenue, engagement, satisfaction for that group). This is why holdouts are kept *small* (often ~1%) and why the decision to run one balances the measurement value against the cost to those users. You use a holdout when knowing the true cumulative value of your ML matters enough to justify the cost, demonstrating ML's overall business impact, catching whether your stream of "wins" actually adds up, having a stable long-term baseline, and you keep it small and reconsider it periodically. The broader lesson holdouts teach is humility about incremental gains: a parade of positive A/B tests does *not* guarantee large cumulative value, because gains overlap, fade, and sometimes do not aggregate, and the only way to know your real total impact is to hold out a baseline and measure against it. This connects to honest measurement throughout the track, just as you benchmark a model against a naive baseline, you benchmark your *entire body of ML work* against a held-out baseline, to know it genuinely created the value the individual experiments suggested. Holdouts are how mature ML organisations keep themselves honest about whether all the work actually paid off.

## Where this fits
You understand holdouts: a small group kept long-term on a baseline to measure the *cumulative* value of all your ML work, catching the compounding, fading, and overlapping effects that individual A/B tests miss, at the deliberate cost of a worse experience for the holdout group. This keeps you honest about real total impact. Tomorrow you assemble the week's A/B-testing knowledge and ship a model-comparison experiment.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a statistically valid model comparison
You assemble the week into a proper A/B test comparing two models, demonstrating that you can validate a model with real-world evidence, not just offline metrics:
- a clear **online outcome metric** defined *before* the test (the real outcome the model should improve, not just AUC).
- a **controlled split** of traffic (or a simulation of one) between the current model (A) and a new one (B), with consistent assignment.
- **valid statistics**, a two-sample test or Bayesian analysis with adequate sample size, a pre-set significance threshold, and no early peeking, yielding a trustworthy verdict.
- the safe-rollout framing (gradual ramp, guardrails) and an honest read of the result.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Model A/B test: statistically valid online comparison + rollout plan"
git push
```

## The deliverable is an evidence-based rollout decision
What makes this project demonstrate real production-ML judgement is that it produces a **statistically valid decision about whether to ship a model**, the thing offline metrics cannot give you. The strongest artifact tells the full story: "model B scored higher offline (0.81 vs 0.79 AUC), so it passed the filter; in the A/B test on [the real outcome], B improved it by 3% with [statistical significance / 95% probability of being better]; the result is trustworthy because I pre-set the sample size and significance and did not peek; therefore I recommend a gradual rollout with guardrails." That narrative demonstrates the entire week: you know offline is not enough, you defined the real outcome, you ran the comparison with statistical rigour, and you reached an evidence-based rollout decision. Crucially, an honest *negative* result is just as valuable, "B won offline but showed no real improvement (or a regression) online, so I am *not* rolling it out", because it proves you let the evidence decide rather than shipping on an offline score, which is exactly the discipline that prevents deploying models that look better but are not.

## What A/B testing established
Step back: you have learned that the verdict on a model is delivered by *real users in production*, not by a held-out test set, and you can now generate that verdict rigorously. You understand the offline-online gap (why a better test score is not a better model), the statistics that make a comparison valid (two-sample tests, Bayesian analysis, sample size, significance, no peeking), the platforms and gradual-rollout patterns that run experiments safely, and holdouts that measure true cumulative value. The deep lesson is that **deploying a model is an experiment and deserves the rigour of one**: you filter candidates offline, decide between them online with statistical validity, and roll out gradually on the evidence, never on faith in an offline number. This is what separates shipping models that *actually* improve outcomes from shipping models that merely look better, and it is the measurement discipline at the heart of trustworthy production ML.

## Where this fits
You shipped a statistically valid model A/B test that decides rollout on real-world evidence, internalising that a model's true verdict comes from production, not the test set. This completes the measurement side of model serving. Next week closes the Model Serving phase with a different and fascinating problem, **recommender systems**, where the prediction depends not just on the item but on the specific *user*, the personalisation problem behind Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify, which standard classification and regression cannot easily solve.

items.body: You want to detect a 3% relative improvement in ROC AUC (from 0.74 to 0.762). Your daily traffic is 500 scored requests. How long will the experiment need to run? Use a power calculator: with alpha=0.05, power=0.80, baseline=0.74, MDE=0.762, the required sample size depends on the variance of your metric. If you need 5000 samples per variant and you get 500 per day split 50/50, you get 250 per variant per day and need 20 days per variant, roughly 3 weeks. For very small effects (1-2% improvement), the required sample size can be 3-6 months at moderate traffic, which is often not practical.
