weeks.title: Recommender Systems, When the Output Depends on the User
weeks.context:
Recommender systems are how Netflix decides what to show you, how Amazon decides what to suggest, and how Spotify builds your Discover Weekly playlist. They are one of the most commercially valuable ML applications and one of the most technically interesting, the output depends not just on the item but on the specific user, creating a high-dimensional personalisation problem that standard classification and regression cannot easily solve.

The fundamental challenge is the sparsity of the user-item interaction matrix. A streaming platform with 1 million users and 100,000 titles has 100 billion possible interactions. The actual interaction data (watches, ratings, clicks) might represent 0.1% of those possibilities, 100 million observations in a 100-billion-entry matrix. Any method that requires explicit ratings for unseen user-item pairs must generalise from 0.1% of data.

Collaborative filtering works by finding similar users (or items) and using their interactions to make predictions. Matrix factorisation decomposes the sparse user-item matrix into two dense lower-rank matrices: a user embedding matrix and an item embedding matrix. Each user and each item is represented as a dense vector in a shared latent space. The predicted rating for any user-item pair is the dot product of their embeddings. This allows generalisation to unseen pairs, users and items that have never interacted but have similar embeddings will have a high predicted dot product.

Alternating Least Squares (ALS) is the standard algorithm for implicit feedback data (clicks, watches, purchases, you know what people did, not how much they liked it). SVD++ extends matrix factorisation to incorporate additional signals (the set of items a user has interacted with, regardless of rating).

The two-tower model is the dominant production architecture. Two separate neural networks, one for users, one for items, each produce a dense embedding. Training: pairs of (user, item) interactions are positive examples; random non-interacted items are negative examples. The model learns embeddings that make positive pair dot products high and negative pair dot products low. At serving time, the item embeddings are pre-computed and stored in a vector database, enabling fast approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## When the answer depends on who is asking
Every model so far gave the same answer for the same input: a flight's features map to one delay probability, regardless of who asks. **Recommender systems** break that, the prediction depends not just on the item but on the *specific user*, so "should we show this movie?" has a different answer for every person. They are how Netflix decides what to show you, Amazon what to suggest, Spotify what goes in your Discover Weekly, one of the most commercially valuable ML applications and one of the most technically interesting, because personalisation creates a high-dimensional problem that standard classification and regression cannot easily solve. This week you build a recommender and learn the ideas, collaborative filtering, embeddings, cold-start, exploration, diversity, that make personalised prediction work.

## Why recommendation is a different kind of problem
A recommender is not just a classifier with the user as an extra feature, the structure of the problem is fundamentally different, and naming why frames the week. The core object is the **user-item interaction matrix**: rows are users, columns are items, and entries are interactions (a watch, a rating, a click). Recommendation is the problem of *filling in the blanks*, predicting which of the vast number of items a user has *not* interacted with they would like. This is different from classification because there is no fixed set of labels, every user-item pair is a potential prediction, and the "right answer" is personal. It is high-dimensional (millions of users times hundreds of thousands of items) and the goal, surfacing the few items each user will love from an enormous catalogue, does not fit the predict-one-target shape of the models you have built. So recommenders need their own methods, which is what makes them a distinct and rich topic.

## The defining challenge: sparsity
The single fact that shapes all of recommendation is the **sparsity** of the interaction matrix, and the numbers are staggering. A platform with 1 million users and 100,000 titles has 100 *billion* possible user-item interactions, but the actual data (the watches, ratings, clicks that really happened) might be 0.1% of that, around 100 million observations in a 100-billion-entry matrix. So 99.9% of the matrix is *empty*, and recommendation is the task of intelligently filling that vast emptiness, predicting preferences for the overwhelming majority of pairs you have *no* direct data on, by generalising from the tiny fraction you do. Any method that needed explicit data for each user-item pair would be hopeless; the whole art is generalising from 0.1% to the other 99.9%. This sparsity is why recommendation needs clever techniques (collaborative filtering, embeddings) that find structure in the sparse data and extrapolate from it, and it is the constraint every idea this week is designed to overcome.

## Where this fits
This week closes the Model Serving phase with recommender systems, the personalisation problem where the output depends on the user, completing your range of production ML applications (serving, monitoring, A/B testing, and now recommendation). It draws on embeddings (from the deep-learning phase) and connects to the exploration/exploitation and A/B-testing ideas you have built. Today's orientation: recommendation predicts personalised preferences by filling in a hugely *sparse* user-item interaction matrix, a fundamentally different, high-dimensional problem from classification, defined by the challenge of generalising from 0.1% of the data. Tomorrow you meet the foundational technique: collaborative filtering.

items.title: Collaborative filtering
items.body:
## Collaborative filtering: people like you liked this
The foundational recommendation technique is **collaborative filtering**, and its idea is intuitive: recommend to a user based on the preferences of *similar* users (or similar items). "People who liked what you liked also liked X, so you might like X too." It comes in two complementary forms:
- **User-based:** find users similar to you (they watched/rated the same things you did), and recommend items *they* liked that you have not seen. Your taste-neighbours' favourites become your recommendations.
- **Item-based:** find items similar to ones you liked (items that tend to be liked by the same people), and recommend those. "Because you watched this, here is a similar one."
The remarkable thing is what collaborative filtering does *not* need: it requires *no* information about the items themselves (no genre, no description) or the users (no demographics), only the interaction patterns, who interacted with what. It finds taste structure purely from the matrix of interactions, which is why it is the workhorse of recommendation.

## Why "collaborative" and why it works on sparse data
The name "collaborative" captures the mechanism: users implicitly *collaborate* by their collective behaviour, your recommendations come from the patterns in everyone's interactions pooled together. This is exactly how it overcomes the sparsity problem from yesterday: even though *you* have interacted with only a tiny fraction of items, *many other users collectively* have interacted with most items, so by finding users similar to you, the system borrows their experience to predict your preferences for items you have never touched. You have not watched item X, but a hundred users with taste like yours have, and they loved it, so it recommends X to you. The structure in the sparse matrix, the fact that users cluster into taste groups and items cluster into preference groups, is what makes generalising from 0.1% possible: you do not need *your* data on an item, you need data from *people like you* on that item, which collectively exists. Collaborative filtering exploits exactly this, finding and using the latent taste structure that pervades the interaction data, which is why it works despite the matrix being almost entirely empty.

## The strengths and limits of collaborative filtering
Collaborative filtering's great strength is that it needs only interaction data and discovers preferences you could never specify by hand, it can surface that fans of one obscure thing tend to love another seemingly-unrelated thing, purely from behaviour, with no notion of *why*. This serendipity (recommending things that are not obviously similar by any content feature, but that similar people love) is a major advantage over content-based approaches and a big part of why it powers real recommenders. Its limits motivate the rest of the week. It struggles with **sparsity at the extremes** (a brand-new user or item with no interactions has no neighbours, the cold-start problem of D4), it can be **computationally heavy** at scale (finding similar users among millions is expensive, which is exactly what the embedding approach in D3 makes efficient), and it tends to recommend **popular** items (which many people interacted with), risking a lack of diversity (D6). So collaborative filtering is the powerful foundation, recommend based on collective taste structure in the interaction matrix, and the subsequent lessons address its weaknesses: embeddings make it scalable and richer, cold-start handling covers the no-data cases, and diversity/exploration counter its popularity bias. Understanding collaborative filtering, and *why* it works on sparse data, is the conceptual core of recommendation.

## Where this fits
You understand collaborative filtering: recommending from the preferences of similar users or items, using only interaction patterns (no item/user attributes), which overcomes sparsity by borrowing the collective experience of taste-similar users, with strengths (serendipity, no metadata needed) and limits (cold-start, scale, popularity bias) that the rest of the week addresses. Tomorrow you see how embeddings turn this into a scalable, modern recommender.

items.title: Embeddings for recommenders
items.body:
## Modern recommenders: embeddings
Classic collaborative filtering compares users and items directly, which is expensive at scale. The modern approach represents users and items as **embeddings**, dense vectors in a shared "taste space", learned so that a user's vector and an item's vector are *close* when the user likes the item. You met embeddings in the deep-learning phase (and in the AI-engineering RAG work); here they power recommendation:
```text
each user -> a vector (their position in "taste space")
each item -> a vector (its position in the same space)
predicted preference(user, item) = similarity(user_vector, item_vector)   (e.g. dot product)
recommend the items whose vectors are closest to the user's vector
```
The model *learns* these vectors from the interaction data, placing users and items so that observed likes correspond to nearby vectors, and then a user's recommendations are simply the items nearest their vector.

## Why embeddings are the right representation
Embeddings solve collaborative filtering's problems elegantly, which is why they dominate modern recommenders:
- **They handle sparsity by learning latent structure.** The model compresses each user and item into a low-dimensional vector that captures the *essential* taste factors (this user likes action and sci-fi; this item is action sci-fi), generalising from the sparse interactions to fill the empty matrix, this is the same latent-factor idea as matrix factorisation, the classic embedding-based recommender. A user's vector summarises their taste from their few interactions, and it then predicts their preference for *any* item via vector similarity.
- **They are efficient at scale.** Once users and items are vectors, recommendation becomes a *nearest-neighbour search* in vector space, find the items closest to the user's vector, which is exactly the fast approximate-nearest-neighbour problem you saw in RAG (the same vector-search infrastructure, HNSW and friends). So instead of comparing a user against millions of others directly, you do an efficient vector lookup, making real-time recommendation over huge catalogues feasible.
- **They blend signals naturally.** Embeddings can incorporate more than interactions, item content, user features, context, into the learned vectors (hybrid recommenders), and they slot into neural recommendation models, the current state of the art.

## The unifying idea: preference as geometry
The deep idea embeddings bring to recommendation is **turning preference into geometry**: by placing users and items in a shared vector space where proximity means affinity, you convert the messy, sparse, high-dimensional recommendation problem into a clean geometric one, recommendation is "find the items near this user." This is the same powerful move you saw with embeddings for text in RAG (meaning becomes proximity) and it is why embeddings are one of the most important ideas in modern ML: they represent complex objects (words, images, users, items) as vectors whose *distances encode relationships*, turning hard problems into tractable nearest-neighbour searches. For recommendation specifically, this geometry is what makes a system both *accurate* (the learned space captures real taste structure from sparse data) and *fast* (recommendation is vector search), and it unifies recommendation with the broader embedding-based ML you have been learning. The takeaway is that a modern recommender learns a taste-space embedding for every user and item and recommends by proximity, which scales to millions of users and items in real time and generalises gracefully across the sparse matrix, the embedding being the representation that makes personalisation tractable.

## Where this fits
You understand embedding-based recommendation: learning user and item vectors in a shared taste space where proximity means preference, which handles sparsity (latent factors), scales via fast nearest-neighbour search (the RAG vector infrastructure), and blends signals, turning recommendation into geometry. This is the modern recommender's core. Tomorrow you handle the case embeddings and collaborative filtering both struggle with: cold-start, recommending for brand-new users and items with no interaction data.

items.title: Cold-start
items.body:
## The no-data problem: cold-start
Collaborative filtering and embeddings both learn from interactions, so they fail for the entities that *have no interactions yet*: a **brand-new user** who has done nothing, and a **brand-new item** nobody has touched. This is the **cold-start problem**, and it is a real, constant challenge because new users and items arrive continuously, a streaming service signs up users every minute and adds titles every week, and you must recommend *something* good to them despite having zero collaborative data. With no interactions, there are no taste-neighbours to borrow from and no learned embedding, so the methods that power your recommender simply have nothing to work with for these entities.

## How to recommend with no interaction data
Cold-start is solved by falling back on information *other than* interactions, and the techniques map to the two cold cases:
- **New user cold-start:** since you have no behaviour, use whatever you *do* know, any signup information (stated preferences, demographics), the context (device, location, time), or simply recommend **popular** items (the broadly-liked safe bets) until the user interacts enough to personalise. You can also *actively* learn fast, ask a new user to pick a few favourites or rate a handful of items during onboarding (the "choose 3 shows you like" flow), bootstrapping a taste signal immediately.
- **New item cold-start:** since nobody has interacted with it, use the item's **content** (genre, description, attributes, creator) to place it near similar items that *do* have interactions, this is **content-based** recommendation, and it is exactly why hybrid systems matter. A new sci-fi film with no watches can still be recommended to sci-fi fans because its *content* matches items they liked.
The common thread is **substitute information for missing interactions**: content features for new items, profile/context/popularity for new users, and active solicitation to gather signal fast.

## Why hybrid systems are the real answer
The deep lesson of cold-start is that **no single recommendation approach is sufficient, and real systems are hybrids** that combine collaborative filtering (powerful when interaction data exists) with content-based methods (which work from the start, using item/user attributes). This is the recommendation version of the recurring "match the method to the situation" theme: collaborative filtering shines once there is interaction data but cannot start cold, while content-based recommendation works immediately from attributes but misses the serendipitous, behaviour-driven discoveries collaborative filtering excels at, so combining them gives you both, content-based to cover cold-start and collaborative to deliver rich personalisation as data accumulates. A new user gets popularity-and-onboarding-based recommendations that quickly become collaborative as they interact; a new item gets content-based exposure that becomes collaborative once it gathers interactions. This graceful transition from content-based (cold) to collaborative (warm) as data accumulates is how production recommenders handle the constant arrival of new users and items, and it is why "which technique?" is the wrong question, the answer is a hybrid that uses each where it is strong. Understanding cold-start, and that hybrids solve it, is understanding why real recommenders are never a single algorithm but a combination engineered to handle the full lifecycle from no-data to rich-data.

## Where this fits
You understand the cold-start problem, no interaction data for new users and items, and its solutions: substitute other information (content features for new items, profile/context/popularity and active onboarding for new users), unified in *hybrid* systems that combine content-based (works cold) with collaborative (rich when warm). Tomorrow you handle a subtle dynamic challenge: balancing exploration and exploitation in what you recommend.

items.title: Exploration vs exploitation
items.body:
## The recommender's dilemma: exploit or explore
A recommender that only ever recommends what it is *most confident* you will like has a hidden flaw: it never learns about your other tastes, and it traps you in a narrow loop. This is the **exploration vs exploitation** trade-off, one of the most important dynamics in recommendation:
- **Exploitation:** recommend the items the model is confident the user will like (based on what it has learned), maximising immediate satisfaction.
- **Exploration:** sometimes recommend items the model is *uncertain* about, to *learn* more about the user's preferences (and to gather data on lesser-known items), at the cost of some immediate hit-rate.
A recommender must do both: pure exploitation gives reliable but stale, narrowing recommendations; pure exploration gives random, unsatisfying ones; the art is balancing them.

## Why exploration is necessary, not wasteful
It is tempting to think exploration is just serving worse recommendations, but it is essential for the system's long-term quality, and understanding why is the insight. Three reasons exploitation alone fails: First, the model only *knows* what it has seen the user interact with, so without exploration it can never discover that you would *love* a genre you have never been shown, it keeps recommending more of the same and never learns your broader taste, a self-reinforcing filter bubble. Second, **new items need exposure to gather data** (the cold-start connection): if the recommender only exploits known-popular items, new items never get shown, never accumulate interactions, and never get a chance, so exploration is how the catalogue beyond the popular head gets discovered. Third, **users and tastes change**, and a purely exploitative model, anchored to past behaviour, never notices, where exploration keeps probing and adapting. So exploration is an *investment*: you give up a little immediate satisfaction now to learn information that makes *future* recommendations better, the same way an organisation invests in R&D. A recommender that never explores slowly degrades into a narrow, stale echo of the user's past, even as it looks "accurate" by exploiting known preferences, which connects to the offline-online gap from W19 (a model that exploits past clicks scores well offline but may engage users less than one that explores).

## Balancing the trade: bandits and beyond
The exploration-exploitation trade-off is formalised by **multi-armed bandit** algorithms, which provide principled ways to balance trying uncertain options against exploiting known-good ones, and you do not need the full theory to grasp the approaches: **epsilon-greedy** (mostly exploit, but a small fraction of the time pick something to explore), **upper-confidence-bound** (favour items that are either known-good *or* highly uncertain, optimistic about the unknown), and **Thompson sampling** (sample from your uncertainty about each option's value, naturally exploring uncertain ones), the Bayesian flavour connecting to W19's Bayesian thinking. The practical takeaway is that a good recommender *deliberately* injects exploration, a controlled fraction of "let's try something to learn", rather than purely exploiting, and tunes how much based on the cost of a worse recommendation versus the value of learning. This is the same explore-to-learn-vs-exploit-to-earn trade that appears across decision-making under uncertainty, and recognising it in recommendation explains a lot of real-system behaviour (why Spotify sometimes serves you something unexpected, it is exploring). The deeper point is that a recommender is not a static predictor but an *interactive learner* that shapes the very data it learns from (it only sees interactions on what it recommends), so it must explore to avoid starving itself of the information it needs to improve, a feedback loop no static model has. Balancing exploration and exploitation is what keeps a recommender learning, fresh, and able to surface the catalogue beyond the obvious.

## Where this fits
You understand exploration vs exploitation: balancing recommending known-good items (exploit) against uncertain ones to learn (explore), essential because the recommender shapes its own training data and must explore to discover broader tastes, expose new items, and adapt, formalised by bandit algorithms (epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling). Tomorrow you handle a related quality dimension: diversity and serendipity, beyond raw accuracy.

items.title: Diversity and serendipity
items.body:
## Beyond accuracy: diversity and serendipity
A recommender optimised purely for *accuracy* (predict what the user will click) can produce a subtly bad experience: a list of items that are all *correct* but all *the same*, ten action movies, or ten variations of what you already watched, technically accurate, practically boring and unhelpful. Two qualities beyond accuracy fix this:
- **Diversity:** the recommendations should *vary*, span different genres, styles, and types, rather than being ten near-identical items. A diverse list is more useful and more interesting, and more likely to contain something the user is in the mood for right now.
- **Serendipity:** recommendations should sometimes be *pleasantly surprising*, items the user would not have found themselves and would not expect, but ends up loving. Serendipity is the delight of discovery, and it is much of what makes a recommender feel magical rather than obvious.
Optimising accuracy alone delivers neither, which is why good recommenders explicitly value diversity and serendipity, not just hit-rate.

## Why accuracy alone is the wrong objective
The key insight is that **the metric you optimise (accuracy) is not the same as the experience you want (a satisfying, engaging recommendation)**, exactly the metric-outcome gap from the A/B-testing week, here within recommendation. A recommender that maximises predicted-click accuracy tends to recommend the *obvious* and the *similar*: items so close to what the user already engaged with that the prediction is safe, which is accurate but redundant (you would have found those anyway, so the recommender added little value) and narrowing (it keeps showing more of the same, the filter-bubble effect). Real value often comes from the *non-obvious* good recommendation, the diverse option that matches your current mood, the serendipitous discovery you would never have found, and these score *lower* on naive accuracy (they are less predictable) while delivering *higher* real satisfaction and engagement. This is why, just as in W19, the offline-accurate model can be the online-worse model: the most "accurate" recommendations (predicting your obvious next click) may engage you *less* than a diverse, serendipitous set. So diversity and serendipity are not soft niceties; they are corrections to accuracy's blind spot, ensuring the recommender delivers *useful* and *delightful* recommendations rather than merely *predictable* ones.

## Balancing the objectives, and the human stakes
In practice you *balance* accuracy with diversity and serendipity, you do not abandon accuracy (irrelevant recommendations are bad too), but you deliberately trade a little predicted-accuracy for variety and surprise, tuning the mix to maximise *real* engagement and satisfaction (measured, as W19 taught, by online outcomes, not offline accuracy). Techniques include re-ranking a candidate list to spread genres, penalising too-similar items, and injecting exploratory or serendipitous picks (connecting to D5's exploration, exploration *produces* serendipity). There is also a genuine **human dimension** worth naming: recommenders that optimise narrow accuracy can create *filter bubbles* (showing people only more of what they already engage with, narrowing their world) and amplify popularity (the rich get richer, niche content starves), which has real effects on what people discover, what creators get seen, and even on society (news and information recommenders shaping what people are exposed to). So building in diversity is not only about engagement metrics, it is also a responsibility, countering the narrowing and homogenising tendencies that pure accuracy optimisation produces. This connects forward to the Responsible ML phase (fairness, the societal impact of ML systems): a recommender is one of the most influential ML systems in people's daily lives, and designing it to be diverse and serendipitous, not just accurate, is both better product and more responsible engineering. The mature recommender optimises for satisfying discovery, balancing accuracy, diversity, and serendipity, not for the hollow accuracy of predicting the obvious.

## Where this fits
You understand diversity and serendipity: that pure accuracy yields redundant, narrowing, obvious recommendations, so good recommenders balance accuracy with variety and pleasant surprise to deliver real satisfaction (the metric-outcome gap again), with a genuine responsibility dimension (filter bubbles, popularity amplification) that connects to responsible ML. items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a recommender system
You assemble the week into a working recommender on a real interaction dataset (movie ratings, music, products), demonstrating the personalisation pipeline end to end:
- **collaborative filtering or embeddings** as the core, learning user/item taste structure from the sparse interaction matrix and recommending by similarity.
- **cold-start handling** (a content-based or popularity fallback for new users/items), making it a *hybrid*.
- attention to **diversity and exploration**, not just raw accuracy, so the recommendations are varied and the system can learn.
- evaluation that goes beyond accuracy (diversity, coverage) and an awareness that the real verdict would come from an online test.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Recommender system: collaborative filtering + embeddings, hybrid cold-start, diversity"
git push
```

## The deliverable shows personalisation and its trade-offs
What makes this project strong is demonstrating that you understand recommendation as more than "predict ratings accurately", that you grasp its real trade-offs. The strongest artifact shows personalised recommendations that clearly differ per user (the defining property), handles a new user/item gracefully (cold-start), and *consciously balances* accuracy against diversity and exploration, with a write-up explaining the choices: "I used embedding-based collaborative filtering for scalable personalisation, a content-based fallback for cold-start, and re-ranked for diversity because pure accuracy gave repetitive lists." Discussing *why* offline accuracy is not the whole story for recommenders (the W19 connection, the real metric is engagement, measurable only online) and the diversity/responsibility dimension demonstrates the mature understanding that distinguishes someone who can build a recommender from someone who just ran a matrix-factorisation library. The personalisation working, plus the awareness of sparsity, cold-start, exploration, and diversity trade-offs, is the deliverable.

## What recommenders, and the Model Serving phase, established
Step back across the week and the phase. This week you learned personalisation, where the output depends on the user, with its own structure (the sparse interaction matrix), techniques (collaborative filtering, embeddings as taste-geometry), and uniquely dynamic challenges (cold-start, exploration-exploitation, diversity, the recommender shaping its own data). The deep ideas, generalising from sparse data, embeddings turning preference into geometry, balancing exploit-vs-explore, and optimising for real satisfaction over naive accuracy, are among the richest in applied ML. And this completes the **Model Serving phase**: you can now take models into production fully, serve them reliably (W17), monitor them for silent drift (W18), A/B test them for real-world value (W19), and build the personalised, interactive systems (W20) that are among ML's most valuable applications. The throughline of the phase is that **a model in production is a living system**, served, watched, tested, and, for recommenders, continuously learning from its own influence, not a static artifact, and you now have the engineering to run that living system.

## Where this fits
You shipped a recommender that personalises from sparse data while balancing cold-start, exploration, and diversity, completing the Model Serving phase: serve, monitor, A/B test, and personalise, the full lifecycle of models in production. Next comes the **MLOps & Monitoring phase** (W21-23), which unifies and automates everything you have built, treating ML training itself as software engineering (pipelines, CI/CD for models), scaling to distributed training and big data, and confronting the responsibilities of ML, fairness, privacy, and explainability, before the final capstone.

There is no guaranteed interpretation for latent factors, they are not directly interpretable the way logistic regression coefficients are. Empirically, some factors correlate with interpretable concepts: one factor might separate action movies from dramas, another might separate blockbusters from art house films. But the model does not guarantee interpretable factors, it finds the mathematical decomposition that best explains the observed ratings, whatever that decomposition captures.

weeks.title: MLOps Pipelines, Training as Software Engineering
weeks.context:
MLOps is the practice of applying software engineering disciplines to machine learning workflows: version control, testing, CI/CD, automated deployment, and monitoring. The reason ML needs its own discipline is that training a model is not a deterministic function, the same code with different data produces different models. The same model with different data distributions produces different predictions. MLOps adds structure to manage this non-determinism while maintaining velocity.

CI/CD for ML differs from web application CI/CD in important ways. The CI for a web app runs unit tests that pass or fail deterministically. The CI for an ML pipeline runs model training that produces a model with a quality metric. "Did the tests pass?" is replaced by "Did the model achieve at least 0.72 ROC AUC on the validation set?" The deployment decision depends on model quality, not just test passage.

Pipeline triggers determine when retraining happens. Code changes: a developer updates the model architecture or the feature engineering code, the pipeline runs automatically. Data changes: a data quality check detects that the new training batch has a different distribution from the reference, the pipeline runs with an alert. Scheduled: the pipeline runs weekly regardless, incorporating new data to maintain model freshness. Manual: a data scientist triggers a training run with specific hyperparameters for an experiment.

Testing ML code is different from testing model quality. Test the code: unit tests for feature engineering functions (does the transform produce the expected columns with the expected types?), data validation (does the training batch meet the expected schema?), and model integration (does the trained model accept the expected input shape and produce output in the expected range?). Test the model: performance above a threshold on the validation set, performance not worse than the previous production model on a comparison set.

weeks.title: Distributed Training and Big Data, When One Machine Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
Single-machine training has a ceiling. When your dataset is larger than RAM, or when your model requires more VRAM than one GPU, or when you want to parallelize training across many machines to save time, you need distributed computing. The transition from single-machine to distributed training is one of the most important scaling decisions an ML engineer makes.

The symptoms that indicate you need distributed: training data does not fit in RAM (Pandas cannot load it), a single GPU epoch takes more than a day, model weights require more VRAM than any available single GPU, or you need to reduce a 2-week training run to 2 days to stay competitive. Each symptom has a different solution, and conflating them is a common mistake.

Apache Spark for preprocessing handles the first case. Spark distributes data processing across a cluster of machines, enabling processing of datasets far larger than any single machine's RAM. The DataFrame API is similar to Pandas but operates lazily, computations are not executed until you collect or write results. This enables Spark to optimise the execution plan before running. Spark is excellent for ETL, feature engineering at scale, and batch inference. It is not a training framework.

Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) handles training a single model on multiple GPUs. Each GPU maintains a full copy of the model and processes a different batch of data. Gradients are synchronised across GPUs after each backward pass. This effectively multiplies your batch size by the number of GPUs. DDP achieves near-linear scaling (2 GPUs produces nearly 2x throughput) because gradient synchronisation overhead is small relative to computation.

Model parallelism handles the case where the model itself does not fit on a single GPU. Different layers are placed on different GPUs. A batch passes through GPU 0 (layers 1-10), then GPU 1 (layers 11-20), then GPU 2 (layers 21-30). This is pipeline parallelism. Tensor parallelism splits individual layers across GPUs. Both are more complex to implement and have lower efficiency than DDP due to communication overhead.

items.body: Your Pandas pipeline loads a 120GB CSV into memory, which exceeds your 64GB RAM. You switch to Spark. What does Spark do differently that allows it to handle this data? Spark processes data in partitions. The 120GB CSV is split into hundreds of partitions, each fitting in memory. Spark processes partitions sequentially or in parallel across worker nodes, never loading the full dataset at once. Additionally, Spark is lazy, computations are not executed until an action (collect, write) is called. This allows Spark to optimise the execution plan, push down filters (reducing data read from disk), and fuse operations to minimise passes over the data.

weeks.title: Responsible ML, Fairness, Privacy, Explainability
weeks.context:
Machine learning systems can harm people. Not through dramatic AI takeover scenarios, but through mundane mechanisms: a hiring algorithm that systematically disadvantages one demographic group, a lending model that charges higher rates to historically redlined communities, a medical diagnosis model that performs worse on underrepresented groups. These harms are not hypothetical, they have occurred in deployed systems. Responsible ML is the set of practices that reduce the likelihood and severity of these harms.

Fairness in ML is not a single concept, it is a family of definitions that are mathematically incompatible with each other in most non-trivial cases. Demographic parity requires equal positive prediction rates across groups. Equalised odds requires equal true positive and false positive rates across groups. Calibration requires that predicted probabilities match actual outcome rates for each group. A model cannot satisfy all three simultaneously when base rates differ between groups. This is the fundamental fairness impossibility theorem, and it forces you to make explicit value judgments about which definition fits your use case.

Measuring bias starts with disaggregated metrics: compute accuracy, precision, recall, and false positive rate separately for each protected group in your dataset. If your flight delay model has 78% accuracy for domestic flights but 61% accuracy for international flights, that is a performance disparity that requires investigation regardless of whether the groups are legally protected. Disaggregated evaluation is the baseline practice that every ML project should perform.

Mitigation falls into three categories: pre-processing (reweight or resample training data to reduce representation imbalances), in-processing (add fairness constraints to the training objective), and post-processing (adjust prediction thresholds separately for each group to equalise a chosen metric). Each approach has tradeoffs in complexity, accuracy cost, and which fairness definition it optimises.

Differential privacy adds mathematical guarantees about individual privacy in model training. An epsilon-differentially private model provides a formal bound on how much any individual's data can affect the model's outputs, limiting the information that can be extracted about training set members.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You compute demographic parity for your loan model across income quintiles. The lowest income quintile is approved at a 15% rate while the highest income quintile is approved at a 62% rate. Is this a fairness problem? The answer requires context. If the base rate of loan repayment (the ground truth) differs across income quintiles in the same proportion, then a model with demographic disparity in approvals may actually be calibrated, it is reflecting the true difference in repayment probability. If the model's approval rate differs more than the base rate difference, it is adding disparity beyond what the underlying data supports. Always compare approval rate disparity to ground truth base rate disparity. Disparity greater than the base rate difference is evidence of algorithmic unfairness.

weeks.title: Capstone, A Full ML System, Shipped
weeks.context:
The capstone is where everything comes together: a full ML system, designed, built, monitored, and shipped. Not just a model. A system, with a data pipeline, a training pipeline, a serving endpoint, monitoring, reproducibility, and documentation. The combination of all these pieces, working together reliably, is what ML engineering produces.

The scoping decision is the hardest part. The instinct is to build something impressive, distributed training, multimodal inputs, real-time monitoring. The right instinct is to build something that works end-to-end with all the engineering quality that implies. A clean, well-monitored, reproducible logistic regression pipeline is a stronger capstone than a messy deep learning system with no monitoring and non-reproducible training.

End-to-end thinking means designing the data pipeline, model, serving, and monitoring as one integrated system before writing any code. Where does the data come from? How does it get preprocessed? Where are the preprocessing artifacts stored so inference uses the same transformations as training? How does the serving endpoint load the model? What metrics does the monitoring collect? What triggers a retraining run? Writing a one-page system design before writing code is the difference between building a system and building a collection of scripts.

The retrospective is as important as the technical work. What decisions turned out to be wrong? What would you architect differently? What took five times longer than expected and why? What would be the first thing to improve in v2? An honest retrospective shows engineering maturity. It demonstrates that you understand the tradeoffs you made, not just the system you built.

Ship something, monitor it, and tell the story. The deliverables: a live endpoint with a public URL, a SYSTEM-DESIGN.md that describes the architecture, an eval report with honest metrics, a monitoring dashboard showing recent predictions, and a retrospective document. The story: a 3-minute demo video and a write-up that explains what problem you solved and why the engineering decisions you made were the right ones.

concept_check.q: You have designed your capstone system. A reviewer asks: "What happens if the prediction endpoint goes down?" Walk through your failure handling. Your answer should cover: (1) health checks, how does?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You have trained your capstone model and the test ROC AUC is 0.77. You present the results. A reviewer asks: "How do you know this model is better than just always predicting the majority class?" Answ?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Your capstone uses XGBoost. A colleague asks why not a neural network. What is your answer? Neural networks require more data, more compute, and more tuning to outperform XGBoost on tabular data. For?

items.title: Finish and ship the week's project
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Build and ship ONE complete ML system to a public URL. It must include: real data pipeline (versioned, scheduled), trained model (with eval suite, hyperparameter sweep, experiment tracking), production serving (containerised, with batching and monitoring), CI/CD (tests + auto-deploy on merge), a small frontend or API that demonstrates value, monitoring dashboard, model card, fairness analysis if relevant. Pick a problem you actually care about, your own data, your own pain. Share the launch on Twitter, HN, your blog, your audience.

Ship checklist:
 - It runs from a clean clone / fresh open, no "works on my machine" steps missing.
 - Commit it to your repo with a short README saying what it does and how to run it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have designed your capstone system. A reviewer asks: "What happens if the prediction endpoint goes down?" Walk through your failure handling. Your answer should cover: (1) health checks, how does the platform know the endpoint is down?, (2) automatic restart, does your hosting platform restart failed containers?, (3) graceful degradation, if the model endpoint is unavailable, does the application fall back to a simple rule-based prediction or does it return an error?, (4) alerting, how do you know the endpoint went down? Walk through all four. A system without failure handling is not production-ready.
